text: Heart rate variability (HRV) biofeedback for emotion regulation typically relies on visual or vibrotactile pacing, yet the suitability of thermal stimulation as a pacing channel for resonance-frequency breathing remains untested. This project investigates whether slow thermal cycles can serve as a viable and distinctively valuable pacing cue, using a two-stage design that avoids over-investing in complex hardware before establishing basic feasibility. In Stage 1, a lab prototype delivers matched thermal and vibrotactile cues at 0.1 Hz on the same body site, allowing direct comparison of perceptual detectability, phase-tracking accuracy, cognitive load, comfort, and immediate autonomic and affective responses. Only if thermal pacing proves at least as entrainable as vibration and equal or superior in comfort and acceptability does Stage 2 proceed to evaluate a minimal wearable implementing fixed-pace thermal cycles, with optional sparse feedback, against vibrotactile and visual biofeedback for training transfer and everyday usability. Primary outcomes include the ability to reproduce elevated HRV without cues and adherence during at-home use. By testing psychophysical assumptions directly rather than embedding them in a larger system, the work either grounds a thermal HRV-training approach or clarifies that simpler haptic cues offer the most efficient route to non-invasive emotion-regulation wearables.

text: This proposal introduces an ultra-brief, low-burden intervention for supporting emotion regulation during cognitively demanding tasks, delivered through existing smartwatches or phones. Rather than requiring guided sessions or continuous respiration sensing, the system provides rare, brief vibration or audio cues a few times per hour; upon each cue, users simply make their next one or two exhalations slightly longer and softer while continuing their activity. The approach leverages the established acute mechanism by which exhale-biased breathing enhances vagal activity and reduces arousal, but applies it in a novel operating regime of very low-dose micro-bouts delivered under load rather than in dedicated breathing blocks. The central problem addressed is poor adherence to breathing exercises during busy periods, when structured sessions feel too time- and attention-intensive. A lab study will randomly assign participants performing prolonged cognitive tasks to micro-exhale prompts, explicit two-minute breathing breaks, or a control condition, measuring subjective stress, tension, perceived disruption, and exploratory physiological markers such as HF-HRV and skin conductance. The key aim is to determine whether micro-prompts reduce subjective stress with substantially lower disruption than standard breathing breaks, and whether they yield any detectable physiological buffering. If even modest benefits emerge at low burden, the findings would validate ultra-low-cost body-focused cues as a practical everyday regulation tool and guide their design in consumer platforms.

label: baseline
text: This proposal investigates whether breathing, and consequently high-frequency heart rate variability (HF-HRV), can be implicitly biased by low-effort, self-locked auditory cues delivered during everyday-like tasks, in contrast to conventional guided breathing that demands sustained attention. The central hypothesis is that consistently tagging each exhalation with a brief, pleasant sound allows the brain to form an implicit phase prediction that gradually lengthens exhalation or overall cycle duration, shifting the exhale-to-inhale ratio and nudging HF-HRV upward. Using a minimal laboratory setup comprising a non-invasive respiration sensor, headphones, and standard HRV recording, we will compare three timing conditions matched for sound content and loudness: self-locked cues time-locked to the participant's own breathing, yoked cues driven by another person's prerecorded breathing, and fixed-tempo cues at a constant rate. A first stage will establish the existence and magnitude of any effect under favorable conditions of low cognitive load and salient, mildly rewarding cues, while a second stage will titrate toward realistic ambient use by increasing task demand and reducing cue salience to identify where entrainment breaks down. Awareness and effort probes will dissociate explicit pacing from genuinely implicit modulation. The findings will determine whether robust ambient entrainment can support attention-sparse emotion regulation in smart environments or whether effective interventions inherently require conscious cooperation.

text: This proposal develops a non-invasive, lab-ready paradigm that pairs breathing with gentle tactile cues and occasionally omits or shifts their timing within a safe context, with an optional wearable adjunct for between-session practice. The central aim is to measure and gently reshape an anxiety-relevant belief, namely the estimated contingency between minor bodily-context oddness and threat. We combine behavioral probes, physiological markers time-locked to cue omissions and jitter, and computational learning models to estimate how quickly individuals down-weight threat likelihood when odd events repeatedly carry no adverse consequence. By providing many benign violations in a bodily rhythm context, the paradigm is expected to reduce the inferred predictive value of such oddness for threat and diminish conditioned autonomic responses, particularly in individuals with elevated anxiety. Breath-locked tactile cues occupy an intermediate level of embodiment between abstract audiovisual expectancy-violation tasks and aversive respiratory-load challenges, enabling frequent, low-distress sessions and clean estimation of prediction errors and contingency updating in insula and anterior cingulate cortex. Rather than a standalone therapy, this paradigm functions as a mechanistic assay, gentle adjunct, and design informant whose parameters can calibrate scalable, app-based or interoceptive exposure protocols. Its contribution is intentionally narrow, bridging aversive interoceptive tasks and purely cognitive safe-surprise training without overclaiming clinical impact.

text: Fear of bodily sensations is central to panic and anxiety, yet the mechanisms governing extinction of interoceptive threat remain poorly understood, particularly the possibility that internal physiological states act as contextual cues. This proposal investigates whether cardiac phase functions as a hidden internal context that gates the retrieval of extinction memories for interoceptive threat. Using a non-invasive, lab-ready paradigm, participants will first acquire a conditioned fear response by pairing a neutral cue with an aversive interoceptive event, such as CO₂-induced air hunger. During a subsequent extinction phase, cue onset will be time-locked via real-time electrocardiogram triggering to either the systolic or diastolic window, and participants will later be tested in either the same or a different cardiac phase, yielding a 2×2 design that contrasts context-congruent and context-incongruent retrieval. We predict that extinction retention, indexed by lower harm expectancy and reduced skin conductance and heart-rate responses, will be stronger when the test phase matches the extinction phase, with careful control for heart-rate distributions and phase-locking accuracy to disentangle phase from general arousal. Robust phase effects would identify internal context shifts as a contributor to relapse and motivate applied strategies to broaden internal context during exposure, whereas null effects would provide an informative boundary condition redirecting effort toward conventional exposure optimizations.

text: This proposal describes a non-invasive, laboratory-based experiment to test whether olfactory input delivered before waking can reliably modulate the cortisol awakening response (CAR), a time-locked and stress-relevant event of the HPA axis. Using a counterbalanced within-subject design, each participant will complete three overnight conditions: a sham night with no odor, a night with a strong constant odor delivered continuously over the final thirty minutes of sleep, and an exploratory night with the same odor ramped gradually to peak intensity across that window. Polysomnography will characterize sleep stages and micro-arousals in the pre-wake window, and CAR will be assessed through serial saliva sampling after awakening, with heart rate variability and subjective reports as secondary measures. The primary analysis estimates the within-subject difference in CAR magnitude between strong-odor and sham nights, adjusted for circadian phase, prior sleep, and other covariates, with success defined as a consistent shift clearly exceeding typical day-to-day noise. A secondary, exploratory analysis compares constant versus ramped delivery to assess whether temporal profile influences CAR beyond total exposure and arousal. By providing a clean effect-size estimate under best-case conditions, the study will determine whether pre-wake olfactory stimulation warrants further mechanistic study or should be deprioritized as an emotion-regulation strategy.

text: Just-in-time adaptive interventions for rumination and stress assume that delivering brief cognitive prompts during elevated negative affect outperforms generic scheduling, yet it remains unknown whether timing matters at a finer scale within a single episode. This proposal tests whether moments exist inside a self-experienced rumination or stress episode when a brief reappraisal cue is substantially more effective than at other moments in the same episode, a phenomenon we frame as a within-episode appraisal-cost gradient. We will build a minimal ecological momentary assessment scaffold delivered through a smartphone app that lets non-clinical participants flag episode onset with a single tap, samples brief self-reports of anxiety, negative-thought intensity, and perceived controllability at fixed offsets, and randomizes whether a standardized one-to-two sentence reappraisal prompt is delivered early, late, or not at all. Analyzing within-person trajectories across these conditions, we will determine both whether micro-reappraisal alters everyday episode trajectories and whether early prompts truncate episodes or reduce peak anxiety more than late prompts. Crucially, this design is decoupled from sensor-based state estimation, answering the foundational question using self-marked episodes and self-report alone. If no robust timing gradient emerges, the field learns that pursuing fine-grained, state-aware timing offers limited return, redirecting effort toward content, engagement, and dosage; if a gradient is found, it establishes a mechanistic target for future sensing and modeling. Either outcome resolves a specific structural uncertainty for non-invasive everyday emotion-regulation interventions.

text: Slow, exhale-weighted breathing at approximately 0.1 Hz can enhance baroreflex resonance and vagal activity, yet everyday adherence to such pacing remains difficult, and it is unclear whether adding vibrotactile cues to common smartphone tools meaningfully improves outcomes. This project develops a minimal breathing aid running on commodity hardware—smartphone, earbuds, and phone or wrist vibration—and tests whether brief two-to-five-minute breathing breaks with audio-plus-vibration guidance outperform audio-only guidance for non-clinical adults under everyday stress. Using a within-subject laboratory design, we compare audio-only, coherent multisensory, and deliberately misaligned multisensory conditions, all cueing the same breathing target, to assess adherence, subjective comfort, and short-term heart rate variability. A central hypothesis is that any autonomic benefit is mediated by improved adherence and reduced perceived effort rather than by vibration acting directly on the heart, and that cross-modal cue coherence functions as a usability lever that shapes how well people breathe. A subsequent field phase examines whether coherent audio-plus-vibration guidance sustains adherence and perceived usefulness during self-initiated breaks across several days. By treating autonomic outcomes as behaviorally and experientially mediated, the study aims to deliver mechanistically transparent, actionable guidance for designing non-invasive, everyday emotion-regulation tools based on slow breathing and simple multisensory support.

label: baseline
text: Slow-breathing and heart rate variability biofeedback protocols reliably improve autonomic function using relatively coarse control of breathing rate and regularity, yet it remains unclear whether precisely timing additional stimulation to cardiac or respiratory phases offers any meaningful benefit beyond enforcing slow, regular breathing. This proposal develops a laboratory framework using only wearable-compatible actuators—paced breathing guidance combined with mild haptic or auricular cues—to quantify the maximum plausible marginal gain that precise timing adds over standard slow breathing for autonomic stabilization. Participants perform guided breathing near 0.1 Hz while identical doses of stimulation are delivered under four timing schemes: breath-phase-locked, cardio-respiratory-aligned, cardiac-phase-locked, and a timing-agnostic random control, with continuous ECG and respiration used to label cardiac and respiratory phase. Stability is defined conservatively through baroreflex-respiratory mechanics, emphasizing respiratory sinus arrhythmia amplitude and coherence, 0.1 Hz baroreflex gain, and reduced non-respiratory heart-rate fluctuations, with pre-specified small effect-size thresholds distinguishing negligible, modest, and substantial timing effects. Because all actuators are realizable in consumer wrist or ear devices, the results yield a clear decision rule: if timing provides negligible benefit, future tools should prioritize adherence, usability, and practice dose, whereas consistent small gains would justify implementing only the simplest effective timing scheme. This project thus offers a mechanistically grounded, well-powered test of whether phase timing is worth exploiting in breathing-based emotion regulation technologies for the general population.

text: Membrane repair deficits contribute substantially to the progressive pathology of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, yet the therapeutic potential of individual repair effectors remains poorly defined. This project quantitatively maps the relationship between expression of Synaptotagmin-7 (Syt7), a calcium sensor required for lysosomal exocytosis and plasma membrane resealing, and both functional benefit and safety liabilities in dystrophic (mdx) muscle. Adopting an explicitly agnostic hypothesis, we will use AAV-mediated delivery of wild-type Syt7 driven by muscle-specific promoters of graded strength to generate a dose-response series, and assess acute resealing kinetics, calcium influx, chronic necrosis, fibrosis, inflammation, and muscle function, alongside markers of lysosomal stress and immune activation. This dose-finding phase aims to identify an expression window in which Syt7 improves repair without provoking lysosomal or immune pathology, or to establish rigorously that no such window exists. In a second phase, the optimal Syt7 condition will be benchmarked head-to-head against established repair effectors MG53 and STX4 to compare efficacy, safety profiles, and potential complementarity at comparable vector burdens. By treating carefully characterized negative and toxicity outcomes as equally valuable to positive findings, the study will clarify whether Syt7 is a rate-limiting, exploitable compensatory node and inform the rational design of future combination gene therapies for DMD.

text: Duchenne muscular dystrophy arises from loss of dystrophin, and upregulating the paralogous protein utrophin is a promising mutation-independent therapeutic strategy. Current approaches based on CRISPR activation require sustained expression of a dCas9-based transgene from adeno-associated virus (AAV) episomes, raising concerns about long-term immune surveillance, promoter silencing, and durability of expression in humans. This proposal develops a systemic AAV gene therapy that installs a minimal set of permanent edits at the endogenous utrophin locus to de-repress its expression, thereby encoding a utrophin-high state directly in the genome rather than the episome. Using a muscle-tropic capsid and transiently expressed compact Cas9, a multiplexed guide RNA cassette will excise a validated inhibitory 3′ untranslated region cluster via non-homologous end joining, with an optional additional deletion of a cis-repressor element if greater upregulation is required. We hypothesize that this de-repression program will produce a stable increase in utrophin, restore assembly of the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex, and improve sarcolemmal integrity across skeletal muscle without ongoing vector expression. The work will refine the minimal edit set in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived myotubes, quantify editing efficiency, utrophin fold-change, functional rescue, off-target activity, and immune responses in dystrophic mice, and directly compare outcomes with CRISPR activation. A quantitative model linking editing coverage and effect size to functional benefit will guide translation toward larger-animal validation, testing whether permanent genomic de-repression is a compelling alternative or complement to sustained CRISPR activation for Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

text: Fibro-adipogenic progenitors (FAPs) drive the chronic fibrosis that undermines muscle function and therapeutic response in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), yet current antifibrotic strategies act broadly and risk impairing normal repair. We propose to use in vivo CRISPR interference and activation as a discovery instrument to define a minimal, FAP-intrinsic regulatory module controlling the chronic VCAM1+ pro-fibrotic state, and then to implement that module as a compact, non-ablative gene therapy. In the first stage, we will integrate mouse and human single-cell transcriptomic and chromatin data to shortlist conserved regulators enriched in VCAM1+ FAPs across disease stages, then deliver a focused AAV-based CRISPRi/a library under a FAP-biased promoter to identify the smallest set of regulators whose partial modulation reduces fibrogenic bias while preserving core FAP identity and acute repair capacity. We will further test whether compact effectors such as tuned microRNA or short-hairpin cassettes and dominant-negative transcription factor fragments can recapitulate this state shift. In the second stage, the validated module will be engineered into a standard AAV cassette and benchmarked against broad antifibrotic approaches for fibrosis reduction, vascular integrity, regeneration quality, and safety. This work introduces state-space compression of stromal control networks as a route to precise, durable antifibrotic gene therapy for DMD.

text: Mast cells can acquire innate memory states—training or tolerance—following exposure to microbial and alarmin signals, yet how systemic stress hormones reshape these established programs in a tissue-relevant setting remains unknown. This project asks how corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) modulates LPS- and IL-33-induced training and tolerance in primary skin mast cells, rather than treating CRH as an independent trainer. We first calibrate a minimal priming–rest–recall assay to reproduce known LPS/IL-33 training signatures, quantifying early histamine and tryptase release separately alongside IL-6 and TNF transcription, receptor expression, and locus-specific chromatin marks at Il6 and Tnf. We then introduce CRH through co-priming and sequential priming schemes to determine whether it amplifies, dampens, or skews these memory phenotypes, and whether such effects persist across rest intervals or reflect only acute, receptor-dependent signaling. Conditions showing clear, history-dependent CRH modulation are escalated to focused transcriptional and chromatin profiling to test whether CRH modifies the chromatin-encoded memory state, followed by in vivo validation in mouse skin using local priming and microdialysis. By benchmarking CRH effects against internal training controls, the project yields interpretable results even when CRH effects are modest, addressing the underexplored question of how stress hormones overlay onto innate immune memory.

text: Understanding how gene expression evolves within individual cells over time remains a central challenge in single-cell biology, as most transcriptomic methods destroy the cell at a single moment, forcing temporal dynamics to be inferred indirectly through pseudotime ordering or population-level metabolic labeling. Here we propose a standardized, scalable assay that transforms gentle serial cytoplasmic sampling—already demonstrated in Live-seq and scanning ion conductance microscopy nanobiopsy—into a routine method for measuring transcriptome trajectories from the same individual cells across seven or more defined timepoints. The approach establishes a stable, reusable access path to each tracked cell using a nanostraw, microcapillary, or nanobiopsy tip, withdraws tiny cytosolic aliquots on a fixed log-spaced schedule following a perturbation, and immediately captures each aliquot in a solution-phase mix carrying both a cell-specific and a timepoint-specific barcode before pooled reverse transcription and sequencing. The result is an explicit cell-by-time matrix of gene counts in which every entry derives from a physical sample taken at a known time from a known cell, enabling classification of genes into discrete-time trend classes such as early versus late and transient versus sustained responders. Because sampling yields sparse, cytosol-biased, Poisson-like snapshots, the analytical framework deliberately emphasizes patterns robust across genes and cells rather than precise kinetic parameters. The principal contribution is organizational rather than chemical: by coordinating validated access hardware, barcoded capture, and pooled sequencing into a canonical protocol, this work converts a bespoke proof-of-concept capability into a broadly adoptable tool for direct, repeated same-cell temporal measurement.

text: Extracellular vesicle (EV) and virus-like particle (VLP) RNA offer a potentially non-destructive window into cell-state dynamics, but their quantitative relationship to intracellular transcription remains poorly characterized. This proposal develops calibrated, program-level mappings that predict exported RNA activity from intracellular transcriptional programs—such as stress, interferon response, EMT, and proliferation—rather than modeling individual genes. We first reanalyze existing paired cellular and EV/VLP datasets to establish how far simple proportional scaling models already capture the exported signal and to identify regimes where they systematically fail. We then perform controlled experiments using engineered exporters and timed perturbations to test whether low-parameter models incorporating fixed lags or simple filters yield reusable improvements, imposing strong regularization and benchmarking each model against naive baselines, cross-perturbation transfer, and deliberate disruption of EV biogenesis. Where robust mappings emerge, we invert them to reconstruct intracellular program trajectories from EV/VLP sampling at the population and clone level without sacrificing cells. Crucially, we report both successes and failures, defining explicit validity regimes for each program and context. The result is a principled, transportable reporter system that turns EV/VLP RNA into a quantitative, non-destructive monitor of specified cell-state programs with known performance bounds.

label: baseline
text: Trajectory-inference methods promise to reconstruct the temporal ordering and branching of cellular responses from sparse, non-destructive measurements, yet rigorous benchmarking is limited by the absence of same-cell ground truth about what happened when. Here we propose to build few-tape, digital DNA recorders that furnish controlled, interpretable trajectories against which such methods can be tested. Each cell carries one or two shared, writable DNA tapes and a compact panel of three to six engineered signal channels—for example, doxycycline-inducible, optogenetic Wnt-reporter, and NF-κB-responsive elements—each driving a distinct guide RNA that stamps a channel-specific symbol using ENGRAM/Typewriter-style symbolic recording. A global recorder is activated across four to seven broad, logarithmically spaced epochs between 30 minutes and 24 hours after perturbation, producing a digital ON/OFF log per channel and epoch that is recovered by a single end-point sequencing readout. By externally varying which channels are stimulated and when, we generate known branching structures, including bifurcations, trifurcations, and delayed responders, whose ground-truth histories are written directly in DNA. Running sparse modalities such as intermittent Live-seq or limited imaging in parallel, we then assess whether trajectory-inference methods can correctly predict these encoded histories. Because all components are established, this design deliberately trades biochemical realism for controllability and interpretability, providing a practical testbed for benchmarking sparse trajectory inference.

label: baseline
text: We propose an externally pulsed DNA recording system that captures coarse molecular trajectories within individual cells across seven or more defined time bins spanning roughly thirty minutes to twenty-four hours after a perturbation, all read from a single endpoint sequencing measurement per cell. The approach combines an append-only genomic tape written by prime editing with a small panel of five to ten samplers, each coupling a signaling pathway or transcriptional program to production of a sampler-specific guide RNA with an engineered, tunable half-life. A fast external gate, controlled optogenetically or by small molecules, restricts editing to brief experimenter-timed pulses, so that each pulse writes an increment reflecting recent pathway activity integrated over a finite window, and the ordered tape encodes a staircase of edit bursts. Trajectories are decoded by partitioning the tape into pulse-wise blocks, computing per-sampler edit increments, and mapping these onto coarse pathway configurations learned from calibration experiments that pair the pulse schedule with destructive single-cell sequencing. This yields same-cell, multi-bin molecular trajectories through interpretable dimensions without per-bin destructive sampling or continuous imaging. We treat the temporal bins as blurred integrals rather than instantaneous snapshots, and identifiability depends on matching guide RNA decay to pulse spacing and on careful calibration. Within these realistic constraints, the design offers a lab-implementable route to trajectory information currently inaccessible with standard destructive or purely computational methods.

label: baseline
text: We propose an RNA-native molecular recording layer that enables individual mammalian cells to report which signaling pathways were meaningfully engaged during a defined perturbation window, encoded as a small set of discrete "history badges" that can be read alongside single-cell transcriptomes at a single endpoint. Rather than reconstructing hour-by-hour dynamics, each pathway-specific cassette records temporally integrated activity into a few qualitative states—such as off, low, or high-sustained engagement—capturing whether and how strongly a pathway crossed activation thresholds. Each badge couples a pathway-responsive promoter to a synthetic transcript carrying a pathway identity barcode and a recording element, using either symbol-counting RNA editing, in which edit number scales with cumulative activity, or a few-state recombinase cassette that yields distinct transcript isoforms. At the experimental endpoint, standard single-cell RNA sequencing simultaneously captures the global transcriptome and the edited state or isoform identity of each badge, allowing straightforward decoding of per-cell pathway engagement classes across multiplexed pathways. Because recording occurs at the RNA level without modifying endogenous genes, this approach is well suited to primary human cells and translational settings where DNA editing is undesirable. By deliberately trading fine temporal granularity for a scalable, transcriptome-compatible layer of coarse pathway history, this system links same-cell signaling history to endpoint fate across thousands of cells and many pathways.

label: baseline
text: Enhancer–promoter communication is thought to depend on both physical contact between regulatory elements and the recruitment of coactivator-rich microenvironments, yet existing perturbation tools conflate these effects, leaving their relative contributions to transcription unresolved. This proposal develops a light-controlled system that drives two matched, CRISPR-targeted perturbations at a single synthetic enhancer–promoter cassette integrated into mouse embryonic stem cells, enabling a direct comparison between mechanical confinement and coactivator condensate formation under identical genomic and optical conditions. The first construct uses a biochemically minimal light-inducible dimerization tether to increase enhancer–promoter contact frequency and dwell time with little added coactivator content, while the second layers coactivator intrinsically disordered regions onto a similar oligomerization backbone to nucleate transcriptional condensates. Parallel quantitative readouts, including dual-color chromatin tracking to measure mean squared displacement, confinement radius, and contact dwell-time distributions, together with MS2 live imaging and single-molecule FISH of transcriptional bursting, will link engineered geometry to gene output. By varying light intensity and duration, we will generate a tunable series of confinement states with and without coactivator condensates and map how burst frequency, duration, and amplitude respond to each. The result will be a quantitative framework distinguishing how much of the transcriptional response reflects stabilized contacts versus specialized coactivator microenvironments, addressing a central ambiguity in condensate-based models of gene regulation. Because all components are standard in current chromatin and transcription laboratories and rely on a single stimulus modality, the approach is both mechanistically informative and practically implementable.

label: baseline
text: This proposal investigates the extent to which modest, geometry-only constraints on enhancer–promoter separation can modulate transcription of activity-regulated genes in human iPSC-derived excitatory neurons. In a primary stage, two dCas9 anchors will be targeted to an enhancer and its cognate promoter at loci such as ARC or BDNF, and bridged by a single bivalent tether with a defined contour length and deliberately neutral biochemistry, allowing us to test whether mechanical and steric linkage alone is sufficient to alter enhancer–promoter contact probability and transcription relative to untethered controls. Readouts will combine live imaging or chromatin conformation methods with single-cell and nascent RNA measurements under defined neuronal activity paradigms, and results will be benchmarked against existing cofactor-recruiting looping tools to isolate the specific contribution of geometry. A contingent second stage, pursued only if robust effects survive anchor-related controls, will replace the static tether with an intramolecularly latching, light-gated element that switches between two inert length states, holding valency and biochemical composition constant while varying end-to-end distance by 20–50 nm. This design enables clean isolation of distance effects and mapping of duty cycles to transcriptional output. By treating small effect sizes as the central deliverable rather than an assumption, the program offers a technically grounded, conceptually distinct framework for quantifying how mechanical constraint alone shapes enhancer–promoter communication in neurons.

text: Chromatin boundaries formed by CTCF and cohesin organize the three-dimensional genome, yet existing tools for perturbing individual boundaries vary in their locality, tunability, and reversibility, and it remains unclear whether new engineered reagents are genuinely needed. This proposal establishes a staged, quantitative program to map how finely current CRISPR-based tools can tune single boundaries before committing to novel tool development. In the first stage, we will systematically explore dCas9-based perturbations—steric blocking with tiled guide RNAs, low-dose KRAB or DNMT recruitment, and partial global CTCF depletion combined with local rescue—across a panel of well-characterized loci in human induced pluripotent stem cells, measuring CTCF and cohesin occupancy, boundary strength, looping, transcription, and reversibility to produce a practical atlas of achievable boundary control. Only where this atlas reveals clear gaps, such as durable epigenetic marks or unacceptable pleiotropy from global manipulation, will we conditionally develop and rigorously benchmark locus-specific CTCF competitors that must demonstrate tunable weakening, minimal global perturbation, and cleaner reversibility. Validated perturbations can then be applied to compare transient boundary weakening against synthetic loop formation and, where required, integrated into inducible or ultrasound-gated frameworks. This design centers problem–solution efficiency, yielding a valuable resource whether existing tools prove sufficient or whether new competitors add demonstrable capability.

label: baseline
text: Enhancer–promoter loops are central to transcriptional regulation during development, yet it remains unclear whether forming a loop or dissolving it is the rate-limiting step for switching gene expression states. This proposal asks whether the characteristic time for loop-driven activation (τ_on) differs from that for loop loss–driven deactivation (τ_off) when the same enhancer–promoter contact is toggled on and off. We will engineer a single, light-controlled loop switch at a defined enhancer–promoter pair of a neural lineage gene in human neural progenitor cells, using dCas9 to target an optogenetic dimerizer that reversibly bridges the two sites upon illumination and releases them in darkness. Loop dynamics and transcriptional output will be measured simultaneously by dual-color locus imaging of enhancer–promoter distance and MS2/MCP reporting of promoter bursting, allowing direct comparison of τ_on and τ_off for the same loop under matched optogenetic kinetics. As a controlled secondary variable, we will slowly tune the strength of a nearby CTCF/cohesin boundary genetically or via a degron to test how native architecture modulates any kinetic asymmetry. Because formation and dissolution act on one engineered contact using identical molecular players, this design cleanly isolates the kinetic bottleneck of transcriptional switching. The results will clarify whether gene regulatory systems respond more sluggishly to the gain or the loss of a loop, with direct relevance to developmental gene control.

text: Cohesin-mediated loop extrusion is thought to be regulated by barriers such as CTCF, yet how the strength of an obstacle quantitatively determines loop formation and downstream transcription remains poorly defined. We propose to construct a calibrated ladder of synthetic chromatin barriers by fusing engineered, sequence-specific DNA-binding modules to catalytically dead Cas9, targeting them to defined genomic loci in K562 cells. A small series of point mutations spanning a range of DNA-binding affinities and residence times will create discrete barrier strengths, each expressed at comparable levels in separate cell lines while endogenous CTCF at the site is modestly attenuated. For every rung of the ladder we will measure barrier occupancy and binding kinetics, loop contact frequency using chromosome conformation and imaging approaches, and transcriptional output of the regulated gene, integrating these data with polymer modeling to derive a transfer function linking barrier strength to loop frequency and gene expression. This static, one-dimensional perturbation series isolates barrier affinity as the primary variable, yielding a mechanistically interpretable map distinct from tether-based approaches. As a subsequent extension, we will incorporate a light-responsive module into a selected barrier design to achieve reversible, real-time toggling between pre-characterized strengths, enabling dynamic control interpreted along the established affinity axis.

label: baseline
text: Whether transcriptional activation by intrinsically disordered activation domains reflects simple multivalent coactivator recruitment or an additional contribution from mesoscale phase organization remains difficult to resolve because sequence, client binding, and condensate formation are experimentally entangled. This proposal develops a minimal, genomically integrated reporter system in which a single-copy fluorescent or luciferase reporter is driven by a synthetic enhancer bearing arrayed guide-RNA target sites, allowing quantitative control of effector engagement. A drug-inducible dCas9–effector scaffold carrying a panel of rationally designed disordered variants, spanning wild-type, truncated, charge-scrambled, and compact activation-domain references, will be titrated across expression levels while measuring effector and coactivator occupancy by chromatin immunoprecipitation, transcriptional output and bursting, and low-dimensional phase descriptors such as punctum fraction and FRAP recovery. These data will populate a multi-variant response surface used to compare two model families: one predicting transcription from occupancy and coactivator recruitment alone, and one adding a phase-state term. By evaluating cross-validated predictive performance and residual structure, the framework tests whether including a phase descriptor materially improves explanation, particularly where phase metrics change sharply without proportional changes in occupancy. Rather than declaring liquid–liquid phase separation present or absent, the approach yields a quantitative, falsifiable, model-based assessment of its explanatory contribution to CRISPR-directed transcriptional control.

label: baseline
text: This proposal investigates whether local perturbation of cohesin's interface at a single CTCF anchor can serve as a distinct control lever for chromatin loops, separate from disrupting CTCF motifs or globally depleting cohesin. Using a tractable human cell line, we will tether a cohesin-interface perturbation module to one anchor of a well-mapped CTCF/cohesin-anchored loop via dCas9 and guide RNAs, characterizing the module's biochemical effect on cohesin in bulk beforehand without presuming its directionality. We will assess local cohesin presence by RAD21 and Smc3 chromatin profiling at the targeted site and neighboring regions, and measure loop strength by locus-focused chromatin conformation assays and gene expression of loop-dependent genes. Effects will be benchmarked against dCas9-only controls, effector tethering at neutral sites, CTCF motif editing, and acute cohesin depletion to distinguish partial, graded loop modulation from complete anchor loss or off-target global perturbation. A positive outcome would establish a usable, anchor-specific cohesin-interface lever, whereas negative or confounded results would define concrete limits on locally tunable cohesin dynamics. Either way, the study provides falsifiable constraints that inform the feasibility and design of future local chromatin control tools.

text: Weight loss, particularly when driven by GLP-1 therapies or structured dieting, frequently produces skin laxity as internal adipose support diminishes and the dermal extracellular matrix undergoes degradation-biased remodeling. Mechanical massage and vacuum-rolling devices can stimulate dermal collagen, elastin, and hyaluronan synthesis, yet their value for preserving skin firmness during active weight loss, and the importance of intervention timing, remains untested. This proposal describes a three-arm, within-subject trial in individuals undergoing intentional moderate weight loss, in which three comparable adjacent regions of the same anatomical area receive no mechanostimulation, late-only rescue mechanostimulation, or early and continuous mechanostimulation using a single standardized commercial device. Outcomes assessed at baseline, mid-, and post-weight-loss include regional fat thickness by ultrasound or MRI, shear-wave elastography, blinded laxity and contour scoring, and patient-reported satisfaction, with optional histological sampling. Analyses will compare each active arm against control and against each other using predefined minimal clinically important differences, applying equivalence testing where appropriate to distinguish whether intervention itself, or its timing, drives benefit. By emphasizing decision-relevant comparisons under realistic anatomical evolution rather than idealized dose-matched mechanics, this design efficiently determines whether mechanostimulation is clinically worthwhile and whether early initiation justifies the additional effort, with a contingent second stage reserved for mechanistic elaboration.

label: baseline
text: Substantial weight loss achieved through GLP-1 pharmacotherapy or bariatric surgery frequently results in skin laxity, yet the optimal timing of radiofrequency (RF) and negative-pressure treatments relative to the weight-loss trajectory remains unclear. This proposal describes a pragmatic, two-arm randomized trial designed to determine whether initiating RF sessions during rapid weight loss provides clinically meaningful benefit beyond treatment begun only after weight has stabilized. Adults scheduled for major weight loss will be randomized to a late-only arm, in which all sessions are delivered after plateau when laxity is visible, or an early-plus-late arm, in which the identical total dose is split between the rapid-loss phase and the post-plateau window, holding session count, energy settings, and treated areas constant so that only timing differs. The trial will be powered around a prespecified minimal clinically important difference, with blinded laxity and contour scores, patient-reported satisfaction, and the need for additional tightening or surgical referral as key endpoints. Analyses will incorporate prespecified stratification by age, diabetes status, and ultraviolet damage, and a nested substudy using high-frequency ultrasound, elastography, and optional biopsies will test whether any clinical advantage reflects measurable extracellular matrix changes. Whether timing proves influential or dose-dominant, the results will yield decision-grade guidance directly translatable to clinical scheduling and practice guidelines.

label: baseline
text: Rapid or massive weight loss frequently results in dermal laxity and maladaptive subcutaneous septal remodeling, yet current strategies focus on correcting these changes only after weight stabilization. This proposal asks whether providing simple, low-modulus volumizing support during weight loss, rather than afterward, measurably reduces tissue laxity and fibrosis, and whether any such benefit is large enough to matter clinically. Using animal models of controlled weight loss, we will compare rapid versus gradual loss and three filler-timing conditions—no filler, filler injected before or during loss, and filler injected after stabilization—delivered through realistic clinical injection patterns rather than idealized dispersions. Primary outcomes will include gross tissue laxity and contour, regional biomechanical stiffness and elasticity, and histological measures of dermal thickness, collagen and elastin organization, and septal integrity, while YAP/TAZ localization and Piezo expression in fibroblasts and adipocyte-lineage cells will serve as mechanotransduction readouts. The design deliberately prioritizes timing over intricate mechanical engineering, using off-the-shelf-like materials to test the core question decisively. A positive result would justify repositioning existing fillers as prophylactic adjuncts, whereas a negative result would redirect the field toward hormonal, metabolic, and post-hoc interventions.

label: baseline
text: Rapid or substantial weight loss unloads the dermis as subcutaneous fat diminishes, reducing fibroblast mechanical strain, downregulating mechanosensitive signaling, and promoting thinning and disorganization of collagen and elastin that manifest clinically as skin laxity and poor recoil. Current hyaluronic acid (HA) strategies address this laxity only after it develops, without exploiting the active remodeling window during which the dermis is being unloaded. This proposal reframes standard intradermal cross-linked and hybrid HA as a temporally targeted, mechanically intentional prophylactic therapy applied during weight loss, using conventional threading and meshing techniques to maintain fibroblast tension and bias local strain fields along defined directions. We hypothesize that early, patterned HA placement guides collagen and elastin deposition to yield a dermis that is thicker and more resistant to creep than isotropic HA or no intervention, then gradually degrades. The concept will be tested against explicit comparators—natural history, early isotropic HA, and patterned HA—using histology, second-harmonic imaging of fiber orientation, mechanical testing, and clinical laxity measures. Because the approach relies on established materials, techniques, and outcome tools, it constitutes a feasible, falsifiable research program that shifts emphasis from treating to preventing weight-loss-related skin laxity.

label: baseline
text: Post–weight-loss skin laxity reflects, in part, the failure of the dermis and superficial fibrous septa as underlying fat volume declines, yet current treatments intervene only after such failure becomes visible. This proposal tests whether short- to medium-term mechanobiologic hysteresis exists in fibroblast-driven remodeling of these tissues during a controlled mechanical unloading event, asking whether stimulation applied before or early in unloading shapes tissue remodeling differently than identical stimulation applied after unloading is established. Using an animal model in which a defined reduction in mechanical load is imposed on a skin region over two to four weeks, we will apply a well-characterized, spatially localized stimulus—an energy-based device or a cyclic micro-stretch apparatus—across three arms: anticipatory (pre/early) stimulation, late stimulation, and unloaded-only control. Densely sampled over the first three weeks, structural endpoints will quantify dermal thickness, collagen composition, and superficial septal continuity and orientation, while molecular endpoints will assess YAP/TAZ and MRTF signaling, myofibroblast activation, and extracellular matrix turnover. Hysteresis would manifest as better preservation of septal organization and a dampened catabolic shift in early-stimulated tissue at matched unloading durations. A positive result would justify clinical timing strategies for preconditioning around unloading, whereas rapid re-equilibration would redirect effort toward ongoing mechanical support, providing a decisive mechanistic answer before complex translational protocols are pursued.

label: baseline
text: Skin laxity following planned, significant weight loss remains a common problem that often necessitates excisional body-contouring surgery, yet the optimal timing of preventive interventions during the weight-loss process is unknown. This proposal describes a pragmatic, mechanistically informed clinical trial that uses only existing, approved tools to determine whether mechanical and anabolic support delivered during active weight loss improves skin outcomes compared with treatment applied after weight stabilization. Adults entering a structured weight-loss pathway, such as bariatric surgery, will be enrolled in a 2×2 factorial design testing standard medical-grade compression garments worn during weight loss and dermal biostimulation applied either early or late. The rationale draws on fibroblast mechanosensitivity, extracellular matrix remodeling under altered dermal tension, and the capacity of biostimulants to increase collagen and elastin production, with the hypothesis that intervening during the adaptive window yields better-organized, more supportive dermal architecture. Primary clinical endpoints include validated laxity and contour scores and the need for or extent of excisional surgery, complemented in a subset by histologic, second-harmonic imaging, and biomechanical assessments of collagen alignment, dermal thickness, and tensile behavior. Weight-loss kinetics and compression adherence will be explicitly modeled to isolate timing effects. Whether positive or null, the results will directly inform whether early mechanobiologic intervention should be integrated into weight-loss care or reserved for post-stabilization management.

label: baseline
text: Massive weight loss, whether achieved through bariatric surgery or GLP-1 pharmacotherapy, frequently results in significant skin laxity and contour deformities, yet current tools for predicting which patients will require body-contouring or skin-tightening procedures rely on noisy clinical factors such as weight-loss magnitude, age, body mass index, and basic skin examinations. Emerging imaging and histological evidence indicates that the retinacula cutis/superficial fascial system (RC/SFS), the tether network connecting skin to deeper tissues, is structurally damaged after major weight loss, but this subsystem is almost never incorporated into risk stratification. This proposal tests the hypothesis that a simple, standardized ultrasound- or MRI-derived RC/SFS index provides independent and clinically meaningful predictive power for post-weight-loss laxity and contouring need beyond established variables. We will first develop a low-dimensional, reliable RC/SFS index based on mean gray value and simple geometric features, prioritizing inter- and intra-operator reproducibility. We will then apply this index within cross-sectional and short-term cohorts of post-weight-loss patients with known laxity and surgical outcomes, evaluating whether it adds statistically significant predictive value and reclassifies patients between risk categories. A supported hypothesis would justify future studies of RC/SFS-targeted interventions, whereas a negative result would efficiently redirect the field toward other determinants, making this a strategic, staged investigation that maximizes clinical impact while minimizing wasted engineering effort.

label: baseline
text: Rapid, intentional weight loss through GLP-1 therapy or bariatric surgery frequently produces skin laxity, ptosis, and contour collapse as adipocyte deflation reduces mechanical strain on dermal and septal fibroblasts, lowering integrin–FAK–YAP/TAZ signaling and collagen and elastin production. Mechanotherapeutic interventions such as radiofrequency, extracorporeal shockwave therapy, and biostimulatory hyaluronic acid fillers can transiently enhance fibroblast activity and extracellular matrix synthesis, but the optimal timing of a limited treatment dose remains unknown. This study asks whether clustering a fixed number of sessions before and at the onset of weight loss confers greater benefit per unit dose than distributing the same total dose evenly as maintenance throughout the weight-loss period. Using off-the-shelf modalities, patients will be randomized to an early-clustered arm or a dose-matched maintenance arm and assessed longitudinally at baseline, mid-loss, and post-stabilization for dermal thickness, collagen and elastin organization, fibrous septa continuity, clinical laxity, three-dimensional contour, and patient-reported outcomes. The primary comparison evaluates whether extracellular matrix, septal, and laxity trajectories differ between arms given equal total dose, and whether early clustering is more dose-efficient. The findings will clarify whether a privileged early window exists for mechanotherapeutic preconditioning, providing actionable guidance for treatment scheduling regardless of outcome direction.

label: baseline
text: Skin redundancy and laxity following major weight loss remain common and clinically challenging, and current mechanical interventions are typically applied reactively after weight has stabilized. This proposal advances a timing principle: that mechanically preconditioning the dermal–septa scaffold before and during rapid adipose loss, rather than only afterward, may alter how the skin–fat composite deforms when internal support shrinks. We hypothesize that collagen and septal reinforcement laid down while fat lobules are still large integrate in a high-tension configuration that increases the load-bearing contribution of septa once fat retracts, thereby reducing visible folds and sagging for a given degree of weight loss. Using extracorporeal shockwave therapy as a well-characterized, clinically available testbed, we will conduct a trial comparing pre-only versus post-only treatment at equal total dose in adults undergoing substantial weight loss, with an optional pre-plus-early arm. Outcomes include ultrasound elastography and thickness, three-dimensional surface topography quantifying redundancy and fold geometry, and blinded clinical laxity grading. A positive result would validate a timing-based preconditioning paradigm generalizable to other mechanical stimuli, while a null result would decisively steer the field toward alternative interventions.

label: baseline
text: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) is a common and burdensome complication of fractional laser treatment in patients with darker skin phototypes, yet current preventive practice is largely empiric, with wide variation in the choice, timing, and duration of topical anti-inflammatory agents. This project aims to define the minimal effective early anti-inflammatory regimen that reduces PIH without impairing wound healing, operationalizing the concept of a narrow, timing-sensitive inflammatory "golden window" following laser injury. Using a single, well-established topical agent already accepted in post-laser care, we will conduct an adequately powered randomized controlled trial in high-risk patients comparing two to three regimens that bracket this window: a very short early course (24–48 hours), a moderate course (4–5 days), and standard care. The primary endpoint will be PIH severity at four to eight weeks, assessed by colorimetry and blinded visual scoring, with key safety endpoints including time to re-epithelialization and early wound complications. An optional mechanistic sub-study will sample early inflammatory markers to support the biological rationale. By identifying the shortest sufficient duration of early anti-inflammatory input, this study will deliver an actionable, evidence-based decision rule that standardizes prophylaxis, reduces unnecessary drug exposure, and provides a benchmark regimen against which future agents can be evaluated.

label: baseline
text: This proposal advances a pharmacodynamics-anchored strategy for preventing post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) and scarring following fractional laser treatment through early, transient RNA interference against key regulatory pathways. Because MITF and the TGFβ/Smad axis govern both pathological and normal wound-healing processes, the central challenge is to suppress these pathways enough to blunt excessive melanin and myofibroblast activation without impairing re-epithelialization, barrier recovery, or tensile strength. To address this, the study first quantifies the depth, duration, and spatial extent of local knockdown and aligns these pharmacodynamic curves with measurable healing milestones, defining treatment regimens by pharmacodynamic targets rather than arbitrary time–dose combinations. Using one target and one vehicle per outcome—MITF via a topical carrier for PIH and a single TGFβ-axis node via a hydrogel or microneedle depot for scarring—it then performs a decisive comparison at matched knockdown levels. Specifically, it tests whether adding a simple enzyme-responsive bias, tyrosinase-cleavable siRNA for PIH or MMP-cleavable crosslinking for scarring, confers a safety–efficacy advantage beyond controlling exposure alone. Because pharmacodynamics is explicitly measured, both outcomes yield actionable guidance, clarifying whether well-controlled ungated delivery suffices or minimal spatial biasing is uniquely beneficial.

label: baseline
text: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) and scarring remain unpredictable complications of fractional laser treatment, particularly in patients with darker phototypes or a history of keloids. This proposal tests whether early patterns of purinergic receptor engagement and downstream Ca²⁺/ERK signaling in human laser wounds predict later PIH and fibrosis beyond established clinical factors, and whether modulating these signals can improve outcomes without impairing wound closure. Rather than assuming a fixed valence for any receptor, the program treats purinergic signaling as context-dependent and empirically maps ATP decay dynamics, calcium transients, and ERK activity in ex vivo human skin and small exploratory in vivo cohorts, using receptor-selective pharmacological perturbations to probe keratinocyte migration and fibroblast and melanocyte activation. A pre-specified decision rule determines whether purinergic markers add measurable predictive value over phototype, keloid history, and inflammation indices, providing an explicit go/no-go gate before any interventional work. If warranted, a short-window topical designed to modestly damp early purinergic tone will be tested as an additive to best-practice care, with re-epithelialization and infection as non-inferiority endpoints alongside PIH and scar outcomes. By coupling a minimal, pre-registered marker set with clear stopping criteria, the study will decisively establish whether receptor-patterned purinergic signaling is a practically relevant lever or a target that should be deprioritized in favor of more direct interventions.

label: baseline
text: This proposal uses fractional laser resurfacing in humans as a controlled, pro-regenerative wound model to test whether early damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) and Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)–related signaling contributes to later scarring and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH). In a prospective cohort enriched for higher scarring and PIH risk, we will map early inflammatory signatures using exudate, tape-strip, and optional biopsy samples, quantifying fibronectin fragments containing the extra domain A (FnEDA), TLR4-responsive cytokines, broader inflammatory profiles, and early fibroblast and myofibroblast markers, and correlate these with instrumented and clinical measures of scarring and pigmentation at follow-up. This observational mapping is the primary contribution and is informative regardless of outcome, since weak associations would indicate that early DAMP/TLR4 amplitude is not a major determinant of outcomes in shallow injury. Contingent on positive predictive findings, a small within-subject randomized trial will test whether standard, low-potency topical anti-inflammatory agents applied during the early inflammatory window shift mechanistic signatures and clinical outcomes without impairing healing. FnEDA is retained as a candidate mechanistic reporter rather than a predetermined therapeutic target. The design emphasizes falsifiability, feasibility, and clarity, aiming to establish whether timing-restricted, local inflammatory control is a genuine lever for reducing fibrosis and pigmentation.

label: baseline
text: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) is a common complication of fractional laser resurfacing, yet it remains unclear whether the early inflammatory signaling triggered by laser injury can be modulated to limit pigment formation without impairing wound repair. This proposal seeks to define whether a brief, early post-laser window exists during which partial modulation of NF-κB/IRF signaling attenuates inflammatory melanogenesis while preserving re-epithelialization and basic tissue integrity. Using ex vivo human skin subjected to standardized fractional laser injury, we will apply one or two skin-compatible NF-κB/IRF modulators as experimental probes across defined early and late treatment windows, together with a high-dose arm and vehicle control, allowing us to attribute pigment effects to timing and strength of modulation rather than generic toxicity. Primary readouts will quantify epidermal melanin, melanocyte number and dendricity, MITF and tyrosinase expression, and paracrine melanogenic mediators, evaluated alongside co-primary repair and viability constraints. Rather than proposing a new therapeutic agent, the study delivers a temporal control map, a quantitative trade-off between pigment suppression and repair, and a go/no-go decision point for early, shared-node intervention strategies. Because NF-κB/IRF is a shared repair–pigment node, a clean controllable window would justify pursuing selective modulators, whereas its absence would redirect attention toward downstream or lineage-specific targets.

label: baseline
text: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) and early hypertrophic scarring remain common complications following fractional ablative laser resurfacing, yet the relative contributions of wound mechanics, barrier restoration, inflammation, and pigment-directed pharmacology to their prevention are poorly separated. This proposal outlines a hierarchical clinical program that first defines and dissects the achievable ceiling of optimized simple care before investing in spatially complex interventions. In Stage 1, a 2×2 factorial randomized controlled trial in patients undergoing facial resurfacing will test a uniform occlusive dressing and an optimized topical/photoprotection regimen, separately and combined, with PIH and texture outcomes assessed at three to six months and a nested biomarker sub-study capturing early erythema, transepidermal water loss, and melanin trajectories. Stage 2, activated only if meaningful residual pathology persists under fully optimized care, will map whether remaining lesions cluster within specific anatomical, geometric, and mobility contexts. Stage 3, conditional on such clustering, will compare uniform versus template-patterned dressings that provide anatomically biased support in high-risk zones. Explicit go/no-go criteria ensure that more complex spatial or mechanistic work proceeds only when justified. The program delivers an immediately actionable standardized care package while rigorously determining whether where local environment modulation is applied truly matters.

label: baseline
text: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) is a frequent complication of fractional CO₂ laser resurfacing, particularly in darker skin phototypes, and is driven substantially by early keratinocyte-derived inflammatory and melanogenic signaling that peaks within days of treatment and largely normalizes by approximately one week. While early topical anti-inflammatory regimens can reduce PIH, the optimal onset and duration of such intervention remain undefined, raising the risk of unnecessarily prolonged suppression that may impair healing or cause steroid-related side effects. We hypothesize that a strictly limited, ultra-short early course of a keratinocyte-centric anti-inflammatory and anti-melanogenic agent, begun immediately or within 24 hours after laser treatment, can blunt the peak of early keratinocyte output sufficiently to prevent PIH while preserving normal re-epithelialization and remodeling. We propose a randomized clinical trial in PIH-prone patients comparing an ultra-short 48–72 hour early course, a standard 7-day early course, a delayed short course started around day 5–7, and standard-of-care control. Primary outcomes are PIH severity and persistence assessed by colorimetry and blinded visual grading at 4–12 weeks, with wound-healing metrics and optional tape-strip assays of key cytokines and melanogenic factors confirming differential shaping of early keratinocyte outputs. By clarifying the temporal leverage of keratinocyte modulation, this study aims to identify the leanest and safest preventive strategy, offering practical guidance implementable with existing agents and infrastructure.

label: baseline
text: Fractional laser resurfacing carries a variable risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) and hypertrophic scarring (HTS), yet current practice typically applies uniform prophylaxis to all treated patients. This proposal develops and validates the Stiffness–Optical Risk Index (SORI), a compact quantitative measure obtained at a single 2–4 week follow-up that combines a static stiffness surrogate (suction-based deformation or ultrasound/OCT-derived elasticity) with an optical and perfusion component (erythema and melanin indices, with optional perfusion mapping), each normalized against adjacent unaffected skin and expected values for anatomic site and laser parameters. Mechanistically, these subacute readouts are hypothesized to reflect emerging fibroblast–myofibroblast activity, matrix deposition, and melanocyte stress that drive later PIH and HTS, although this predictive value is treated as an empirical question rather than an assumption. The research plan will prospectively recruit fractional-laser patients, record clinical predictors, acquire stiffness and optical measures using off-the-shelf devices, and track outcomes at 6–12 months to compare a clinical model, a SORI-only model, and a combined model. SORI will then define simple risk tiers that gate the intensity and duration of standard prophylaxis, such as topical steroid or tacrolimus and silicone or pressure therapy. A follow-on randomized study will test whether SORI-gated intensified prophylaxis improves outcomes relative to usual care. The central contribution is a reproducible, mechanistically informed framework for risk-stratified prevention that determines who needs stronger intervention rather than applying a one-size-fits-all regimen.

label: baseline
text: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) and hypertrophic remodeling are common complications of fractional laser resurfacing in high-risk patients, yet the optimal timing and duration of preventive anti-inflammatory or anti-fibrotic modulation remain undefined. This proposal aims to identify a narrow, safe window of early post-laser modulation that prevents these adverse outcomes without impairing normal wound healing. We will conduct a within-patient randomized trial in high-risk individuals selected by validated criteria, applying standardized fractional laser treatment to symmetric fields and randomizing those fields to control skincare or brief anti-inflammatory modulation initiated at varying times and durations after laser exposure. Primary outcomes will include PIH incidence and severity assessed by objective colorimetry and blinded photographic scoring, alongside early hypertrophic tendencies and safety endpoints such as time to re-epithelialization. In a subset of participants, minimally invasive sampling will quantify inflammatory and profibrotic markers together with transepidermal water loss and erythema at early time points, allowing us to explain why particular timing regimens succeed and to model whether biomarker-based stratification could spare unnecessary exposure. This design establishes practice-relevant timing guidance while providing mechanistic insight to inform future, potentially stratified preventive strategies.

label: baseline
text: Mitochondrial pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductases PYCR1 and PYCR2 are frequently essential in hypoxic cancer cells, yet whether this dependency reflects a generic redox function or additional, non-substitutable roles remains unclear. This proposal develops a two-stage, hypothesis-explicit framework to distinguish when PYCR1/2 dependency can be neutralized by generic mitochondrial redox rewiring from when it reflects functions insensitive to such rewiring. All experiments are performed under defined hypoxia with abundant extracellular proline and intact transport, using isoform-agnostic PYCR1/2 double knockouts and matrix-localized manipulations. In Stage 1, cells with and without matrix-targeted LbNOX are profiled for mitochondrial NADH/NAD+ and NADPH/NADP+ balance, reactive oxygen species, purine synthesis flux, mTOR-pathway signaling, and proliferation, classifying contexts by full, partial, or minimal rescue. Stage 2 conditionally deepens partial- and no-rescue contexts through nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase modulation and pathway-specific or structural rescues targeting purine pools, mitochondrial dynamics, and collagen/extracellular matrix production. By pre-specifying redox, signaling, and structural hypotheses and probing them in a staged manner, the framework yields a mechanistically partitioned map that clarifies when PYCR functions as a replaceable redox valve versus an irreplaceable organizational hub.

label: baseline
text: Proline metabolism supports the survival of many tumors, but it remains unclear whether the mitochondrial localization of the pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductases PYCR1 and PYCR2, rather than their catalytic activity per se, constitutes a distinct therapeutic vulnerability in cancers dependent on proline dehydrogenase (PRODH). This proposal introduces a compartment-swap genetic strategy to resolve this question in bona fide PRODH-dependent cancer models. We will construct a minimal three-state system comprising wild-type cells, PYCR1/2 double-knockout cells, and knockout cells reconstituted with either mitochondrially targeted or cytosolically retargeted PYCR1/2, with all rescue constructs calibrated for matched expression and catalytic capacity. Each state will be characterized using stable-isotope proline and glutamine tracing to quantify PRODH-derived anaplerosis, subcellular metabolite profiling of proline and pyrroline-5-carboxylate pools, compartment-specific redox biosensors, and functional assays of ATP, reactive oxygen species, and viability under metabolic stress, alongside pharmacologic PRODH and pan-PYCR inhibition comparators. A predefined decision framework will distinguish whether total PYCR activity or its mitochondrial localization drives PRODH dependence, or whether alternative bypass routes dominate. Regardless of outcome, the results will clarify whether mitochondrially biased PYCR1/2 inhibition represents a genuine spatial choke point or whether simpler PRODH- or pan-PYCR-directed strategies suffice, thereby sharpening translational priorities.

label: baseline
text: The proline–P5C cycle, driven by proline dehydrogenase (PRODH) and pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductases (PYCR1/2), plays context-dependent roles in cancer cell survival and death, yet it remains unclear whether it can be exploited as a self-damaging metabolic trap. This proposal tests the hypothesis that in a PYCR-high, electron-rich mitochondrial environment, activating PRODH forces its FADH2-derived electrons toward oxygen rather than the ubiquinone pool, converting proline oxidation into a net pro-oxidant flux. Using a single well-characterized cancer line, we will construct two isogenic states—PYCR-high with PRODH off and PYCR-high with inducible PRODH—alongside wild-type controls, holding all other pathways and media conditions constant. We will characterize the mitochondrial redox background through NAD(P)H and Q-pool reduction measurements, quantify proline-derived electron flux with stable-isotope tracing and oxygen consumption, and measure mitochondrial reactive oxygen species to compute the ratio of ROS generated per proline oxidized. By varying extracellular proline and modestly perturbing NAD(P)H generation, we will determine whether additional proline deepens the oxidative burden or is buffered. The central falsifiable prediction is that this ROS-to-oxidation ratio rises with Q-pool reduction, revealing a physically constrained “substrate weaponization” regime; a flat or declining ratio would instead indicate a buffered cycle better targeted by classical inhibition.

label: baseline
text: This proposal develops a minimal, genetically defined system to determine whether the direction of proline flux at the pyrroline-5-carboxylate (P5C) node governs the vulnerability of PYCR-dependent cancer cells. Using a single cellular background maintained under constant high extracellular proline, we construct two to three genotypes: a wild-type control, a strong PYCR1/2 loss-of-function line, and PYCR-deficient cells engineered with doxycycline-inducible PRODH or P5CDH targeted to their native mitochondrial locations. Because P5C is chemically unstable, we define flux direction operationally through stable-isotope labeling of extracellular proline, tracking enrichment in glutamate and TCA intermediates alongside proliferation, survival, and bulk NADH/NAD⁺ and NADPH/NADP⁺ ratios. The central prediction is that if mitochondrial proline serves a uniquely reductive role through PYCR, then inducing oxidative routing in PYCR-deficient cells will fail to rescue and may further impair growth and redox balance despite increased anaplerotic input; conversely, partial normalization would indicate that oxidative handling can substitute for reductive proline usage. Inducible, within-line comparisons minimize compensatory adaptation and clarify cause and effect. By enforcing a persistent, genetically defined flux bias at the mitochondrial node, this parsimonious design cleanly distinguishes substitution from non-substitution of proline usage in a way that systemic pharmacologic inhibition cannot readily achieve.

label: baseline
text: The enzyme PYCR1 is essential for the survival of hypoxic tumors, yet loss of PYCR1 is frequently not rescued by exogenous proline, suggesting that its critical function extends beyond proline synthesis. This proposal seeks to determine whether the non-rescuable dependency on PYCR1 reflects a specific requirement for mitochondrial matrix NADPH support or, alternatively, a role for PYCR1 as an NADH/TCA cycle valve independent of NADPH supply. Using one or two well-characterized models in which PYCR1 is required for hypoxic proliferation and cannot be fully rescued by extracellular proline, we will perform orthogonal manipulations of mitochondrial NADPH under hypoxia and saturating proline. Specifically, we will compare wild-type cells, PYCR1-deficient cells, and PYCR1-deficient cells in which matrix NADPH supply is augmented with a targeted NADPH-generating enzyme or NADPH demand is reduced through partial suppression of matrix antioxidant systems. Readouts will include viability, mitochondrial ROS, iron–sulfur and respiratory integrity, compartment-targeted redox biosensors, and isotope tracing to separate cofactor usage from carbon flux. By testing whether these manipulations rescue or exacerbate PYCR1 loss, the project will discriminate between the two proposed functions and establish a foundation for rational targeting of the PYCR–mitochondrial redox node in cancer.

label: baseline
text: Targeting the mitochondrial enzymes PYCR1/2 is an emerging anticancer strategy, but extracellular proline may undermine such therapies by supporting cell fitness through bypass routes, and it remains unclear when this matters. Here we propose a context-aware, two-phase framework to decide, for a given cancer lineage, whether extracellular proline can be ignored, requires modest co-targeting, or signals complex therapeutic escape. In the first phase, PYCR1/2 loss-of-function is established and a minimal functional rescue test is performed, assessing growth, viability, and optional stress-signaling markers with and without proline in both two-dimensional monoculture and at least one stromal or three-dimensional context; lineages showing no reproducible rescue are classified as proline-irrelevant, and the program stops. Only lineages exhibiting rescue advance to the second phase, which uses targeted isotope tracing and a limited set of single-node perturbations, including PRODH, PYCRL, and proline transporters, to map how proline supports fitness and to identify small perturbation sets that neutralize rescue. Lineages are then designated as controllable, when one or two co-targets suffice, or as complex escape, when parsimonious combinations fail. By gating relevance on function rather than preselected metabolic sentinels and allowing distributed bypass routes, this parsimonious, laboratory-implementable framework directly informs the design and de-risking of PYCR1/2-targeted therapies.

label: baseline
text: Cancer cells reprogram amino acid metabolism, and the mitochondrial enzymes PYCR1 and PYCR2, which mediate proline synthesis and proline–P5C cycling, are frequently implicated in tumor growth. Whether cancer cells possess a genuinely noncompensable dependence on this activity, however, remains unclear, because glutamine and proline metabolism is generally flexible and extracellular proline uptake could substitute for de novo synthesis. This proposal tests the hypothesis that acute, isoform-complete loss of PYCR1/2 is functionally noncompensable even when alternative nutrients and recycling routes remain fully available. Using doxycycline-inducible CRISPR or degron systems to achieve rapid, near-complete dual ablation, we first perform a minimal whole-cell test under permissive metabolic conditions, measuring short-term survival, proliferation, bulk redox and ROS states, and de novo proline synthesis by focused isotope tracing. Only if this reveals a strong, non-rescuable vulnerability will we proceed to a compartment-resolved dissection using matrix-targeted redox sensors, organelle-aware proline/P5C tracing, and mitochondria-focused rescue experiments to determine whether the lethal phenotype reflects a specific failure of mitochondrial redox buffering. This staged, compartment-aware design provides a rigorous and parsimonious way to establish whether mitochondrial PYCR activity is uniquely non-redundant and to localize the underlying mechanism.

label: baseline
text: Pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductase (PYCR1/2) represents a promising therapeutic target in several cancers, yet it remains unclear whether the vulnerability arises from the catalytic conversion of P5C to proline within the mitochondrial glutamate–P5C–proline cycle or from the enzyme's embedding within a specific redox and adhesion microdomain, such as the PINCH-1/kindlin-2/DRP1 axis. This distinction is decisive for drug development, determining whether efforts should target active-site inhibition or the disruption of recruitment interfaces.
