We propose to resolve this question in PYCR1/2-null cancer cells reconstituted with controlled re-expression, using three convergent and mechanistically distinct perturbations: a mutant pair separating catalysis from localization (catalysis-dead/localization-intact versus catalysis-intact/localization-defective), a matrix-targeted heterologous P5C reductase providing catalysis without mammalian scaffolding, and disruption of the PINCH-1/kindlin-2 recruitment machinery in cells expressing wild-type PYCR. Each condition will be assessed with 13C-glutamine and 13C-proline flux tracing, compartment-specific redox measurements, and oncogenic phenotypes including stress survival, ECM output, and mitochondrial dynamics. By emphasizing glutamate-derived proline flux and working within PYCR-null backgrounds, this design controls for extracellular proline uptake and isoform redundancy. Together, these experiments will falsify either the catalysis-dominant or embedding-dominant model, thereby clarifying the mechanistic basis of PYCR1/2 dependency and guiding rational therapeutic strategy.

label: baseline
text: Mitochondrial redox balance constrains aspartate and purine synthesis in many tumors, yet the enzymes PYCR1 and PYCR2 are typically regarded as auxiliary contributors to NAD+ regeneration under hypoxia rather than principal control points. This proposal asks whether PYCR1/2 can become a dominant matrix redox gate for aspartate and purine output, and if so, in which tumors and under what pre-existing constraints. Rather than surveying all cancers, we first pre-select models that are already aspartate-limited and constrained in malate–aspartate shuttle capacity, using existing omics data followed by a functional screen in which aspartate supplementation strongly rescues proliferation and nucleotide labeling under hypoxia or mild electron transport chain inhibition. In this enriched subset, we apply a lean three-lever design that compares matched perturbations of PYCR1/2, malate–aspartate shuttle components, and complex II, together with exogenous aspartate rescue, using isotopic tracing to quantify aspartate and de novo purine flux. A PYCR-anchored gate is defined when PYCR perturbation reduces flux comparably to or more than canonical gates and is only partially relieved by aspartate. Optional redox reporters and targeted probes will refine mechanism if a gate is identified. Either outcome yields a decisive, quantitative boundary on PYCR's biosynthetic role.

label: baseline
text: This proposal establishes a mechanism-based discovery program to test whether mitochondrial pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductases (PYCR1/2) can be exploited to activate proline-like pro-toxins within PYCR-addicted cancer cells. The central concept is to design stable proline-core analogs, or masked precursors that generate a PYCR substrate in the mitochondrial matrix, that the enzyme reduces using its native, stereospecific hydride-transfer chemistry, such that the resulting product becomes toxic or creates a metabolic trap. Rather than assuming such molecules exist, the work defines strict mechanistic criteria for a genuine PYCR-activated pro-toxin, requiring measurable enzymatic turnover in vitro, PYCR-dependent product formation in cells, and cytotoxicity that tracks catalytic conversion rather than uptake or nonspecific inhibition. A small, rational library informed by structural and inhibitor data will be screened to distinguish turnover from competitive inhibition, and hits will be characterized for effects on respiration, redox pools, and proline metabolism in matched PYCR-high and PYCR-low cell lines with genetic perturbations. Critically, PYCR-activated analogs will be benchmarked against generic mitochondria-targeted redox-consuming pro-drugs to determine whether PYCR activation confers a selectivity window that promiscuous activation lacks. The project is explicitly exploratory and falsifiable, with clear decision points to pivot toward classical PYCR or PRODH inhibition if PYCR proves an inadequate activating gate. A positive outcome would define a mechanistically crisp vulnerability that converts a proline-cycle compensation enzyme into a selective executioner of PYCR-dependent tumors.

label: baseline
text: This proposal investigates whether neuron-derived signals initiate or accelerate localized epidermal barrier deterioration beyond epithelium-intrinsic Th2 drift in atopic dermatitis, redefining barrier disruption as a multidimensional state rather than a single tight-junction defect. Using three-dimensional human epidermal equivalents conditioned with IL-4/IL-13 (with or without IL-22) to establish an atopic dermatitis-like baseline, we apply a shared readout panel spanning junctional architecture, differentiation markers, protease activity, lipid organization, mechanical stiffness, and integrative transepithelial measures. In a parallel design, we first test whether physiologically plausible neuron-derived mediators, such as substance P and a SEMA7A-family ligand, shift the composite barrier state, and concurrently establish a minimal co-culture with induced pluripotent stem cell-derived pruriceptors carrying a chemogenetic actuator to test whether controlled neuronal activation drives barrier changes. Receptor blockade and neuronal silencing provide causality checks on both the epithelial and neuronal sides. Contingent on positive findings, targeted transcriptomics and spatial structuring will resolve which barrier dimensions are most neuron-sensitive and which keratinocyte subpopulations respond. By distinguishing cytokine-driven from neuron-initiated barrier shifts in a human-relevant system, this work aims to identify neuro-epithelial pathways whose blockade could stabilize the barrier and inform combinatorial therapeutic strategies.

label: baseline
text: Inflammation in atopic dermatitis (AD) is typically framed in terms of cytokine dose, yet cells may also respond to the temporal pattern, or waveform, of cytokine exposure. This proposal tests whether AD-relevant keratinocytes decode cytokine dynamics in ways that go beyond cumulative dose, and whether pericellular heparan sulfate and other glycosaminoglycans (HS/GAGs) act as distinct kinetic control nodes rather than simple modulators of signaling strength. In Phase 1, two-dimensional keratinocyte cultures will be exposed to matched-dose ligand waveforms—continuous, pulsed, and ramped—while measuring pSTAT dynamics and barrier and inflammatory gene expression to detect robust history effects beyond area-under-the-curve. In Phase 2, HS/GAG availability will be perturbed through coatings and enzymatic manipulation and compared directly against pathway inhibition tuned to equivalent signaling metrics, testing whether matrix modulation reshapes temporal decoding in ways that inhibitors cannot reproduce. Explicit decision points determine whether to proceed: if responses depend only on dose, or if HS effects merely rescale signaling, the project concludes early. Only confirmed waveform dependence with HS-specific temporal effects justifies Phase 3 extensions to immune co-culture, organ-on-chip, and transgenic models. This disciplined, mechanistically grounded design efficiently evaluates whether extracellular matrices provide an exploitable temporal control axis in epithelial inflammation.

label: baseline
text: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is thought to become self-sustaining when early-life skin injury imprints durable immune and sensory circuits, yet it remains unclear whether transient neonatal keratinocyte programs can prevent this "locking" even under chronic barrier failure. This proposal tests, in mice with constitutive barrier defects (FLG−/− or DSG1−/−), whether brief neonatal manipulation of keratinocyte modules can durably block establishment of pro-AD immune circuits and pro-itch sensory remodeling. Locking is defined by long-lived, biologically anchored endpoints, including skin-resident memory T cell and ILC2 pools with type 2 cytokine bias, intraepidermal innervation density, and itch-associated dorsal root ganglion subtypes, all measured well after manipulation ceases. Using inducible, keratinocyte-targeted tools, we will first determine whether any single module—alarmin signaling (IL-33/TSLP) or innervation control (Sema3a/NGF)—can override chronic drive when activated only during the first postnatal week. If confirmed, a three-way comparison against barrier reinforcement will rank modules using a predefined composite locking index integrating immune, neural, and behavioral outcomes. Targeted single-cell profiling will validate module specificity and refine cell-type definitions. The results will identify which keratinocyte-controlled axis most effectively prevents durable AD circuit formation, prioritizing early-life interventions for translational development.

label: baseline
text: Atopic dermatitis (AD) frequently involves persistent barrier fragility and heightened itch even after obvious triggers are removed, suggesting that early insults may leave a durable imprint on the skin. This project tests whether Staphylococcus aureus quorum sensing (QS), governed by the agr system, drives a path-dependent, partially irreversible barrier and itch defect in AD-prone skin, and whether early agr suppression combined with standard barrier care can prevent this transition. Using filaggrin-deficient three-dimensional human epidermal models or skin-on-chip systems, we will expose tissue to agr-active bacteria, an isogenic agr-inactive strain, and generic damage controls at matched injury levels, then remove bacteria and cytokines and apply standardized repair conditions across at least one keratinocyte turnover cycle. We will assess barrier differentiation, protease balance, cytokine milieu, and inducible IL-31/Th2 responsiveness, using targeted single-cell RNA sequencing to determine whether persistent abnormalities localize to basal or early spinous progenitor compartments. A filaggrin-deficient mouse model will confirm whether agr-active colonization produces lasting barrier fragility, itch bias, and exaggerated challenge responses after clearance. If a QS-imprinted state is confirmed, we will test whether agr suppression during the insult window prevents imprinting. The framework is falsifiable and designed to yield actionable conclusions about whether agr-targeted prevention can meaningfully alter long-term AD trajectories.

label: baseline
text: This proposal investigates whether the disease phase at which a brief, low-dose local intervention is delivered materially alters the durability of remission in atopic dermatitis, independent of total drug exposure. Using an MC903-induced mouse model engineered to produce a controlled flare–remission–relapse cycle, we will define biologically grounded disease phases based on transepidermal water loss and clinical scores, distinguishing a mid-flare plateau from an early-remission phase. We will test the falsifiable hypothesis that delivering an identical short course of a topical immune-axis intervention, such as a JAK inhibitor, during early remission produces at least a two-fold increase in median time to relapse relative to delivery during mid-flare. Three primary arms—mid-flare-timed, early-remission-timed, and a pragmatic fixed-schedule or threshold-reactive comparator—will be compared against a vehicle control, with time to relapse as the pre-specified primary outcome. Targeted single-cell RNA sequencing of extreme-phenotype lesions and a parallel skin-on-chip model will help interpret why timing does or does not confer leverage. A positive result would reveal an underused control lever for anchoring remission, whereas a negative result would establish that dose and basic monitoring dominate, providing a clear, decision-relevant answer either way.

label: baseline
text: Atopic dermatitis (AD) frequently relapses after treatment withdrawal, yet clinicians lack skin-level biomarkers that predict which patients will maintain remission beyond generic measures of reduced inflammation and restored barrier function. This proposal tests whether a mechanistically specific tolerance–resident memory T cell (TRM) axis, capturing tuned keratinocyte danger responses and regulatory, barrier-supporting resident immune programs, improves prediction of AD relapse beyond transepidermal water loss (TEWL) and Staphylococcus aureus load. We first mine existing human and mouse AD datasets to define generic disease axes as controls and to derive a pre-specified, low-dimensional tolerance–TRM score, testing whether it is partially independent of overall inflammation and preferentially enriched in long-term remitters. We then conduct a focused relapse experiment in an AD-like mouse model with S. aureus dysbiosis, applying a short course of anti-Th2 or JAK inhibitor therapy and comparing nested predictive models for relapse timing and severity. Finally, a minimal skin-on-chip system probes causal levers, such as commensal timing and AhR activation, that install this desirable state. The results will clarify whether a skin-intrinsic resolution signature can guide tapering decisions and adjunct therapies, or whether generic normalization suffices.

label: baseline
text: In atopic dermatitis, keratinocytes overproduce alarmins such as TSLP and IL-33 while barrier and antimicrobial functions deteriorate, yet it remains unclear whether tuning upstream sensing pathways can improve these outcomes beyond what clinically validated cytokine blockade already achieves. This proposal poses an explicit comparative question: can defined upstream inputs—calcium entry via STIM/Orai and TRPV4, redox and NRF2 signaling, and NLRP3 activity—drive keratinocytes toward transcriptional states with lower alarmins and clinically acceptable barrier and antimicrobial function that match or surpass direct IL-4Rα/IL-13 inhibition? Using stratified human keratinocyte air–liquid interface cultures exposed to defined atopic cytokine milieus, we will apply upstream perturbations alongside downstream blockade comparators and map alarmin, barrier, antimicrobial, and proliferation outputs at single-cell resolution across multiple timepoints. We will anchor acceptability to clinically grounded reference bands derived from cytokine-blockade responses, then test whether any upstream regime reaches or exceeds these benchmarks. Promising regimes will undergo conditional dynamic characterization with genetically encoded calcium and redox sensors and limited in vivo validation. Regardless of outcome, the study delivers a strategic answer about whether keratinocyte-intrinsic sensing represents a therapeutically useful control point.

label: baseline
text: Atopic dermatitis patients treated with IL-4/IL-13 blockade frequently show incomplete responses, with residual barrier fragility and itch that current adjunct strategies address unsystematically. This proposal develops a patient-anchored, stratified framework to define the residual keratinocyte and immune programs that persist after Th2 pathway suppression and to determine in which residual profiles purine or sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) targeting adjuncts are the rational choice relative to other adjunct classes. In a core stage, we will combine targeted single-cell RNA sequencing with protein and metabolite panels from dupilumab partial responders and controlled responders to define endotypes as stable transcriptional and receptor wiring patterns rather than transient ligand elevations, and then test endotype-guided adjunct shortlists in lean two- and three-dimensional keratinocyte models under Th2-blocked, stressed conditions using barrier, danger, and pruritogen readouts. Purinergic- or S1P-dominant endotypes will be declared only when both biopsy-derived wiring and in vitro adjunct performance converge. An optional second stage will use a simple innervated, microbiome-competent co-culture to dissect neuro-immune coupling in a single endotype where purine or S1P mechanisms remain ambiguous. This staged design yields a practical residual endotype map and endotype-specific adjunct priorities, directly informing rational combination therapy for dupilumab partial responders.

label: baseline
text: Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) inhibitors rapidly suppress the itch, inflammation, and barrier dysfunction of atopic dermatitis, yet symptoms frequently return once treatment ceases, and it remains unclear which tissue compartment must stay JAK1-suppressed to prevent relapse. This proposal introduces a spatial minimal-controller test in which an in vivo JAK1-OFF background is established through systemic or broad topical inhibition, optionally combined with keratinocyte- or neuron-specific conditional knockouts, and small JAK1-ON islands are then restored in one compartment at a time. Under a standardized submaximal relapse drive held constant across animals and regions, we ask whether atopic dermatitis-like lesions preferentially reappear within these islands compared with surrounding suppressed skin. Outcomes are assessed across four domains—skin barrier integrity, immune infiltrate and cytokine composition, neuro-immune activation and scratching behavior, and site-matched microbiome shifts—using standard, spatially resolved readouts. Preferential relapse within keratinocyte, neuronal, combined, or immune-intact islands would identify the compartment sufficient to re-ignite multi-axis disease, distinguishing single-compartment, distributed, and immune-dominant control. Focused single-cell profiling and innervated skin-on-chip models will resolve ambiguous patterns. By reframing the question from whether JAK1 matters to where it must remain suppressed, this tractable framework directly informs whether skin-restricted, neuro-immune, or systemic JAK1 targeting is required to sustain remission.

label: baseline
text: Atopic dermatitis (AD) arises from coupled interactions among skin barrier dysfunction, type-2 immune skewing, and Staphylococcus aureus colonization, yet whether the temporal order of these insults determines disease trajectory remains untested. This proposal asks whether biologically plausible differences in the order and coarse timing of barrier injury, IL-4/13 exposure, and S. aureus colonization can bias an AD-like skin circuit into distinct, semi-stable regimes that resist strong but non-destructive late interventions, providing evidence for timing-sensitive hysteresis rather than effects of intensity or chronicity alone. We will use a three-phase, stepwise-complexity program on 3D epidermal-equivalent and organ-on-chip platforms, beginning with keratinocyte and myeloid constructs, then adding live S. aureus, and finally incorporating Th2 T cells and an optional neuronal compartment. Simple barrier, immune, and microbial indices will classify system regimes, and pre-validated, non-destructive barrier-repair and antimicrobial interventions will test reversibility, with acute controls and ordinary differential equation models distinguishing true multistability from slow kinetics or irreversible damage. Selected regimes will be profiled by single-cell transcriptomics to identify cellular memory states. Robust timing principles will then be validated in barrier-defective AD-prone mouse models. The anticipated outcome is regimen-level timing strategies, such as barrier-first versus antimicrobial-first sequencing, grounded in mechanistic understanding of when the coupled barrier–immune–microbiome system is most susceptible to flare-like regimes.

label: baseline
text: This proposal develops a bounded-capacity, adipocyte-localized hormone source for the long-term management of body weight, designed as a hybrid homeostat that couples an embedded biological actuator with external, clinician-directed control. The system uses mature-adipocyte–biased promoters to restrict expression of a single well-characterized effector—a GLP-1 analogue, an FGF21 analogue, or a GLP-1/FGF21 fusion—to subcutaneous white adipocytes following one-time AAV or lipid nanoparticle delivery. Expression is governed by a strictly off-by-default, exogenous ligand–inducible transcriptional layer, so that hormone output can be raised or lowered over months by titrating an inducer according to simple clinical measures such as weight, BMI, and waist circumference. Potency and half-life are tuned so that even maximal induction keeps circulating levels within established therapeutic windows, ensuring bounded exposure and reversibility on both fast (inducer withdrawal) and slow (basal leak) timescales. The central hypothesis is pharmacokinetic and adherence-related rather than mechanistic: a distributed, low-output source may yield flatter plasma profiles with lower peak concentrations and improved tolerability relative to bolus injections or constitutive liver-directed gene therapy. We will test this in animals by comparing weekly peptide injections, liver-directed gene therapy, and the adipocyte-local inducible system at matched average exposure, evaluating defended weight, fat mass, hormone pharmacokinetics, and side-effect proxies to determine whether this anatomical and control topology improves weight control and tolerability.

label: baseline
text: We propose to develop and evaluate a minimal, adiposity-referenced control rule for GLP-1 maintenance dosing that functions as a simple physiological thermostat. In this framework, a smoothed estimate of body-fat status—derived from frequent home weights anchored by periodic clinic measures of body composition and waist circumference—serves as the state variable, and drug dose is adjusted to keep adiposity within a jointly agreed clinical target band. The rule is deliberately austere: at fixed intervals the dose is held at the lowest effective level when adiposity is within band, stepped up when it drifts persistently above, and reduced or paused when it falls below, with automatic re-engagement on subsequent upward drift and an explicit non-response condition that halts escalation near the maximal tolerated dose. This approach targets two persistent limitations of GLP-1 therapy: weight regain following fixed-course cessation and unnecessarily high chronic dosing under indefinite maximal regimens. We will test the rule in a multi-year randomized controlled trial in patients who have already achieved initial weight loss, comparing the thermostat against a fixed low-maintenance dose and an optional fixed-course/stop arm. Primary outcomes include average adiposity, regain fraction, cumulative drug exposure, side-effect burden, and patient-reported acceptability. The decisive contrast is whether explicit fat-referenced feedback yields lower adiposity at similar or reduced drug exposure without added harms, thereby demonstrating clinical value beyond simply continuing therapy at a constant dose.

label: baseline
text: We propose a macroencapsulated endocrine cell therapy that delivers metabolic hormones in a state-selective, temporally integrated manner to improve the safety of anti-obesity interventions. The engineered cells sense plasma free fatty acids through a fatty-acid-responsive module that drives a synthetic transcription factor, while a glucose-responsive promoter imposes a fed-state veto that prevents activation during fasting or illness, when elevated fatty acids reflect adaptive catabolism. A slowly accumulating integrator protein couples these inputs so that hormone output ramps only when high fatty acids and fed-range glucose persist over hours to days, filtering out transient metabolic noise and tapering gradually when conditions resolve. Downstream, an asymmetric dual-output circuit prioritizes secretion of an energy-expenditure-enhancing FGF21-like hormone, with a weaker, higher-threshold anorectic signal engaged only under more severe or sustained overload. Because each module—fatty-acid sensing, glucose-responsive repression, long-lived integrators, and macroencapsulation—has been demonstrated independently, the design is buildable and tunable through promoter strength, protein half-life, and activation thresholds. This controller can be directly benchmarked against instantaneous fatty-acid-only circuits to test whether combined fed-state and chronicity gating widens the therapeutic window, offering an incremental but clinically relevant advance in synthetic metabolic hormone delivery.

label: baseline
text: Melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R) neurons in the paraventricular hypothalamus (PVH) are central regulators of energy balance, yet they are anatomically heterogeneous and coupled to sympathetic and counter-regulatory systems, leaving unclear whether a simple, sustained bias in their output could safely lower defended body fat. This project builds an anatomically resolved, long-timescale perturbation map of projection-defined PVH MC4R subcircuits to test whether any subpopulation supports a stable "sweet spot" of tonic activation that reduces defended adiposity while preserving core starvation defenses and maintaining acceptable cardiovascular risk. In diet-induced obese animals, we will partition PVH MC4R neurons into two or three projection-defined classes, including spinal-projecting sympathetic premotor cells and brainstem-projecting neurons, and impose chronic, graded chemogenetic activation at several discrete gain levels over weeks. After the network adapts, we will quantify outcomes across three axes: defended adiposity set point, integrity of low-fat defense under caloric restriction, and cardiovascular and autonomic cost. For each projection, we will determine whether a contiguous, clinically relevant trade-off window exists in which adiposity is meaningfully reduced, starvation defenses remain functional, and cardiovascular changes stay within a predefined safety envelope. The resulting dose-response profiles will provide go/no-go guidance on whether projection-targeted tonic PVH MC4R bias is a rational basis for a synthetic anti-obesity homeostatic layer or whether more complex, state-dependent strategies are fundamentally required.

label: baseline
text: Maladaptive adipocyte hypertrophy, characterized by insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, and hypoxia in expanded white adipose tissue, remains difficult to target selectively with gene-based therapies because existing adipocyte promoters cannot distinguish pathologically stressed cells from healthy or benignly remodeling ones. This proposal aims to determine whether promoter-level regulatory logic can materially improve the selective sensing of maladaptively hypertrophic, stressed white adipocytes. We will design and benchmark two promoter classes: synthetic constructs combining adipocyte identity motifs with stress-responsive elements, and minimal native enhancers of genes selectively upregulated in inflamed, insulin-resistant adipocytes, comparing both against standard promoters and inflammation-inducible modules. Using human and mouse adipocyte models, we will systematically vary hypertrophy, receptor activation, inflammatory and hypoxic signals, mechanical cues, and beiging stimuli, employing reporters with defined kinetics to bias toward chronic rather than transient stress. Top candidates will be validated in vivo across diet-induced obesity, cold exposure, drug-induced expansion, systemic infection, and weight-loss paradigms, using a predefined pathologic selectivity index to quantify performance. Whether synthetic constructs, native enhancers, or neither prove superior, the study will deliver rigorous quantitative metrics and datasets to guide the design of future adipose-targeted gene circuits.

label: baseline
text: This proposal addresses a central design question for chronic soft neural probes: once mechanical compliance and miniaturization are optimized, does any realistically manufacturable, fouling-surviving surface topography improve neuronal integration enough to justify added fabrication complexity? We adopt a two-stage, explicitly gated approach that treats mechanics and size as fixed and topography as a candidate secondary lever. In Stage 1, we fabricate smooth control and engineered multiscale surfaces on a single probe platform and matched coupons, expose them to serum, brain extracellular matrix, and short-term implantation, and quantify band-limited power spectral density and curvature statistics in biologically relevant scale bands of roughly 100 to 500 nanometers and 1 to 5 micrometers. A predefined persistence threshold determines whether measurable geometric distinctions survive fouling; if they collapse, testing stops. If distinctions persist, Stage 2 chronically compares the most robust roughness design against smooth zones within the same animals, measuring neurite versus glial process density, encapsulation architecture, single-unit yield, signal quality, and, where applicable, optical stimulation dose. An a priori effect-size threshold determines whether topography is a validated design axis. Either outcome yields actionable guidance for probe engineering.

label: baseline
text: Chronic optogenetic probes combine light delivery with electrical recording, yet it remains unclear whether the photonic and thermal dose experienced by the electrode–tissue interface itself contributes to long-term single-unit instability, independent of mechanical mismatch and surface chemistry. This proposal isolates that variable by using a model-guided spatial offset between the optical outlet and the recording electrode, allowing the neural modulation near the electrode to be held constant while systematically varying the photon fluence and temperature rise at the metal surface. We will first build coupled optical–thermal models of a soft optrode in cortex to identify offset positions that preserve local firing-rate modulation while producing at least a two- to three-fold change in surface fluence or a 0.5–1 °C change in temperature, proceeding to fabrication only if such regimes exist. We will then fabricate otherwise-identical co-located and offset optrodes on a common flexible platform, implant them, and titrate light power in vivo to match local neural modulation across designs. Over weeks to months we will track single-unit yield and stability, impedance and noise, and endpoint histology, with intermittent micro-thermometry validating modeled thermal contrasts. Whether or not offset designs age more favorably, the outcome will decisively establish whether electrode-local photonic stress is a primary or secondary design concern for durable optogenetic implants.

label: baseline
text: Conductive polymer coatings based on PEDOT are widely used for neural electrode interfaces, yet their long-term electrochemical stability remains inconsistent, and the specific role of dopant mobility in this aging process is poorly resolved because it is typically confounded by tissue mechanics and geometry. This proposal establishes a minimal, controlled in vitro platform to mechanistically test how dopant mobility shapes the trajectory and variance of PEDOT electrochemical aging. Two closely matched PEDOT films on planar microelectrodes will be compared: one with covalently tethered anionic dopants acting as fixed charges, and one with conventional large but only sterically confined mobile dopants, prepared to have similar thickness, roughness, and mechanical support so that dopant mobility is the primary systematic difference. Films will be aged in defined saline and protein-containing electrolytes under standardized and accelerated pulsing protocols, with electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, charge-storage capacity, and redox measurements tracked over time, emphasizing drift and replicate variance rather than end-point means. Orthogonal assays of swelling, mass uptake, and microstructure, including optionally labeled dopants, will distinguish dopant redistribution from swelling or fouling effects. The hypothesis is that tethered dopants will not prevent over-oxidation but will stabilize local ion transport, yielding narrower distributions and slower drift. Whether differences are significant or negligible, the results will clarify whether dopant immobilization is a first-order design lever, directly guiding investment in future neural interface coatings.

label: baseline
text: Chronic intracortical neural interfaces suffer from mechanical mismatch and foreign body responses, and while both soft, low-tether designs and liquid-infused (SLIPS-like) lubricated surfaces have been proposed to mitigate these problems, existing comparisons confound softness, geometry, lubrication, and surgical variability across different animals. This proposal introduces a twin-probe assay that isolates surface lubrication as the single designed variable by co-implanting two nominally identical soft shanks through the same craniotomy, one with a fluorinated liquid-infused outer layer and one with the same solid chemistry but no infused liquid. Both shanks carry matched on-shank strain traces and electrodes, enabling within-animal, within-site differential readouts of cyclic strain, electrode impedance, and noise over time, with common-mode confounds largely cancelled and endpoint histology characterizing local glial density, vascular markers, and scar thickness. Sustained divergence in these differential measures would indicate a genuine, quantifiable chronic benefit from lubrication beyond softness, whereas rapid convergence would suggest that any advantage is purely acute or negligible. The design accepts an irreducible ambiguity between insertion-phase and chronic micromotion effects but substantially improves attribution over current practice. Built from established soft two-state backbones, SLIPS-like coatings, and standard co-implantation methods, the approach offers clear falsification criteria and readily generalizes to larger arrays and primate models.

label: baseline
text: Chronic neural implants degrade over time due to persistent gliosis and recording drift, yet it remains unclear whether ATP/ADP-mediated purinergic signaling continues to drive these failures once state-of-the-art mechanical, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory strategies are already in place. This proposal aims to determine whether purinergic signaling is a significant and usefully targetable design lever for next-generation implants, delivering a clear attribution answer and decision framework rather than assuming a new coating is warranted. In a first stage, we will quantify the maximum plausible impact of purinergic modulation using deliberately simple perturbations, including microglia-specific and global P2Y12/P2X7 knockout or antagonist models alongside local, time-limited delivery of receptor antagonists or soluble ectonucleotidases near best-in-class implants. These experiments will assess both benefits, such as reduced glial sheath formation and improved signal stability, and costs, including disruption of microglial surveillance and neuroprotection, yielding one of three decision outcomes. Only if a large, spatially localized benefit with manageable side effects emerges will we pursue an exploratory, tightly constrained second stage to translate the effect into a device-local, ATP/ADP-reducing surface. By design, the program stops when the biology indicates that purinergic modulation is weak, harmful, or better addressed systemically, providing the community with actionable guidance regardless of outcome.

label: baseline
text: Chronic neural implants fail in part because reactive oxygen species contribute to oxidative tissue damage, glial encapsulation, neuronal loss, and signal degradation, yet it remains unclear how spatially confined antioxidant action must be to improve long-term outcomes. This proposal addresses that design question directly by asking over what spatial range surface-anchored antioxidant activity needs to operate to meaningfully influence implant performance, rather than pursuing novel antioxidant chemistries. Using established, translatable technologies such as immobilized ceria-like particles and antioxidant polymers, we will fabricate three matched coatings on otherwise identical probes: a high-capacity, surface-anchored, locally acting coating; a diffuse coating with equivalent total capacity but broader tissue distribution; and an inert control. Reaction–diffusion estimates will guide formulation to ensure physically realistic near-surface reductions in oxidative markers, and in vivo studies will quantify spatially resolved oxidative damage and glial phenotypes at early time points and encapsulation, neuronal survival, and recording performance at chronic time points. Comparing confined versus diffuse antioxidant action against inert controls will distinguish whether total antioxidant dose or fine spatial confinement governs outcomes. The results will provide quantitative design guidance indicating whether interface-proximal redox engineering warrants prioritization or whether effort should shift to other stabilization strategies.

label: baseline
text: Glioblastoma tumor–associated microglia and macrophages (TAMs) sustain immunosuppression in part through STAT3 signaling, yet current STAT3-targeting therapies lack the specificity to spare homeostatic microglia and peripheral myeloid cells. This proposal tests whether regulatory elements exist that are sufficiently biased toward GBM TAMs to enable selective, transcriptionally targeted STAT3 inhibition with acceptable off-target activity. In Phase I, we will construct a comparative regulatory atlas of myeloid states using single-cell RNA-seq and chromatin accessibility data spanning GBM TAMs, healthy microglia, non-tumor CNS inflammatory conditions such as stroke, viral infection, and demyelination, and peripheral monocytes and macrophages. Candidate promoters and enhancers with consistent TAM-biased activity will be quantified for effect size, validated in reporter assays across primary myeloid cells, and benchmarked in vivo through systemic delivery across multiple pathologies. Contingent on identifying elements that meet predefined specificity thresholds, Phase II will build a minimal STAT3-suppressing cassette driven by the best regulatory module and benchmark it against state-of-the-art STAT3 antisense platforms for knockdown depth, selectivity, and toxicity. By making the existence and magnitude of GBM TAM-biased regulation the central testable hypothesis, this work will define whether transcriptional engineering can meaningfully widen the therapeutic window or whether delivery optimization remains the more rational strategy.

label: baseline
text: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains difficult to control at its infiltrative margin, where peritumoral astrocytes lose homeostatic functions—particularly glutamate uptake via EAAT2 and potassium buffering via Kir4.1—while adopting a reactive, scar-forming phenotype that promotes hyperexcitability, seizures, and tumor invasion. This proposal tests whether restoring a single core astrocyte function, glutamate and potassium buffering, at the resection margin can measurably reduce GBM invasion and network hyperexcitability beyond what mechanical extracellular matrix stiffening and CHI3L1/STAT3 pathway inhibition achieve alone. We will implement a minimal, single-axis intervention driving EAAT2-like and Kir4.1-like expression in astrocytes using an AAV construct under an astrocyte-biased promoter, avoiding complex synthetic circuitry. In GBM–neuron–astrocyte co-cultures, organotypic slices, and rodent GBM models exposed to tumor-like cytokine pressure, we will compare this restoration head-to-head and in combination with stiff hydrogels and CHI3L1/STAT3 inhibition, measuring invasion distances, extracellular glutamate and potassium dynamics, neuronal firing, seizure-like discharges, and tumor regrowth. Both outcomes are informative: a positive result identifies astrocyte buffering restoration as a concrete, transplantable lever for edge control, whereas a negative result quantitatively falsifies a central astrocyte-centric premise and redirects the field toward simpler mechanical or tumor-targeted strategies. This falsifiable, lab-ready design uses standard neuro-oncology tools to resolve whether re-installing lost astrocyte homeostasis is a meaningful third therapeutic axis.

label: baseline
text: This proposal presents a focused, two-step mechanistic study examining whether human oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC) migration can be predictably steered through defined adhesion parameters, using a motor–clutch framework relevant to white-matter invasion in glioblastoma. In the first step, we construct a minimal pair of brain-relevant substrates—myelin-mimetic aligned microtracks and softer, isotropic lesion-mimetic pads with distinct extracellular matrix compositions—and empirically characterize the adhesion systems OPCs use in these contexts, profiling integrins, CD44, and focal adhesion components while measuring traction forces, migration speed, and dwell time. These data are used to place OPCs qualitatively on a simple motor–clutch model and to generate a model-based prediction of how altering a chosen adhesion axis should shift their behavior. In the second step, we perform a single, quantifiable perturbation—either tuning integrin density/affinity or introducing a nanoscale glycocalyx layer that modifies force transfer—and test in paired assays whether OPC persistence and lesion dwell change as predicted, and whether effects differ between tracks and pads. The primary readout is whether scalar tuning of one parameter moves OPCs along the predicted motor–clutch branch in a substrate-dependent manner. Positive results would establish that OPC surface mechanics are rationally tunable and justify progression to organotypic, multi-parameter models for courier-based therapies, whereas negative results would constrain future design by demonstrating that naïve single-axis tuning is insufficient for robust navigation control.

label: baseline
text: Glioblastoma (GBM) grows within the rigid confines of the skull, generating chronic mechanical compression and solid stress that tumor cells decode through PC1/Piezo1-mediated mechanotransduction and downstream signaling. This proposal reframes intracranial compression not as an abstract force but as a definable transcriptional program, and seeks to exploit it as an intrinsic, skull-linked control lever for therapy. We will first establish a discovery framework using chronic three-dimensional spheroid compression models to identify genes that are reproducibly induced by sustained mechanical load and whose induction depends on PC1/Piezo1 activity while remaining minimally responsive to hypoxia, cytokines, or stiffness alone. This compression program will be mapped in vivo across intracranial versus extracranial GBM and non-neoplastic brain injury models to characterize its spatial and contextual specificity. We will then repurpose one or a small panel of native, compression-inducible promoters within a GBM-biased delivery backbone to drive a single suicide or cell-cycle arrest effector, so that compression-adapted tumor cells self-eliminate. By combining GBM-preferential transduction with compression-dependent promoter activation, the system implements a conjunctive, partially specific logic linking tumor identity and mechanical state. The primary product is a validated map of the chronic-compression program, with the suicide switch serving as a concrete demonstration that a pro-tumor mechanical adaptation can be converted into a pressure-linked therapeutic vulnerability.

label: baseline
text: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains incurable in part because rare, plastic tumor cells escape treatment and drive relapse, and while direct conversion of GBM cells into non-proliferative neuron-like states is a promising strategy, its durability is unknown. This project asks a tightly defined question: after best-available GBM→neuron conversion, what is the frequency of cells that can still form tumors, and do these rare escapees converge on a discrete, targetable axis? Using two leading conversion paradigms—transcription-factor-based (NGN2 with SOX11 or NeuroD1) and microRNA-based (miR-9/9* with miR-124)—applied across multiple human patient-derived xenograft models, we will barcode individual cells and link a reprogramming reporter to distinguish genuinely converted from non-converted populations. Sorted fractions will undergo high-n limiting-dilution orthotopic transplantation to quantify tumor-initiating cell frequency, establishing a rigorous upper bound on relapse-capable cells. Escape tumors will be profiled with a focused panel to test reactivation of candidate stemness and chromatin axes, followed by a prospective causal test in which SOX2/OLIG2 are suppressed during and after conversion. If suppression collapses tumorigenicity, we identify an actionable therapeutic target; if not, we obtain an equally informative result redirecting the field toward delivery and safety.

label: baseline
text: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) lacks targeted therapies, motivating strategies that concentrate cytotoxic drugs at disease sites while sparing normal tissue. This proposal develops an intraductal chemotherapy platform that exploits mammary duct anatomy as the primary source of selectivity, delivering high drug concentrations to the ductal epithelium and early invasive fronts with minimal systemic exposure. Within this route, we treat pH-responsiveness as an empirically testable enhancement rather than an assumed benefit, directly comparing three intraductal regimens: free drug, a pH-insensitive controlled-release depot, and a mildly pH-responsive depot tuned to release faster in the acidic tumor microenvironment. Using rodent models of ductal carcinoma in situ and early invasive TNBC, we will evaluate each formulation by therapeutic index, quantifying tumor control against damage to normal ductal epithelium and periductal stroma, with coarse pH measurements providing supportive interpretive context rather than serving as a hard design requirement. The central decision rule retains pH gating only if it yields clear, reproducible gains in tumor-versus-normal selectivity, otherwise advancing the simpler depot. This outcome-driven framework establishes when microenvironment-responsive features add value beyond anatomical targeting, offering a parsimonious, laboratory-ready approach generalizable to other local therapies.

label: baseline
text: This proposal develops a staged, phenotype-first classifier to determine whether triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) constitutes a distinct fate-response class under a validated non-thermal ultrasound "mechanoptosis" regimen, relative to non-TNBC breast cancers and normal mammary epithelial cells. In the first phase, a panel of TNBC lines, non-TNBC (ER+, HER2+) lines, and at least one normal epithelial line will be exposed to a single published ultrasound protocol in standard two-dimensional culture, and each line will be assigned to pre-specified outcome categories—acute death, durable clonogenic failure, or recovery—using apoptosis markers, growth curves, and clonogenic assays. We will test whether TNBC lines cluster together in outcome space more tightly than with other tumors and distinctly from normal cells, benchmarking against simple predictors such as tumor-versus-normal status and baseline proliferation. Only if a TNBC-specific or TNBC-enriched response class emerges will a second phase examine candidate mechanotransduction correlates, including Piezo1/2 and YAP/TAZ expression and cortical stiffness, and assess whether the response persists in soft and stiff three-dimensional matrices. This lean, explicitly staged design yields a falsifiable answer about whether TNBC warrants specialized non-ablative ultrasound strategies or fits within generic tumor mechanoptosis frameworks, avoiding unnecessary mechanistic complexity while remaining globally informative.

label: baseline
text: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) remains prone to metastasis, and although matrix stiffness is known to shape tumor cell behavior, it is unclear whether stiffness-controlled mechanosensing and metabolism can be therapeutically exploited without merely redistributing disease between local invasion and distant colonization. This proposal tests the hypothesis that the sequence of soft and stiff mechanical environments—termed stiffness history—imprints distinct metabolic and signaling states, with soft priming generating fatty acid oxidation (FAO)-dependent colonizers, stiff exposure driving ATR–β-catenin-mediated epithelial-mesenchymal transition and immune remodeling, and integrin β1 acting as a context-dependent node whose inhibition may help or harm. In a first tier, TNBC cells will be exposed to defined stiffness histories in tunable 3D hydrogels, profiled for FAO flux, ATR–β-catenin activation, integrin status, and EMT phenotype, and transferred into secondary niche mimics to assess colonization fitness and responses to targeted modulation. Only if narrow, favorable intervention windows emerge will a second tier evaluate peri-operative FAO (with optional ATR-axis) inhibition in orthotopic models with characterized mechanical baselines. This staged, falsifiable design will clarify how stiffness history governs metastatic behavior and define whether short, timed metabolic intervention can neutralize soft-primed colonizers. The outcome will either identify a targeted strategy for mechanically defined TNBC subsets or establish why stiffness-based trapping cannot serve as a safe, global therapeutic lever.

label: baseline
text: LINE-1 retrotransposition depends on ORF1p condensates that concentrate nucleic-acid substrates, yet it remains untested whether exogenous nucleic acids can meaningfully compete with endogenous L1 substrates within these condensates in living cells. This proposal develops a minimal, stepwise in-cell framework to determine whether added exogenous load produces a sharp, ORF1p-specific change in how condensates handle endogenous L1 substrates, or only a smooth, bulk-like modulation. Using short fluorescently labeled L1-like and length- and chemistry-matched control probes introduced at graded doses, we will measure condensate partitioning by quantitative imaging and functional consequences with a validated retrotransposition reporter, generating a combined load–partition–retrotransposition surface. Specificity will be established through ORF1p mutants with altered nucleic-acid binding, ORF1p-negative cells, and comparison to other RNP granules, while innate immune activation is monitored and kept sub-threshold. The central goal is to identify whether a discrete, non-linear competition regime exists in which exogenous substrates override ORF1p's cis bias and markedly alter retrotransposition. Only if such a regime emerges will we extend the analysis to mitotic chromatin docking and genome instability, interpreting these phenotypes against the quantitative surface. This parsimonious design cleanly distinguishes a specific condensate gating window from generic nucleic-acid stress.

label: baseline
text: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) exhibits intrinsic features—elevated polyunsaturated fatty acid content, labile iron, and redox stress—that may predispose it to ferroptotic cell death, yet current sonodynamic ferroptosis platforms rely on large, poorly translatable perturbations. This proposal tests a single decisive question: whether a clinically plausible, sub-cavitation ultrasound regimen combined with a modest, single-axis ferroptosis perturbation (partial GPX4 inhibition or mild glutathione depletion) creates a meaningful selectivity window between TNBC and matched normal mammary cells. We will first define one or two ultrasound protocols that produce measurable but sublethal stress without overt cavitation, thermal ablation, or dominant necrosis. We will then titrate a single ferroptosis axis across a dose range, with and without ultrasound, in TNBC and matched normal epithelial and stromal cells, using lipid peroxidation markers, ferrostatin-1 and iron-chelator rescue, and competing death-pathway readouts to define an effective threshold for entering a ferroptosis-dominant regime. By comparing thresholds across cell types and conditions, we will determine whether ultrasound selectively lowers the ferroptosis threshold in TNBC, yielding a concise, mechanistically interpretable rule about the minimal augmentation required. Promising windows will be confirmed in ex-vivo breast tissue slices. The work clarifies whether a lighter-touch, clinically straightforward ferroptosis strategy is even theoretically achievable.

label: baseline
text: Triple-negative breast cancers with BRCA deficiency and high homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) exhibit pronounced chromosomal instability and DNA-repair defects, yet it remains unknown whether this genomic state produces a reproducible, practically exploitable microenvironmental or surface signature that could safely guide cell-based therapies. This proposal tests, rather than assumes, whether a small set of combined features can distinguish BRCA-deficient/HRD-high tumors from low-HRD triple-negative cancers, other instability-high tumors, and chronically inflamed non-malignant tissues. In a discovery stage, we will use spatial transcriptomics, single-cell RNA and protein profiling, and targeted genomics to jointly map HRD and instability metrics alongside tumor, stromal, and immune states, and search explicitly for low-complexity, temporally robust logic gates that persist under chemotherapy, PARP inhibition, and radiotherapy, benchmarking them against instability-agnostic combinatorial strategies. Only if a clearly discriminative and implementable pattern emerges will a contingent engineering stage build locally delivered CAR T or natural killer cells whose activation logic encodes the identified signature, leveraging the anatomical accessibility of breast lesions to limit off-tumor activity. If no such advantage is found, we will conclude that HRD-anchored gating offers no practical benefit and that HRD status is better used to guide drug combinations with conventional platforms. Either outcome yields a decisive, field-useful answer about whether genomic instability should organize receptor-agnostic targeting in this high-risk subset.

label: baseline
text: This proposal investigates whether subcellular localization, and specifically enzyme-gated access to the plasma membrane, is a dominant lever for widening the therapeutic window of ferroptotic photodynamic therapy in triple-negative breast cancer beyond gains from optimized light delivery, pharmacokinetics, and systemic ferroptosis sensitizers. The work is organized as a two-stage, decision-gated program built on a single porphyrin core. In the first stage, interchangeable targeting motifs bias the photosensitizer toward the plasma membrane, mitochondria, lysosomes, or endoplasmic reticulum, allowing the effect of localization alone on the tumor-versus-normal kill differential to be isolated under clinically realistic superficial conditions with optimized illumination. If membrane localization clearly outperforms other organelles, the second stage compares constitutively membrane-preferring, conventional enzyme-activatable, and polarity-flip constructs in which matrix metalloproteinase cleavage exposes a lipophilic anchor to drive tumor-selective membrane partitioning. Key readouts include normal-tissue tolerance, tumor control, membrane lipid peroxidation, and ferroptosis markers, with pre-cleavage leakiness and enzyme geography treated as primary variables. Regardless of outcome, the study yields actionable design rules for exploiting membrane-localized ferroptotic stress while minimizing normal-tissue toxicity.

label: baseline
text: This proposal establishes a deliberately pessimistic upper bound on how much reactive oxygen species (ROS)-gated erosion of polyethylene glycol (PEG) coatings can alter the adhesion of glyco-decorated vesicles and extracellular vesicles under vascular flow conditions. We construct a kinetic envelope using the fastest reported ROS-cleavable linker chemistries at upper-end physiologic ROS levels, assuming spatially homogeneous exposure to maximize the plausible loss of PEG coverage over both single-vessel transit and cumulative near-wall timescales. We then combine this envelope with the steepest local slope of adhesion versus PEG coverage extracted from existing static adhesion data, yielding a best-case bound on the dynamic adhesion change that deliberately favors the responsive design. This bound is compared against the dynamic range already accessible through static tuning of ligand multivalency and PEG density, and against typical experimental variability under flow. Optional minimal experiments with paired static and dynamic synthetic vesicles, and a strictly secondary extracellular vesicle check, serve only to confirm compatibility with the bound. The expected contribution is a parameter-anchored no-go region showing that ROS-gated masking offers little unique leverage for fast, damage-state-selective vascular adhesion, thereby redirecting future targeting efforts toward more promising encoders.

label: baseline
text: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte (hPSC-CM) grafts hold promise for cardiac repair, but their propensity to generate arrhythmias, particularly under ischemic and catecholaminergic stress, remains a major barrier to clinical translation. This proposal advances an integrated strategy that engineers grafts as quiescent-yet-excitable, energetically buffered follower tissue and deploys them within a pre-specified macro-environment that biases the host ventricle toward electrical dominance. At the cellular level, we implement a minimal, energetically grounded triad of genetic edits: upregulation of the Na⁺/K⁺ pump coupled to enhanced mitochondrial capacity to sustain ionic gradients under stress, elevation of the inward rectifier current to stabilize a negative resting potential, and suppression of pacemaker and Ca²⁺-clock currents to remove intrinsic automaticity while preserving robust host-driven excitation and contraction. In parallel, moderate-sized epicardial patches are placed and coupled to the infarct border zone along a gradual, in silico-defined trajectory that keeps graft–host coupling within a safe conductivity window, ensuring the larger host myocardium remains the dominant electrical sink. We hypothesize that combining pump-metabolic hardening with constrained geometry yields superior robustness, reducing graft-initiated ectopy and limiting propagation of any focal events. Using computational modeling and hPSC-CM engineering with established maturation protocols, we will test whether this approach systematically decouples conduction competence from automaticity and biases the graft–host system toward host control across realistic stress conditions.

label: baseline
text: Engraftment-associated ventricular arrhythmias remain a major barrier to human pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte (hPSC-CM) therapy, arising largely from the immature electrophysiology of graft tissue that permits pacemaker activity, calcium-driven delayed afterdepolarizations, and focal ectopy under permissive source–sink conditions. This project engineers a minimal quiescent-yet-excitable hPSC-CM line by editing three validated ionic determinants: knockout of HCN4 to remove pacemaker current, tuned KCNJ2 (Kir2.1) overexpression to restore adult-like inward-rectifier current and stabilize resting potential near −80 mV, and graded suppression of SLC8A1 (NCX1) to constrain calcium-driven inward current. On a common high-IK1, HCN4-knockout background, we compare a full NCX1 knockout benchmark against a partial NCX1 suppression candidate to determine how much sodium–calcium exchange is compatible with arrhythmia safety while preserving physiological calcium handling. Using detailed electrophysiological and tissue-scale models, engineered in-vitro syncytia challenged with β-adrenergic stimulation, calcium loading, and partial uncoupling, and large-animal or high-fidelity computational benchmarking, we quantify an ignition floor as a measurable graft property. The primary endpoints are engraftment ventricular tachycardia and ectopic burden, with secondary assessment of conduction, contractility, and long-term calcium handling. This lean, implementation-ready study either validates a safe corridor for partial NCX suppression or defines the quantitative boundary justifying full knockout, refining the tradeoff between maximal arrhythmia safety and durable calcium physiology.

label: baseline
text: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte (hPSC-CM) grafts hold promise for treating myocardial injury, but their arrhythmic risk remains a major barrier that cannot be resolved through single-parameter tuning of ionic currents or graft geometry alone. This proposal develops a unified design and deployment framework that treats inward-rectifier potassium current (IK1), sodium-potassium pump activity, and calcium-handling/action potential dynamics as a coupled stability triad, expressed through a small set of measurable composite indices rather than an abstract high-dimensional manifold. On the cellular side, we define a diastolic stability index, a stress–action potential reserve index, and an excitability–contractility index, each computed from detailed models and targeted engineered-tissue experiments across realistic ionic configurations under potassium, ischemia, and adrenergic stress. On the tissue side, we define a patch source–sink index and a substrate-adjusted risk index that link patch mass, conduction velocity, and scar topology to simulated ventricular tachycardia incidence in three-dimensional ventricle models. For both axes we identify risk gradients and derive robust quantitative thresholds separating safe follower behavior from graft-driven arrhythmia, stress-testing these thresholds against heterogeneity and time-varying host–graft coupling. The framework is explicitly falsifiable: it succeeds only if non-obvious, decision-changing thresholds emerge, yielding concise, mechanistically grounded constraints for engineering and deploying host-dominated, IK1-rich grafts safely.

label: baseline
text: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte (hPSC-CM) grafts can be engineered to be quiescent-yet-excitable to reduce arrhythmia risk, yet it remains unclear how far their electrical stabilization can be pushed before conduction and capture are compromised in the hostile early graft–host environment. This proposal develops a focused, quantitative design atlas that anchors on established large-animal constructs—those silencing depolarizing drivers such as funny current, T-type calcium, and sodium-calcium exchange while up-titrating inward-rectifier potassium and sodium-potassium pump activity—and explores small, mechanistically guided perturbations around these origins. Rather than an unconstrained global sweep, we evaluate a local neighborhood in ionic parameter space using multi-scale models spanning single cells, one-dimensional cables, two-dimensional sheets, and simplified border-zone geometries with controlled partial coupling and anisotropy, all probed under catecholamine, ischemia, and pacing stress. Robustness is assessed across optimistic and pessimistic coupling-evolution scenarios to identify safety plateaus rather than knife-edge optima, quantifying capture margin, conduction integrity, and ectopy or reentry propensity. A small set of candidate recipes is then implemented via CRISPR in hiPSC-CMs and validated in engineered tissues with patterned coupling and border-zone geometry using optical mapping and electrophysiology. The result is a compact atlas of one to three static ionic edit recipes, each with quantified safety margins and explicit failure boundaries, directly informing preclinical and clinical graft design.

label: baseline
text: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte (hPSC-CM) grafts promise myocardial regeneration but risk acting as independent arrhythmia sources when transplanted into injured hearts. This proposal seeks to design grafts that electrically integrate and contract in synchrony with host myocardium while remaining passively driven, by explicitly decoupling conduction competence from automaticity at the genetic design stage and verifying safety at the tissue level under adrenergic, ischemic, and electrolyte stress. Rather than exhaustively searching a large design space, we will compare a small number of mechanistically distinct genome-edit programs—ranging from a canonical hard-quiescent line to calcium-preserving and high-conduction-velocity alternatives—within a shared quantitative state-space framework that captures resting membrane potential, sodium channel availability, triggered-activity propensity, and repolarization heterogeneity. Each program will be mapped from single cells to multicellular and tissue models to identify the edit set offering the best trade-off between arrhythmia suppression and graft function for in vivo testing. In parallel, in silico infarct-plus-graft models will optimize delivery geometry and coupling and then test, as a strict yes/no question, whether a thin passive epicardial conductivity layer suppresses residual edge-anchored arrhythmias beyond further tuning of conduction velocity and geometry. Only a reproducible computational benefit would justify focused large-animal validation, ensuring efficient allocation of experimental resources. This hierarchical, comparison-driven strategy identifies the minimal combination of cell edits and tissue-scale adjustments needed for safe, host-driven grafts without unnecessary over-engineering.

label: baseline
text: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte (hPSC-CM) grafts hold promise for cardiac remuscularization after myocardial infarction, but engraftment arrhythmias remain a safety concern even as gene-edited, automaticity-suppressed grafts have markedly reduced lethal events in large animals. It remains unknown how much additional safety margin, if any, could be gained by manipulating host-side electrophysiology once grafts are already edited and standard electrophysiologic care is applied. This project addresses that question by treating the perigraft host border as a control surface and computing a quantitative upper bound on its incremental benefit. We develop a family of two- and three-dimensional infarct-plus-graft models calibrated to experimental and clinical data, set realistic worst-case ectopy burdens from large-animal studies, and perform directed sweeps over pharmacologically plausible ranges of border-zone properties such as sodium recovery, IK1, action potential duration, and coupling under baseline, ischemic, adrenergic, and electrolyte-stress conditions. We then cross-check the most promising model-predicted regimes using transient pharmacologic perturbations in engineered heart tissues and small-animal infarct models challenged with programmed ectopy and stress, tightening or relaxing the modeled bound accordingly. By comparing achievable risk reduction against background post-infarction ventricular arrhythmia risk, the project delivers a model-anchored, experimentally informed estimate of the maximum value of host-side intervention, directly informing go/no-go decisions on complex host-engineering strategies.

label: baseline
text: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte (hPSC-CM) grafts hold promise for myocardial repair, but graft-origin arrhythmias remain a major barrier to clinical translation. This project proposes to co-design the ionic phenotype and graft architecture of hPSC-CM patches, rather than optimizing ion channel edits in isolation, to achieve robust, host-driven electrical integration with minimal arrhythmic burden. Starting from a validated "quiescent-yet-excitable" multi-edit reference line, we will define its residual vulnerabilities—particularly calcium-driven ectopy under catecholaminergic and ischemic stress—and construct a small, structured panel of paired candidate configurations that combine specific ionic and calcium-handling edits with matched patch geometry, delivery pattern, and coupling regimes. Computational models spanning single-cell electrophysiology and calcium handling to tissue-scale graft-host constructs with time-evolving coupling will be used to stress-test each configuration under a standardized battery of β-adrenergic, ischemic, and coupling perturbations, ranking them by arrhythmia robustness and preserved conduction, action-potential, and contractile function. The most promising configuration will be implemented as a single edited hPSC-CM line with a matched delivery protocol and validated through single-cell assays, engineered co-culture tissues, and large-animal infarct models against unedited and reference grafts. By treating ionic design, calcium handling, and coupling geometry as jointly determining arrhythmia risk, this approach offers a practical, laboratory-implementable path to safer, functionally integrated myocardial patches.

label: baseline
text: We propose a minimal, method-agnostic validation tool for in situ cryo-electron tomography that ranks competing reconstructions by their ability to predict a small set of held-out tilts under a shared image formation model. For each tilt series, a single standardized split separates training tilts from held-out tilts, and a common alignment—including any elastic deformation fields—is estimated once and applied identically to every method, so that geometry and alignment errors become shared confounds rather than sources of bias. Each method reconstructs a tomogram from the training tilts, which is then forward-projected to the held-out angles using a shared single-scattering projector with per-tilt contrast transfer function and dose weighting, yielding per-tilt prediction error maps and a simple normalized comparative score. The tool operates directly in tilt space, respecting the anisotropic, missing-wedge-dominated nature of the data, and is explicitly relative: it identifies which reconstruction best predicts unseen measurements rather than estimating absolute truth. A key application is testing whether half-map Fourier shell correlation rankings are trustworthy, since correlation can favor over-regularized or denoised maps that in fact predict new tilts worse. By adding one simple step to existing workflows, this approach provides an experiment-based criterion for algorithm and regularization selection that is easy to implement and hard to misinterpret.

label: baseline
text: Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) is limited by anisotropic sampling arising from the restricted tilt range and the resulting missing wedge, which can make certain structural features irrecoverable regardless of the reconstruction algorithm used. This proposal develops a minimal, geometry-first validation rule that determines whether specific structural aspects of oriented features—such as membrane thickness, filament twist, or complex asymmetry—are in principle recoverable given the acquisition geometry. The method relies on only two orientation angles per feature direction, the angle to the tilt axis and the angle to the nearest missing-wedge boundary, together with a coarse global anisotropy summary, deliberately avoiding tensor calculations or detailed thickness models. Using controlled simulations of filaments and membranes across orientations and signal-to-noise levels, alongside a small set of real datasets with known ground truth, we will calibrate empirical orientation bands that classify each feature direction as safe, caution, or forbidden for structural interpretation. An optional qualitative flag will highlight cases where geometry-limited directions nonetheless display strong fine-scale structure, indicating high risk of denoiser-induced hallucination. The result is a compact, reconstruction-agnostic, and shareable look-up chart that integrates easily into existing pipelines. This validation layer will help experimentalists make principled decisions about what in situ cryo-ET data can legitimately support.

label: baseline
text: In situ cryo–electron tomography is increasingly used to resolve macromolecular structures within cells, yet the field lacks standardized procedures for validating and comparing reconstruction quality across imaging centers. This proposal develops a minimal, laboratory-ready protocol for cross-center benchmarking that uses standard internal complexes, such as ribosomes, nuclear pores, or an added well-characterized virus, as embedded biological rulers evaluated through a single shared sub-tomogram averaging pipeline. Participating centers process common phantoms and internal rulers under harmonized acquisition and metadata standards, then compute plain metrics including global and directional resolution and anisotropy indices to determine whether embedded biology reconstructs comparably across sites. As an optional interpretive layer, physics-informed digital-twin simulations generate coarse envelopes of expected behavior from tilt geometry, contrast transfer function, dose, and thickness, allowing residual cross-center differences to be checked against physically plausible bounds rather than assumed per-complex accuracy. By formalizing ad hoc internal-ruler checks into a reproducible ring-trial design with explicit decision points, the project quantifies whether phantom- and metadata-based standards suffice or whether biological-context validation and simulation-referenced envelopes add measurable diagnostic value. All required components already exist, making the study feasible and directly applicable to multi-center cryo-ET standardization efforts.

label: baseline
text: Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) acquisition planning requires microscopists to balance lamella thickness, tilt range, dose distribution, and missing-wedge anisotropy, yet these trade-offs are often navigated through tacit expertise that is difficult for smaller labs and new users to access. We propose a minimal, rule-based planning tool that makes these trade-offs explicit and quantitative without claiming to predict achievable resolution. Given a proposed lamella thickness, tilt scheme, dose distribution, and basic contrast-transfer settings, the tool computes an idealized Fourier-space coverage map that weights each tilt slab by contrast, dose, and thickness-dependent attenuation, and extracts a small set of interpretable indices, including a thickness-compatible tilt window index, an anisotropy ratio at target resolution bands, and an optional edge-tilt reliance measure. These indices are compared against transparent, editable thresholds derived from established simulation studies and community practice, producing clearly labeled planning-time risk flags, quantitative margins to guidelines, and interactive coverage plots rather than resolution guarantees. A lean, multi-lab validation will correlate computed indices with simple outcome measures, such as fiducial visibility and tomogram anisotropy, to sanity-check the rule set and adjust thresholds where systematically too lax or too pessimistic. By packaging physical constraints and heuristic knowledge into a lightweight, integrable module compatible with tools such as SerialEM, this work lowers the expertise barrier for wedge-aware acquisition planning while explicitly respecting the physical information ceilings that limit cryo-ET.

label: baseline
text: In situ cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) is increasingly used to study macromolecular organization within cells, yet the field lacks standardized benchmarks for evaluating detection, localization, and reconstruction algorithms under realistic imaging constraints. We propose a two-track, wedge-aware benchmarking standard that decouples these algorithmic challenges to address current evaluation gaps. The first track establishes an in-cell detection and localization benchmark based on a mammalian reference line expressing an inducible, genetically encoded rigid multimeric particle of known geometry, from which a canonical dataset is acquired across defined lamella thickness bins and tilt schemes, with population-level ground truth distributions and comprehensive metadata publicly released. The second track uses purified rigid particles and high-fidelity simulations, where exact structures, orientations, and missing-wedge geometries are known, to benchmark wedge-aware reconstruction and anisotropy correction. Benchmark tasks and metrics are explicitly constructed around known failure modes of widely used tools, including thickness-dependent detectability loss, wedge-induced localization bias, denoising-driven artefacts, and anisotropic resolution. By anchoring evaluation in shared canonical datasets rather than requiring each lab to reproduce ground truth, this standard provides a portable, tomography-native reference for validating cryo-ET methods.

label: baseline
text: Template matching (TM) is a central tool for locating macromolecules in cryo-electron tomograms, yet its raw or normalized scores lack a clear absolute meaning, forcing practitioners to rely on heuristic, manually tuned thresholds that vary across datasets and laboratories. This proposal develops a minimal calibration layer that converts existing wedge- and CTF-aware TM scores into tomogram-internal confidence values by building empirical null distributions from random positions and orientations sampled within the same tomogram. In its simplest mode the method assumes an approximately stationary background and uses a single global null, but data-driven diagnostics can trigger optional spatial zoning when thickness gradients, defocus variation, or distinct compartments make backgrounds strongly non-uniform. From these nulls, empirical tail probabilities are computed for each candidate hit and mapped to FDR-controlled acceptance thresholds, yielding interpretable, comparable hit lists across datasets. The framework explicitly guards against realistic failure modes, reporting conservative confidence bounds under target-rich null contamination and emphasizing practically relevant FDR ranges where heavy-tailed clutter makes extreme p-values unreliable. Requiring no phantoms, external standards, or additional physics modeling, this lightweight wrapper around current TM engines is immediately implementable and ready for benchmark validation against high-confidence baselines.

label: baseline
text: Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) has become central to in situ structural biology, yet the field lacks reliable ground truth for validating reconstruction, denoising, and deep-learning algorithms, since simulations capture only modeled physics and biological standards offer real physics but no known structure. We propose a community physical phantom framework built on nanofabricated beacon phantoms—reproducible three-dimensional nanostructures such as layered gratings and dot lattices patterned on Si₃N₄ supports with geometry characterized to nanometer tolerance using orthogonal methods including FIB/SEM cross-sectioning and high-dose tomography. These phantoms will be imaged under realistic cryo-ET conditions across multiple facilities, capturing genuine detector response, noise, charging, beam-induced motion, ice morphology, missing-wedge effects, and thickness-dependent scattering, and paired with their known geometry to form labeled benchmark datasets with defined metrics and standardized training and validation splits.
