By co-locating full-fidelity instrument physics with a fixed, known target, the framework enables objective quantification of feature recovery, direction-dependent resolution, and artefact or hallucination rates, and reveals where simulation-trained methods are over-optimistic. Multi-site contributions will expose how different microscopes distort identical structures, allowing cross-lab algorithm comparison that isolates processing from sample variation. Ultimately, this open benchmark lowers the expertise barrier, letting non-expert laboratories adopt tools with demonstrated robustness on physical ground truth.

label: baseline
text: Cryo-electron tomography refinements in RELION-4.0 rely on internal Bayesian bookkeeping that balances likelihood and priors to weight each tilt, yet current validation tools such as Fourier shell correlation are volumetric and angle-averaged, obscuring direction-specific failure modes. This proposal develops a standardized, projection-domain, angle-resolved validation protocol that operates entirely on the outputs of a single RELION-4.0 refinement, using the per-tilt log-likelihood contributions, residual maps, and per-frequency noise variances that RELION already computes. Rather than introducing a competing noise model, the method normalizes raw per-tilt scores by RELION's own effective information weights, producing an internally consistent, tilt-angle-resolved measure that flags discrepancies between what the model trusts and what actually fits. From these normalized scores the protocol derives tilt-angle performance curves, angle-binned residual summaries, and particle-level consistency measures, together with reproducible decision rules for tilt-range trimming, down-weighting, and particle pruning. It can further apply targeted, RELION-consistent partial refinements to disambiguate suspect tilt bands. Because all required quantities are already present in RELION-4.0, implementation requires only extraction and aggregation, offering a feasible, statistically coherent quality-control standard that advances in situ cryo-ET beyond ad hoc inspection.

label: baseline
text: Subtomogram averaging (STA) in situ cryo-electron tomography campaigns often consume substantial acquisition and computational resources before it becomes clear whether a target can reach the desired resolution, motivating tools that assess feasibility at the planning stage. This proposal aims to develop and validate an orientation-aware feasibility index that predicts, for a given target and acquisition geometry, the probability of achieving a user-specified resolution at or above a minimum particle count. The core of the method is an orientation-uncertainty-aware conditioning scalar that combines a coarse orientation prior for the target class with tilt geometry, lamella thickness, and dose to quantify how well Fourier components near the target resolution are sampled and supported by signal-to-noise ratio, accounting for the missing wedge and high-tilt path length. Conditioning values are aggregated across plausible orientations and calibrated against curated historical STA campaigns to yield an interpretable feasibility band supporting go/no-go decisions. A key aim is to test whether a small set of empirical features can match the fuller conditioning calculation, allowing the tool to be simplified toward a lookup table when justified. Validation will compare predictive performance against thickness-and-tilt heuristics and expert triage using standard classification metrics. The resulting index targets geometry- and dose-driven failures, offering a reproducible, lightweight planning aid that can reduce wasted STA effort in typical laboratory settings.

label: baseline
text: The SUMO-targeted ubiquitin ligase RNF4 has been proposed as a therapeutic effector for clearing SUMO2/3-decorated nuclear polyglutamine aggregates, yet RNF4 also governs PML body homeostasis and SUMO-dependent DNA-protein crosslink repair, raising the question of whether its activity can be enhanced selectively enough to be druggable. This project tests whether a minimally nuclear-biased, wild-type RNF4 admits any practical operating window in which it preferentially clears nuclear polyQ-ATXN7 inclusions while leaving PML bodies and DNA-damage-associated SUMO condensates functionally intact. Using a single, tightly titratable construct with an unmodified SIM array and RING domain and only a modestly strengthened nuclear localization signal, we sample a graded range of expression in a cell model of ATXN7 aggregation. At each level we quantify aggregate clearance, PML and repair sentinel integrity, and, critically, the relative occupancy of tagged RNF4 across aggregates, PML bodies, and repair condensates by live imaging of co-localization and dwell time. Occupancy is calibrated against arsenic-induced PML degradation to ground RNF4 engagement in a physiologic high-stress benchmark. A usable window is defined as substantial aggregate reduction with sentinels within tolerance and preferential, stress-comparable occupancy at aggregates. The outcome will determine whether naïve nuclear enhancement of RNF4 is viable or whether substrate-specific, geometry-gated strategies are fundamentally required.

label: baseline
text: Osteoarthritis (OA) pain is heterogeneous and incompletely explained by classic protein mediators, yet the potential contribution of an oxidized-lipid danger axis remains untested in humans. This proposal poses a narrow, mechanistic question: do some OA patients exhibit a distinct oxidized-lipid–driven endotype, characterized by high oxidized phospholipid and oxidized lipoprotein burden and an oxidized-lipid–sensitive TLR4 signaling component, such that transient perturbation of this chemistry reproducibly reduces pain? We will first define this endotype in patient plasma and, where clinically available, synovial fluid, combining targeted measurement of oxidized lipoproteins with a standardized human TLR4 reporter assay performed with and without an in-vitro oxidized-lipid scavenger to quantify the oxidized-lipid–sensitive fraction of TLR4 agonism. In identified high-burden patients, we will then apply a short-course apoA-I mimetic peptide (D-4F class) as a mechanistic probe, measuring time-linked changes in oxidized-lipid metrics, TLR4 reporter activity, and joint pain, with an optional intra-articular E06-derived feasibility sub-study. A positive result would establish a chemically distinct, potentially druggable stratification axis complementary to existing OA therapies. A negative result would be equally informative, rationally deprioritizing oxidized-lipid danger signaling relative to better-validated nodes and directing resources accordingly.

label: baseline
text: Osteoarthritis (OA) is characterized by frequent discordance between structural joint damage and reported pain, yet it remains unclear which biological mechanisms best explain this decoupling and could guide patient stratification. This proposal aims to conduct a lean, adequately powered study in a pain-discordant OA cohort to comparatively rank a small set of pre-specified mechanistic axes—central sensitization, danger-associated molecular pattern and pattern-recognition receptor (DAMP/PRR) signaling, nerve growth factor/innervation drive, and basic inflammatory cytokines—for their ability to explain pain–structure discordance. High-pain and low-pain patients matched for structural severity, age, sex, and body mass index will be assessed using quantitative sensory testing and compact, analytically robust fluid biomarker panels, each summarized as a composite axis score. Pre-specified regression models will quantify the incremental variance in pain explained by each axis beyond standard clinical stratifiers, using effect sizes and information criteria to identify axes that meet an explicit decision-changing threshold. This design deliberately excludes biopsy, nerve staining, and omics work from the primary phase, reserving them for axes that demonstrate substantial incremental predictive value. The resulting ranking will provide an actionable, quantitative basis for prioritizing mechanistic targets and designing biomarker-enriched trials in OA.

text: Bone marrow lesions (BMLs) in knee osteoarthritis are strongly associated with pain and nociceptive sensitization, yet their underlying biology remains poorly defined and current antiresorptive approaches do not isolate the responsible mechanism. We hypothesize that netrin-1/Unc5B signaling supports the retention and survival of osteoclasts and myeloid cells within subchondral niches corresponding to BMLs, sustaining local inflammation and ongoing nociceptive drive. To test this, we propose a two-tier translational program using systemic netrin-1/Unc5B blockade as a mechanistic probe. In the first tier, a human bridge study in patients undergoing knee arthroplasty will map netrin-1/Unc5B expression and myeloid/osteoclast markers in BML versus non-BML bone and determine whether very short-term antibody dosing perturbs niche composition, providing pharmacodynamic, safety, and tissue-level evidence. In the second tier, a three-to-six-month trial in symptomatic, MRI-confirmed BML-rich osteoarthritis will assess whether antibody-mediated blockade reduces pain, normalizes sensitization, and diminishes BML volume and activity. By linking clinical and imaging outcomes to shifts in myeloid and netrin-axis markers, this program aims to establish the netrin-dependent niche as a specific, druggable organizer of BML-linked pain, distinct from generic osteoclast suppression.

text: Osteoarthritis (OA) pain frequently persists despite modest structural damage, driven in part by central sensitization and by joint tissue senescence that sustains a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), including nerve growth factor and vascular endothelial growth factor. Unlike analgesics or anti-NGF agents that block signals while leaving the source tissue intact, senolytics aim to eliminate senescent chondrocytes, synoviocytes, and osteocytes, potentially producing more durable reductions in peripheral nociceptive drive. This proposal tests a decisive mechanistic question: when a clinically feasible systemic senolytic regimen lowers joint SASP in patients with disproportionate pain and central sensitization, do central pain processing and clinical pain improve in tandem, and by how much. In a mechanistically focused pilot, adults with knee OA (Kellgren–Lawrence 2–3), high pain, and baseline central sensitization will undergo intermittent senolytic dosing with repeated synovial fluid and plasma SASP measurements, quantitative sensory testing, conditioned pain modulation, and clinical pain outcomes, modeling within-person trajectories and responder analyses. A contingent second stage adds targeted imaging and limited biopsies only if meaningful SASP–central coupling emerges. By directly measuring both SASP and central gain, the design yields interpretable go/no-go guidance, distinguishing insufficient SASP change from entrenched, senolysis-resistant central sensitization.

text: Osteoarthritis (OA) remains without effective disease-modifying therapies, and identifying targets that simultaneously address pain and structural progression is a pressing need. The acid-sensing ion channel ASIC3 is activated by the acidic, inflamed microenvironments characteristic of OA joints and has been implicated in both nociception and early structural changes in animal models, yet its relevance in human disease is unclear. This proposal presents a staged target-triage program designed to determine, with minimal but decisive human-tissue experiments, whether ASIC3 is worth pursuing as a dual pain/structure target in OA. In Stage 0, we will map ASIC3 expression, localization, and functional proton responsiveness across human OA cartilage, synovium, subchondral bone, and meniscus, and test whether ASIC3-rich regions co-localize with acidic, metabolically stressed niches and structural pathology. Only if positioning is supportive will Stage 1 proceed to focused explant assays that use gene silencing and pharmacological probes to assess whether ASIC3 perturbation shifts structural markers beneficially relative to an established dual-action comparator. A highly contingent Stage 2 would explore intra-articular blockade should both prior stages and a credible antagonist support it. By grounding decisions in human biology first, this program efficiently clarifies whether ASIC3 merits further investment beyond niche analgesia.

text: Osteoarthritis pain and structural progression are strongly linked to subchondral bone marrow lesions (BMLs), where heightened osteoclast activity drives microdamage, acidic resorption, and release of netrin-1 that promotes aberrant sensory nerve sprouting and nociceptive sensitization. Current anti-resorptive and pain therapies lack joint specificity and risk disrupting normal bone homeostasis when delivered systemically. We propose a systemic prodrug that remains largely inert in circulation and normal tissues but is preferentially activated within active BMLs, delivering a single focused action that dampens osteoclast activity and reduces osteoclast-derived netrin-1 signaling. Lesion-selective activation is achieved through a linker gated by cathepsin K and a secondary lesion-enriched protease, with additional lability under the mildly acidic conditions of resorption lacunae, so that release of the active anti-resorptive/anti-netrin-1 moiety is strongly enriched in osteoclast-rich, high-turnover bone. We will characterize differential activation in BML versus normal bone and evaluate effects on osteoclast markers, netrin-1 levels, nerve density, BML volume, cartilage integrity, and pain behavior in established preclinical models. We further outline a biomarker-enriched trial design selecting patients with MRI-defined symptomatic BMLs and elevated turnover markers, hypothesizing that greatest lesion burden predicts greatest structural and analgesic benefit. This approach tests whether locally reducing osteoclast–netrin-1 coupling is sufficient to improve both structure and pain while preserving systemic homeostasis.

text: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) driven by inflammatory synovitis remains inadequately treated, and although positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) of the α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor offer a plausible anti-inflammatory and analgesic mechanism, it is unclear whether they can produce a quantitatively sufficient effect in human synovium, particularly given the human-specific modulatory gene CHRFAM7A. This proposal centers on a single decisive parameter, the synovial α7-PAM responsiveness index, defined as the percentage suppression of a small NF-κB/NLRP3-linked marker pair at clinically tolerable drug exposure, normalized to the CHRFAM7A/CHRNA7 ratio. In a preliminary phase, a type I α7-PAM will be characterized in human synovial macrophages and fibroblast-like synoviocytes across defined CHRFAM7A/CHRNA7 strata to define concentration-effect relationships and validate a minimal marker pair. Stage 1 will then measure the responsiveness index directly in KOA patients receiving short pre-surgical drug exposure, using synovial fluid, tissue, and serum, with an explicit go/no-go threshold based on the fraction of patients achieving biologically meaningful suppression. If favorable, Stage 2 will conduct a lean 12–16 week phase 2a trial in an inflammatory, macrophage-skewed KOA endotype, testing whether systemic treatment reduces WOMAC pain with concordant serum marker suppression. By concentrating on this quantitative parameter and integrating CHRFAM7A dependence throughout, the program aims to determine cleanly whether α7-PAMs merit further development for osteoarthritis.

text: Osteoarthritis (OA) pain and cartilage catabolism have been mechanistically linked in preclinical models to a pathway in which aggrecanase activity generates the aggrecan 32-mer fragment, which activates TLR2/MyD88 signaling on nociceptors and joint cells; however, the quantitative and therapeutic relevance of this fragment in human disease remains unresolved. This proposal addresses whether the 32-mer is a sufficiently important driver of human OA pain to merit a bespoke systemic therapy, or whether the field should instead prioritize upstream aggrecanase inhibition or generic TLR2 modulation. We propose a disciplined, top-down, two-stage strategy that uses the clinical success or failure of ADAMTS-5 inhibition as the primary gatekeeper. In the first stage, existing or minimally extended ADAMTS-5 inhibitor programs will test whether robust aggrecanase inhibition improves pain and structure when aggrecan fragments are suppressed, and whether 32-mer changes co-move directionally with TLR2-linked biomarkers and pain. If these signals are coherent, a small, phenotyped cohort will receive intra-articular 32-mer neutralization as a local mechanistic stress test of TLR2 signaling and joint nociception. Rather than relying on brittle variance partitioning, interpretation emphasizes biologically plausible directional signals, yielding an actionable go/no-go decision. The project will thus determine whether a 32-mer-responsive patient phenotype exists and where the field should invest next.

text: Osteoarthritis (OA) involves both persistent pain and progressive joint destruction, yet current therapies rarely address the loss of endogenous inhibitory mechanisms that normally prevent minor tissue damage from being amplified into chronic pathology. This proposal reframes OA as a failure of biological "volume control" and systematically tests two independently validated inhibitory layers to determine which dominates in different patient-like endotypes. The first arm reprograms dorsal root ganglion (DRG) macrophages toward a pro-resolving phenotype, using IL-4/IL-10 mimetics or MerTK agonists to normalize nociceptor sensitization while preserving protective pain signaling. The second arm activates intrinsic anti-catabolic and anti-inflammatory transcriptional brakes, including NR4A1 and comparators such as Nrf2 and LXR, in chondrocytes and synovial cells using joint-biased delivery strategies. Through animal OA models, we will apply each intervention alone and in combination to map bidirectional joint-to-DRG and DRG-to-joint signaling, measuring structural, inflammatory, electrophysiological, and behavioral outcomes to identify the dominant brake in each context. This mechanistic mapping will support endotype-based stratification, matching pain-dominant, structure-dominant, or coupled patients to the most appropriate brake-restoring therapy, thereby increasing the likelihood of clinically meaningful benefit.

text: Chronic partial sleep restriction degrades vigilance, yet practical countermeasures such as napping or caffeine are often constrained in operational settings, and it remains unclear whether structured breathing offers advantages over the simplest available intervention. This study evaluates whether a standardized paced slow-breathing micro-break at approximately 0.1 Hz produces an operationally meaningful improvement in psychomotor vigilance compared with equal-duration eyes-closed quiet rest under experimentally imposed sleep restriction. Healthy adults will complete a within-subject crossover in which two matched micro-breaks per critical day, delivered before and during a sustained task period, precede repeated psychomotor vigilance testing. The primary endpoint is reduction in lapses and reaction-time variability in the 30–60 minutes following each break, benchmarked against published caffeine and nap effect sizes so that the design can either detect or rule out practically relevant benefits. Secondary measures include resting heart-rate variability and baroreflex indices during spontaneous breathing, subjective sleepiness, and monitoring of micro-sleep incidence to ensure that any advantage of rest or breathing is not confounded by brief dozing. Rather than adjudicating resonance-specific mechanisms, the study delivers a decision-relevant verdict on whether the added complexity of a cued breathing protocol is justified.

text: Chronic modest sleep loss is common in operational, clinical, and shift-work settings, yet it remains unclear whether investing in the complexity of a ketogenic diet offers meaningful advantages over simpler carbohydrate moderation for preserving function under such stress. This proposal tests which steady-state dietary backdrop better maintains neurocognitive, metabolic, autonomic, and immune function during imposed partial sleep restriction. Participants will be randomized to a standard mixed diet, a low-glycemic/low-sugar diet, or a nutritional ketogenic diet and will fully adapt to their assigned diet over three to four weeks with normal sleep preserved. All groups will then undergo a controlled period of modest sleep restriction of five to six hours per night for one to two weeks, allowing us to probe the stable dietary state rather than the combined burden of diet, adaptation, and sleep loss. Outcomes include sustained attention and decision-making, continuous glucose monitoring and insulin dynamics, heart-rate variability and blood pressure, and a core panel of cytokines and cortisol. Rather than relying on aggregated composite scores, we will interpret patterns across these axes to characterize the distinct benefits and trade-offs of each dietary backdrop. The findings will directly inform practical dietary policy for settings where sleep loss is unavoidable while remaining mechanistically grounded.

text: Glymphatic-like clearance of interstitial solutes is markedly enhanced during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, but the extent to which this advantage reflects mechanical drivers such as posture and respiratory pulsation, as opposed to state-dependent factors including neuromodulation, interstitial volume, and aquaporin-4 polarization, remains unresolved. This proposal tests how much of the sleep–wake difference in solute transport can be recovered in electroencephalography-verified wakefulness through maximally feasible, physiologically tolerable mechanical manipulation alone. Using a within-animal rodent tracer experiment, we will compare four conditions: wake control, wake with mechanical boosting (optimized posture plus a validated respiratory or airway-pressure manipulation), NREM control, and optionally NREM with boosting. Time-resolved tracer kinetics will serve as the primary outcome, while cerebrospinal fluid and vascular pulsation metrics, respiratory variables, and blood gases will be analyzed as covariates to confirm the achieved boost and control for systemic confounds, and simultaneous electroencephalography and electromyography will verify brain state. By quantifying how far mechanical boosting narrows the wake-to-NREM clearance gap, the study will define the ceiling of mechanically permissive enhancement versus state-locked resistance. The results will directly inform whether posture and breathing interventions could support recovery-related clearance during wakefulness in humans.

text: Short-term sleep restriction is known to induce sympathetic, inflammatory, and metabolic strain, yet its effect on the cellular proteostatic stress-response system remains poorly characterized. This study proposes a mechanistic within-subject 2×2 crossover experiment to determine whether several nights of curtailed sleep alter both the baseline state and the inducibility of the HSF1–HSP72 heat-shock response in healthy humans. Participants will complete four laboratory sessions combining two sleep conditions (habitual versus 3–5 nights of restriction) with two thermal conditions (controlled whole-body hyperthermia targeting a tolerable ~1°C core temperature rise held for 60–90 minutes, versus thermoneutral sham). Whole-body hyperthermia will serve as a standardized in vivo activator of heat-shock machinery, while an ex vivo standardized heat-shock challenge of peripheral blood mononuclear cells will index intrinsic cellular response capacity independent of participants' vascular and thermoregulatory state. Primary outcomes include peripheral blood mononuclear cell HSP72 levels, HSF1 activation, and stress-kinase phosphorylation at baseline and across multiple post-intervention timepoints, with secondary metabolic, inflammatory, autonomic, and cognitive measures. By comparing basal status, in vivo inducibility, and ex vivo capacity, the design decomposes sleep effects into baseline tone, intrinsic proteostatic bandwidth, and effective thermal dosing. This approach provides an interpretable test of whether inadequate sleep constrains a core cellular repair program.

text: Sleep supports restorative processes linked to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) movement and reduced noradrenergic tone, yet the relative contributions of mechanical drivers and neuromodulatory state to these signatures in humans remain unclear. This proposal describes a minimal, causal perturbation experiment in awake humans that manipulates two levers: a strong mechanical input (0.1 Hz paced deep breathing with controlled tidal volume and end-tidal CO₂) and a neuromodulatory downshift (low-dose clonidine or an equivalent noradrenaline-reducing agent). Participants will be studied across four conditions crossing normal versus reduced noradrenergic tone with spontaneous versus paced breathing, with readouts including heart rate variability, baroreflex sensitivity, and, in a subgroup, MRI-based measures of CSF oscillation amplitude and low-frequency BOLD pulsations. Because the two levers are not perfectly independent, mechanics and CO₂ will be measured under each pharmacologic state and used as covariates to estimate noradrenaline-linked changes in CSF and autonomic gain at fixed mechanical input. The design tests competing predictions: a mechanics-dominant model in which paced breathing largely reproduces sleep-like patterns, versus a noradrenaline-gated model in which reduced tone multiplicatively amplifies these effects. The resulting response map will define the constraints that any wakeful strategy aiming to mimic sleep's restorative features must respect.

text: Chronic partial sleep restriction degrades vigilance and increases subjective sleepiness, yet extending sleep is often impossible for workers and students, motivating scalable in-wake countermeasures. Slow breathing and heart rate variability biofeedback are widely promoted, with breathing at the cardiac–respiratory resonance frequency (~0.1 Hz) presumed to confer special benefit, but whether this specific tuning matters more than generic slow breathing or quiet rest remains unresolved. We propose a two-arm parallel randomized controlled trial that compares scheduled resonance breathing (six breaths per minute) against an expectancy- and time-matched control practice (non-resonant slow breathing or eyes-closed quiet rest) across a standardized multi-day sleep-restriction protocol. Primary outcomes are behavioral trajectories of psychomotor vigilance performance and subjective sleepiness collected daily across baseline and restriction days, with brief resting heart rate variability recordings serving as minimal secondary physiological characterization rather than mechanistic proof. This lean design maximizes informational value per participant and yields an actionable answer: if resonance breathing outperforms control, resonance specificity is supported and justifies richer follow-up; if the arms are equivalent, simpler slow breathing or relaxation suffices, and precise frequency tuning is unnecessary. The study thus provides the first disciplined head-to-head test of resonance specificity as a fatigue countermeasure under controlled sleep loss.

text: This proposal investigates how much realistically achievable manipulation of sleep architecture can compensate for insufficient sleep compared with simply extending nocturnal time in bed. We will conduct a nap-free, 2×2 factorial study in which participants sleep at a fixed circadian phase under four conditions crossing short (4.5 h) versus long (7–8 h) time in bed with closed-loop acoustic stimulation (CLAS) during non-rapid-eye-movement sleep versus sham. Rather than treating CLAS as a large lever, we use it as a fine-grained probe and characterize the full architecture bundle it produces, including slow-wave activity, sleep stages, total sleep time, and fragmentation, over several nights to reach a steady state. Outcomes span neurocognitive, autonomic, immune, and exploratory metabolic domains, allowing us to determine which functions are duration-locked and which are architecture-sensitive. Primary contrasts quantify the benefit of additional sleep minutes at constant circadian timing, while secondary contrasts estimate the realistic ceiling of architecture-based enhancement under both restricted and adequate sleep. By calibrating the true dynamic range of these interventions, the study will clarify when protecting sleep duration is essential and when targeted architecture aids may offer meaningful, domain-specific gains.

text: Sleep deprivation produces characteristic changes in waking electroencephalographic (EEG) activity that reliably track sleep pressure and normalize with recovery sleep, yet it remains unknown whether any simple quiet waking state can transiently modulate these same EEG dimensions or whether the benefits of restful wakefulness reflect only generic relaxation. This proposal describes a lean, EEG-centric, within-subject experiment that uses partial sleep restriction to induce a well-characterized sleep-deprivation signature in resting EEG and then compares several minimal quiet waking states, including passive dark-room rest, paced 0.1 Hz resonance breathing, and a standardized non-sleep deep rest or mindfulness script. A pre-registered set of EEG markers, including spectral features and microstate parameters, will be defined from well-rested baseline and recovery-sleep profiles to establish sleep-deprived and recovered reference patterns, with autonomic indices recorded as arousal context and sparse endocrine sampling used only to confirm the expected day-level phenotype. The central question is whether any guided state shifts these markers toward the recovered profile more than passive rest, and whether distinct EEG sub-components respond differentially across states. Time-matched, counterbalanced blocks and standardized circadian and lighting conditions minimize confounds and enhance interpretability. By anchoring analysis in validated EEG markers rather than broad arousal measures, the design yields informative results whether positive or null, clarifying whether quiet waking states meaningfully engage sleep-related EEG homeostasis and identifying credible targets for future countermeasure development.

text: Sleep restriction reliably impairs executive and working-memory performance while modestly shifting autonomic balance toward sympathetic dominance and elevating inflammatory markers, yet it remains unclear whether transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) can buffer these effects or through which physiological channel it might act. This study addresses a narrow but critical mechanistic question: under controlled sleep restriction, which channel—autonomic (heart rate variability) or inflammatory—responds most reliably to taVNS, and does that response track improvements in executive cognition? Healthy adults will undergo several consecutive nights of restricted sleep while receiving fixed-schedule auricular taVNS or sham stimulation, with executive/working-memory performance as the primary functional outcome and HRV and inflammatory markers assessed as parallel, non-assumed mechanistic channels. Vigilance, metabolic readouts, and subjective states will be captured as exploratory context. Channels will be analyzed both separately and jointly to identify which combinations of cognitive and physiological effects actually occur, rather than presuming they move together. By mapping these relationships, the study will clarify whether any physiological channel makes taVNS a viable component of a multiaxis recovery strategy under sleep loss, informing subsequent applied trials or redirecting resources when effects are absent.

text: This project addresses a development-relevant question in allergic rhinitis: whether intranasal pentosan polysulfate (PPS), under clinically plausible nasal formulations and dosing, can approach the efficacy of standard-of-care therapies and of best-in-class glycosaminoglycan-like comparators. The primary aim is a head-to-head in vivo comparison in established allergic rhinitis animal models, in which PPS delivered as a simple aqueous spray and as retention-enhancing formulations is benchmarked against a GAG-like scaffold and standard intranasal steroid or antihistamine therapy. Each agent will be tested under its own best practical intranasal formulation to avoid biasing results toward one chemistry, and dose–response curves will be generated up to a tolerability-limited ceiling using clinical-proxy endpoints such as sneezing, nasal rubbing, airway resistance, and secretions, alongside inflammatory readouts including eosinophilia, Th2 cytokines, alarmins, and epithelial repair markers. Mechanistic pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic analyses are secondary and will be deployed only where in vivo efficacy meaningfully diverges, to explain observed differences rather than to decide outcomes a priori. By anchoring decisions on comparative in vivo efficacy and applying targeted mechanistic work selectively, the study will determine whether PPS merits further optimization or whether development should pivot to alternative scaffolds, while potentially informing endotype-sensitive therapeutic choices.

text: Siglec-8 is an attractive target for allergic rhinitis because it can inhibit mast cells while also affecting eosinophils, yet whether a safe, mast-cell-selective therapeutic can be achieved by engineering the engagement format—rather than by local formulation—remains unresolved. This proposal tests, in a defined nasal-mucosal context that mimics allergic airway inflammation, whether any biologically plausible Siglec-8 engagement format can deliver strong mast-cell inhibition with acceptably low eosinophil harm before any intranasal delivery is considered. Using primary human mast cells and matched-donor eosinophils cultured under allergic cytokine milieus and physiologically relevant sialylation states, we will compare three mechanistically anchored formats: an Fc-active IgG1-like antibody, a rigorously Fc-null multimeric antibody, and a high-valency sialoside-mimetic ligand. For each format we will measure exposure-ranged mast-cell degranulation, mediator release, and proximal signaling alongside eosinophil apoptosis and functional impairment, and we will apply a pre-registered binary decision rule requiring a defined therapeutic window. A negative outcome would indicate that Siglec-8 biology intrinsically couples benefit and risk in this context, justifying early abandonment of local-only strategies, whereas a positive outcome would establish a clear mechanistic basis for subsequent, streamlined intranasal formulation work.

text: Epithelial barrier dysfunction contributes to allergic rhinitis, yet some patients retain residual macromolecular leak despite intranasal steroids and Th2-directed therapies. In the intestine, a tight junction–biased pool of myosin light chain kinase isoform 1 (MLCK1) drives rapid, reversible macromolecular leak, but MLCK1 biology has been essentially unexplored in nasal epithelium. This project asks, in a deliberately narrow and graded manner, whether MLCK1 is spatially deployed at or near nasal tight junctions and whether its abundance and activity covary with leak that persists after suppression of Th2 signaling. We will map MLCK1 expression, isoform composition, and junctional localization, together with phosphorylated myosin light chain, in allergic rhinitis versus non-allergic nasal tissue using high-resolution imaging. In parallel, primary human nasal air–liquid interface cultures exposed to one or two validated allergic-like conditions will be used to relate transepithelial resistance and FITC-dextran flux to MLCK1 localization before and after steroid-like and IL-4Rα/JAK-pathway interventions. Carefully titrated, exploratory pharmacologic probing will provide supportive, non-definitive evidence. By emphasizing localization and correlation rather than over-claiming therapeutic causality, this efficient study will decisively indicate whether MLCK1 merits future targeting in allergic nasal barrier disease.

text: Autophagy plays a dual role in cancer, promoting survival under stress but also potentially driving cell death, yet the conditions that determine this valence remain poorly defined. This proposal tests the falsifiable hypothesis that, in specific genomically biased tumor contexts, combining a defined stress state (AMPK-high/mTORC1-low) with inhibition of a dominant co-regulator axis unmasks a MiT/TFE–FOXO-dependent, autophagy-dependent lysosomal death state mediated by lysosomal membrane permeabilization and cathepsin release. Using MYC-high, autophagy-addicted pancreatic cancer as a model, we will impose controlled stress alongside HDAC inhibition and employ gain- and loss-of-function of TFEB/TFE3 and FOXO3a, together with autophagy inhibition, to determine whether any resulting death is MiT/TFE-, autophagy-, and LMP-dependent. If validated, we will define a compact, candidate-first module of lysosomal-stability and cathepsin-handling regulators under direct MiT/TFE–FOXO control, using targeted causality filters and optional epigenetic analyses. A negative outcome would itself be informative, steering the field toward simpler TFEB activation and lysosome-targeting strategies. This minimal, mechanism-first design provides a clear decision point with direct implications for the rational design of autophagy-directed anticancer therapies.

label: baseline
text: Autophagy plays a dual role in cancer, both clearing damaged cellular components (cleanup) and recycling nutrients to fuel biosynthesis and growth (refuel), which complicates its therapeutic targeting. This proposal asks whether a realistic lysosomal mTORC1 (LYNUS) configuration exists in which quality-control autophagy and MiT/TFE-dependent lysosomal programs remain robust while autophagy-derived amino acids fail to restore anabolic biosynthesis and growth after therapy-induced stress, even though the same cells can still use exogenous nutrients to recover. Rather than relying on engineered mTOR components or exhaustive combinatorial screening, we test a small, predefined panel of LYNUS perturbations with documented substrate-selective effects, including FLCN inactivation, RagC/D nucleotide-state mutants, and moderate Ragulator disruption, introduced into mTORC1-dependent cancer cell lines. For each configuration, we will verify substrate-selective signaling, confirm that stress genuinely increases autophagic flux, and directly compare cleanup capacity against refueling efficiency specifically from autophagy-derived amino acids, using exogenous nutrient add-back as a critical control. An explicit early go/no-go decision point determines whether any configuration achieves meaningful separation before further investment, and candidate states will be challenged with oncogenic signals to assess robustness. A successful outcome would demonstrate that a MiT/TFE-permissive, refueling-impaired LYNUS state exists, is accessible through realistic perturbations, and resists rescue by parallel oncogenic pathways, providing a concrete mechanistic target for anticancer strategies that preserve cleanup while blocking refuel; a negative result would decisively redirect future efforts toward more direct nutrient-sensing interventions.

label: baseline
text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) relies on metabolic plasticity, using glutamine, fatty acid oxidation, and macropinocytosis-derived nutrients to survive stress, and the transcription factor TFEB has been implicated in coordinating several of these catabolic programs. It remains unclear, however, whether TFEB narrows PDAC's metabolic solution space into a targetable dependency or instead broadens plasticity by enabling switching among fuel sources. This proposal will construct a state-resolved, comparative map of nutrient dependencies across three axes: basal PDAC with endogenous TFEB activity, TFEB loss-of-function, and defined TFEB-activating stresses including glutamine deprivation and KRAS/ERK inhibition, with optional lipid limitation. In each state we will confirm MiT/TFE nuclear activity, CLEAR gene induction, and autophagic flux, then systematically perturb glutamine, macropinocytosis-lysosomal, and lipophagy/FAO pathways while measuring viability, energetic and redox status, and metabolic flux by isotope tracing. The central analysis will determine whether TFEB presence sharpens dependence on a specific nutrient axis, revealing supra-additive lethality of dual inhibition only under particular stresses, or whether it merely amplifies escape routes. Either outcome is actionable: identifying a TFEB-dependent metabolic choke point would define a concrete therapeutic niche, whereas its absence would justify TFEB-independent, multi-axis inhibition strategies. This mechanism-first program leverages established genetic, epigenomic, and metabolic tools to clarify TFEB's therapeutic relevance in advanced PDAC.

label: baseline
text: This study investigates whether minimal editing of the cis-regulatory sequence of a single p53-linked autophagy and lysosomal effector, DRAM1, can measurably shift the balance between therapy-induced lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP)-linked cell death and survival autophagy, beyond what simple DRAM1 overexpression or upstream TFEB/TFE3/BID perturbation achieves. We will build two complementary minimal systems in p53-wild-type cancer cells: isogenic lines carrying base- or prime-edited p53/FOXO and CLEAR/TFEB-like motifs at the native DRAM1 promoter, and synthetic comparators in which DRAM1 knockout cells are rescued using tunable neutral, p53-responsive, or TFEB-responsive promoters. Crucially, DRAM1 expression will be matched across genotypes and benchmarked against graded inducible overexpression and TFEB/TFE3 or BID perturbations, allowing us to define preferential lysosomal death as a higher death-to-flux ratio than any point within this control phenotype space. Across genotoxic, starvation, and combined stresses, we will quantify DRAM1 induction, LMP-linked death, and bulk autophagy flux, then test whether cis-tuned configurations escape the range spanned by simpler manipulations. Because DRAM1 intrinsically couples LMP to flux, any measured effect represents an upper bound on single-locus cis-tuning. Whether cis wiring confers unique leverage or DRAM1 behaves as a graded effector, the results will guide whether future autophagy-directed strategies should pursue locus-level rewiring or higher-level network control.

label: baseline
text: MiT/TFE transcription factors, including TFEB, TFE3, and oncogenic fusions such as ASPSCR1–TFE3, control both basal autophagy/lysosomal homeostasis and stress-induced, therapy-protective autophagy through largely overlapping CLEAR gene networks, yet it remains unclear whether these dual roles can be uncoupled. This project asks whether any MiT/TFE activation state selectively compresses stress-induced autophagy relative to basal autophagy, weakening chemoprotective "survival autophagy" while preserving tonic autophagy sufficient for cell viability. To test this, we will construct a minimal, mechanistically interpretable panel of MiT/TFE states in isogenic cancer models dependent on MiT/TFE-driven autophagy, spanning wild-type factors, AMPK-phospho-dead mutants, mTORC1-site localization mutants, and an oncogenic fusion, with matched expression and verified signaling behavior. For each state, we will quantitatively map basal versus stress-induced autophagy using LC3 flux, p62 turnover, lysosomal function, and viability, computing a basal autophagy index and a stress response gain, and correlating these with chemoresistance metrics. Promising states showing preserved basal but compressed stress autophagy will be dissected by RNA-seq and ChIP-seq, and, if warranted, by targeted cofactor-interface mutations to identify the mechanistic basis of compression. If instead all states shift autophagy proportionally, the result would indicate that MiT/TFE control of basal and stress autophagy is effectively one-dimensional, redirecting therapeutic strategies toward downstream or combinatorial levers. Either outcome delivers a concise, MiT/TFE-proximal test of whether transcriptional mode bias of autophagy is biologically exploitable for anticancer therapy.
