text: Certain advanced tumors, most clearly MiT/TFE-driven renal cell carcinomas, depend on the transcription factors TFEB and TFE3 to activate autophagy and lysosome genes, rendering them addicted to autophagic flux for survival under metabolic and therapeutic stress. Although autophagy blockade impairs viability in these contexts, tumors frequently escape by rewiring upstream signaling or engaging compensatory catabolic and stress programs, limiting the durability of such approaches. This project tests the hypothesis that MiT/TFE-high, autophagy-addicted tumors rely on non-redundant chromatin cofactor modules at MiT/TFE-controlled target genes that are distinct from generic repressive machinery and can be exploited therapeutically. Using cell lines and organoids with confirmed autophagy addiction, we will perform focused CRISPRi screens to identify functional target-gene bottlenecks whose repression impairs survival or sensitizes cells to autophagy inhibition, then map the chromatin state and associated cofactor complexes at these loci through profiling and mass spectrometry. Candidate cofactors will be perturbed with genetic and pharmacologic tools to define dependencies whose disruption selectively collapses bottleneck gene expression, robustly enhances sensitivity to autophagy blockade, and cannot be rescued by alternative complexes. The work will deliver a ranked set of MiT/TFE target genes and biochemically tractable chromatin cofactors that represent selective vulnerabilities for combination with autophagy inhibitors, opening an underexplored therapeutic avenue in autophagy-addicted cancers.

label: baseline
text: Combining chemotherapy with autophagy/lysosome-targeted agents has yielded inconsistent clinical results, in part because patient selection often relies on static autophagy markers or broad assumptions of pathway dependence rather than regimen- and microenvironment-specific predictors. This proposal develops a minimal, therapy-induced molecular signature that predicts when adding an autophagy/lysosome-directed drug to a given chemotherapy regimen will substantially increase tumor killing. Using panels of pancreatic, triple-negative breast, and glioblastoma models in 2D, organoid, and co-culture systems under niche-mimicking stresses, we will profile transcriptional and proteomic changes after short-interval treatment with chemotherapy with and without inhibitor, and quantify the added benefit of the inhibitor. Regularized predictive models will identify the smallest robust panel that forecasts this benefit, and an unbiased model will be compared head-to-head with a model restricted to MiT/TFE (TFEB/TFE3) targets to determine whether MiT/TFE-centric features are sufficient or whether broader stress-adaptation modules are required. The causal role of the selected features, particularly TFEB/TFE3, will then be tested using CRISPRi and degron-based perturbations to distinguish MiT/TFE-driven from MiT/TFE-independent mechanisms. The resulting panel will be translated into a clinically tractable assay for ex vivo–treated patient samples to guide combination decisions and enable biomarker-informed early-phase trials.

label: baseline
text: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) support tumor growth partly by exporting nutrients such as lactate and by sustaining high autophagic flux, yet whether these two functions represent separable therapeutic targets remains unclear. This proposal seeks to determine, in a quantitatively rigorous way, whether CAF nutrient export and CAF autophagy are independent axes for weakening mTORC1-high, oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS)-dependent tumors, and whether targeting export alone is sufficient. We adopt a two-stage design in which a rapid pharmacologic stage first tests dependency on stromal export and autophagy across tumor panels pre-stratified by mTORC1 activity and metabolic phenotype, using MCT1/4 and autophagy inhibitors together with isotope tracing to quantify stromal carbon contribution to tumor metabolism. Only if these tests are encouraging will we proceed to a focused genetic stage that cleanly separates CAF-specific MCT4 suppression from titrated, inducible CAF autophagy knockdown, thereby resolving whether autophagy is a primary target, a secondary amplifier, or redundant once export is blocked. Finally, we will use AMPK, MiT/TFE, and FOXO perturbations with chromatin mapping to explain the mechanistic coupling between autophagy and export. With explicit decision points enabling early pivots, this efficient, lab-implementable program aims to define which stromal metabolic axis is truly actionable against defined tumor phenotypes.

label: baseline
text: Advanced tumors frequently survive therapy by biasing stress responses toward survival rather than death, yet it remains unclear whether this bias is most effectively targeted at broad transcriptional and epigenetic regulators or at specific downstream autophagy–lysosome effectors. This project directly compares two regulatory tiers—global rheostats such as MYC, HDAC, BRD4, MiT–TFE, and p53–mTOR–FOXO, versus local effectors such as DRAM1, lysosomal membrane permeabilization machinery, and lysophagy receptors—within a focused panel of tumor cell lines and matched normal-like controls under standardized, clinically relevant stresses. Autophagy and lysosomal pathways are treated as one modulatory layer within a broader damage context that includes mitochondrial permeabilization and BCL2-family signaling, avoiding over-interpretation of their centrality. In Stage 1, parallel perturbations of each tier are assessed for effect size, stress-conditionality, and consistency across genotypes using readouts of autophagy flux, lysosomal membrane permeabilization, lysophagy dynamics, cell death, and clonogenic survival, guided by predefined decision rules. Only loci showing tier-comparable or superior, chromatin-gated, stress-conditional control proceed to Stage 2, where dCas9-based epigenetic editing tests whether local chromatin modulation offers unique therapeutic leverage. Either outcome is informative, clarifying where in the regulatory hierarchy tumors most stably encode survival bias and where intervention is most efficient.

label: baseline
text: Incomplete penetrance in preclinical autoimmunity remains poorly understood: individuals with comparable genetic and serologic risk frequently diverge in whether they progress to clinical disease. This proposal tests the hypothesis that genotype-calibrated immune function in blood explains part of this residual variability, reflecting a mismatch between an individual's genetic wiring and the functional output of accessible immune pathways. Using existing autoantibody-positive at-risk cohorts for lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, and type 1 diabetes, we will first fit the best available progression models from polygenic risk scores, HLA, autoantibodies, and resting transcriptional modules to identify misclassified strata, namely high-risk non-progressors and low-risk progressors. We will then apply simple, robust ex vivo stimulation assays with disease-tailored stimuli and low-dimensional cytokine and sentinel-transcript readouts, computing mismatch metrics that compare observed stimulated responses against genetic pathway scores. We will test whether these metrics improve prediction within misclassified strata beyond existing features and replicate across cohorts and timepoints. Only if simple assays demonstrate robust incremental value will we escalate to a pathway-resolved Genotype–Stimulus Response Index using targeted transcriptomics. Regardless of outcome, this staged, hypothesis-driven design clarifies whether penetrance determinants are meaningfully encoded in blood-based function or lie predominantly in tissue and environmental axes.

label: baseline
text: Serum proteomic, metabolomic, and polygenic risk score (PRS) signatures can stratify individuals for nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) progression, yet they do not explain why some high-risk patients progress while others remain stable. This proposal develops a targeted, dynamic hepatocyte-like cell assay as a mechanistic follow-up platform to interpret established serum+PRS strata rather than to serve as a standalone clinical test. Using a single, standardized human iPSC-derived hepatocyte lineage as a measurement probe, we apply time-structured repeated pulses of pooled or fractionated serum drawn from pre-defined risk groups and monitor a minimal endogenous circuit spanning NF-κB/STAT3 signaling, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and lipid handling. From these responses we derive quantitative adaptation phenotypes—activation thresholds, relaxation half-times, and degree of hysteresis—that characterize how hepatocytes process recurrent inflammatory and metabolic hits. We then map these phenotypes back to specific serum features and PRS components to identify which axes drive maladaptive persistence versus resilient recovery. By linking abstract risk signatures to concrete regulatory tipping behaviors, this focused, hypothesis-driven approach provides mechanistic grounding for existing biomarkers and may guide rational refinement of serum+PRS models.

label: baseline
text: We propose a single-donor, multi-stimulus blood assay that generates a per-patient "wake-up map" describing how an individual's disease-risk genetic architecture manifests under defined immune challenges. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells from a genotyped donor are exposed to a small panel of standardized stimuli, and functionally dangerous states are defined primarily by secreted cytokines and surface activation markers, yielding a condition-specific functional response score relative to that donor's baseline. For stimuli flagged as dangerous, bulk RNA sequencing at a few timepoints is used to characterize the coarse temporal behavior of risk-linked gene modules, which are summarized into phenomenological dynamic classes such as early-, sustained-, or late-dominated rather than inferred kinetic parameters. By linking disease-risk variants to nearby pathways through public regulatory maps, the assay distinguishes individuals who show similar protein overshoot but differ in which risk modules are engaged, for example interferon versus NF-κB biased responses. External priors on transcript stability and dynamic response quantitative trait loci are overlaid to generate non-causal mechanistic hypotheses for follow-up. The resulting interpretable stimulus-by-module matrix uses only routine assays and offers a condition-specific, dynamics-aware predictor of clinical events and treatment responses that extends beyond baseline polygenic risk scores and static endotypes, ready for prospective testing.

label: baseline
text: Genetic risk scores identify individuals at elevated risk for complex diseases, yet many high-risk individuals remain healthy, and the functional determinants of this incomplete penetrance are poorly understood. This proposal tests whether a single-stimulus, single-time-point whole-blood perturbation assay can explain why some genetically high-risk individuals develop disease while others remain resilient, and, critically, how much functional immune complexity is genuinely required beyond polygenic risk scores and simple markers. Within a high-polygenic-risk stratum for a chosen autoimmune disorder, we will contrast penetrant and resilient individuals using a standardized whole-blood assay measuring a targeted panel of transcripts and cytokines at baseline and 4–6 hours post-stimulation, from which we derive a small set of predefined, interpretable pathway-level indices spanning type I interferon, TNF/NF-κB, regulatory, and stress axes. We will fit a pre-registered hierarchy of models ranging from polygenic risk alone and simple clinical markers to full and deliberately compressed perturbation signatures, evaluating discrimination, reclassification, and calibration under strict analytical constraints that minimize overfitting. By pitting the assay against the harshest simple baselines and pre-specifying compression schemes and success thresholds, we identify the smallest adequate functional signature and accept a finding of no gain as a valid, publishable outcome. This disciplined design clarifies whether, and how simply, a lab-ready blood perturbation assay can inform penetrance among high-risk individuals, with direct implications for mechanistic understanding and clinical deployment.

label: baseline
text: Incomplete penetrance of immune-disease risk alleles remains poorly understood, and it is unclear why some carriers of identical risk genotypes remain healthy while others develop autoimmune or inflammatory disease. This proposal tests the hypothesis that resilience reflects a favorable distribution of signaling capacity across competing immune cell fates rather than uniformly higher or lower signaling strength. We will develop a minimal, clinically compatible phospho-flow assay that applies one or two pre-selected low doses of IL-2 and a Toll-like receptor ligand to whole blood or peripheral blood mononuclear cells and quantifies the fraction of responding cells within key subsets. From these measurements we will compute cross-subset responder ratios, such as effector-to-regulatory T cell responses under low-dose IL-2 and pro-inflammatory-to-tolerogenic myeloid responses under low-dose stimulation. Within fixed genotype strata, we will test whether these ratios distinguish resilient from affected carriers better than single-subset signaling metrics, basic immunophenotypes, or polygenic risk scores, using pre-registered benchmarking with explicit falsification criteria. If validated, cross-subset signaling balance would provide a mechanistically interpretable readout of resilience and a candidate target for therapies that bias immune signaling toward a protective configuration.

label: baseline
text: Incomplete penetrance in immune-mediated diseases remains poorly explained, even for risk loci with established effects on expression in specific immune cell states. This proposal tests whether within-genotype, within-trajectory heterogeneity of gene expression in accessible peripheral blood cells provides information about which risk-allele carriers convert to overt disease or develop severe phenotypes, beyond what per-genotype mean expression and allele-specific expression already capture. We will anchor the analysis in mechanistically implicated (locus, gene, trajectory) triplets identified from existing single-cell eQTL, transcriptome-wide association, and Mendelian randomization evidence in autoimmune, systemic inflammatory, and selected hematologic conditions. For each triplet, we will derive a compact, interpretable set of per-carrier features spanning level (mean, allele-specific imbalance), heterogeneity (a dispersion index and a single upper-tail metric), and stimulus responsiveness, and compare baseline models using polygenic risk and mean expression against augmented models incorporating heterogeneity features, evaluating cross-validated discrimination, likelihood, and calibration with replication across cohorts. We will assess test–retest reliability and robustness to batch effects and state misclassification to ensure any gains are not artifacts. Whether heterogeneity features improve prediction or not, the results will meaningfully redirect efforts in explaining penetrance and in designing targeted immune assays.

label: baseline
text: This proposal investigates whether cell-intrinsic bioenergetic traits of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), measured at single-cell resolution, provide stable and non-redundant information that modifies disease risk beyond standard clinical variables and cheaper biomarkers. Focusing on immune-metabolic diseases with plausible mitochondrial or redox involvement, such as atherosclerosis, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, and selected autoimmune conditions, we ask whether NAD(P)H fluorescence lifetimes—a label-free readout of the balance between free and enzyme-bound cofactors—capture a distinct axis of risk within high polygenic risk score (PRS) individuals. In an initial phase, we will recruit participants across PRS strata and collect genotypes, clinical covariates, plasma markers, immunophenotyping, subset-specific NAD(P)H lifetimes, and simple functional assays, using mixed-effects and variance-components models to separate stable traits from short-term fluctuations and to test incremental prediction. A conditional second phase applies targeted, mechanism-aligned perturbations only if a trait-like, subset-specific signature emerges, evaluating whether dynamic response indices add further predictive value. NAD(P)H lifetimes are treated not as an assumedly superior modality but as a specific, testable window subjected to head-to-head comparison against simpler measures. Whether or not these metrics add value, the study delivers a clear, mechanistically honest boundary result on the utility of PBMC bioenergetic phenotyping.

label: baseline
text: Incomplete penetrance—where individuals carrying high genetic liability for a disease nevertheless remain healthy—represents an underexploited window into biological resilience, yet the space of potentially relevant immune readouts is prohibitively large. This proposal develops a staged prioritization pipeline that begins with individuals matched on polygenic risk score and contrasts affected with unaffected high-risk carriers to identify stable, mechanistically interpretable immune signaling phenotypes associated with resilience. Rather than attempting definitive causal inference, the framework functions as a disciplined screening engine that narrows candidate readouts through successive stages of increasing complexity, each governed by explicit stopping rules. Stage 0 broadly screens blood-based cell frequencies, basal phosphorylation, and serum proteins; Stage 1 focuses on functional readouts within a genetically implicated pathway and cell type; and Stage 2 applies compact dose–time sampling and a minimal ex vivo pharmacologic perturbation to probe circuit-level properties. Repeat sampling and, where feasible, sibling or cohabiting pairs are incorporated to distinguish stable traits from transient disease state and to flag environmental contributions. The deliverable is a ranked, evidence-annotated shortlist of resilience-associated signaling phenotypes suitable for subsequent causal and genetic dissection. This approach offers a principled, genotype-informed, and practically implementable strategy for reducing the field’s search space.

label: baseline
text: Autoimmune diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatoid arthritis have well-characterized genetic risk profiles, yet some individuals with substantial genetic burden experience better-than-expected clinical courses, a phenomenon commonly described as resilience but rarely defined rigorously. This proposal develops a behaviorally anchored, minimal-complexity framework that defines resilience on a longitudinal outcome axis—delayed onset, fewer flares, or lower inflammatory burden relative to expectations set by polygenic risk—rather than by a single cross-sectional measure of low inflammation. Using existing longitudinal cohorts with linked genotype and clinical or validated preclinical data, we will classify individuals within polygenic risk strata as following resilient or vulnerable trajectories and, in a subset sampled during clinical stability, isolate CD14+ monocytes for bulk RNA sequencing at baseline and after a single standardized ex vivo stimulus. We will compute activity scores for a pre-specified panel of disease-relevant pathways and regulons and, in a two-step analysis, first test whether these blood-accessible responses track outcomes and then whether polygenic risk modifies or explains these associations. This design quantifies the fraction of outcome variance explained by standardized blood responses and identifies polygenic-risk-by-pathway interactions indicative of protective immune profiles. Whether signals prove strong or weak, the study yields either behaviorally validated blood correlates of resilient trajectories or robust upper bounds, thereby guiding future attention toward tissue-local or environmental mechanisms.

label: baseline
text: Incomplete penetrance in systemic autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus means that individuals with comparable genetic risk can differ substantially in disease activity, yet the immunological basis of this divergence remains poorly defined. This proposal tests whether within-subset response heterogeneity in peripheral blood immune cells, rather than mean activation alone, distinguishes primed but stable from primed but fragile individuals sharing similar polygenic risk. We propose to expose peripheral blood mononuclear cells to a single, disease-relevant ex vivo stimulus targeting a mechanistically implicated pathway, such as type I interferon or TLR4 signaling, and to profile cells at a single timepoint using a targeted single-cell readout. From each subject we will derive a compact heterogeneity fingerprint capturing mean module activity, upper-tail response fractions, and abnormal co-activation of normally decoupled modules across major immune subsets, stratified by polygenic risk score bands. The central hypothesis is that tail and co-activation features improve prediction of near-term flare beyond clinical indices, serum biomarkers, known subset frequencies, and mean stimulated responses. The design is explicitly falsifiable, treating absence of predictive gain as an informative negative result that would justify simpler monitoring strategies, while a positive outcome would yield an interpretable, blood-based fingerprint amenable to distillation into practical risk-stratification assays.

label: baseline
text: This proposal introduces a two-stage framework to quantify the mixing ratio of exosomes derived from two predefined sources during manufacturing, addressing conditions where genomics and bulk markers cannot attribute vesicle origin. In the development stage, multiplex single-vesicle surface phenotyping using DNA-barcoded affinity probes generates high-dimensional marker vectors that are read out by sequencing or digital PCR, enabling statistical models of the two source distributions and explicit tests of their separability. Separability and stability are treated as empirical properties rather than assumptions, so that when the two populations overlap substantially the system declares the problem ill-posed instead of forcing a number. When separability is adequate, the high-dimensional model is compressed into a minimal set of composite markers or engineered epitopes that implement a locked discriminant in a simple, manufacturing-compatible low-plex assay. This routine assay estimates the source fraction with propagated credible intervals and flags samples as indistinguishable when uncertainty exceeds predefined thresholds. Periodic profiling of reference lots monitors drift, triggering either model refreshment through brief high-dimensional re-profiling or suspension of quantitative use. The approach thereby maximizes information extraction, delivers a practical quality-control format, and transparently acknowledges the limits of origin attribution.

label: baseline
text: This proposal describes the development of a quantitative method for deconvolving extracellular vesicle (EV) mixtures derived from two distinct producer cell lines. The approach relies on engineering two cell lines, each packaging a distinct optical reporter (for example, complementary luciferases or fluorescent proteins) into exosomes through fusion with the tetraspanin CD63, using matched reporter architectures and expression strategies to minimize differential perturbation of EV biogenesis. A calibration framework first characterizes each line in monoculture by fitting a linear model relating bulk optical signal to label-free particle concentration, thereby absorbing detection biases into line-specific coefficients. Controlled co-culture experiments, benchmarked against a laborious reference method, then map the operating envelope within which the linear model yields acceptable error and document conditions requiring recalibration. In routine use, two bulk optical measurements and an optional particle count are solved as a small linear system to report either absolute contributions or robust relative fractions, with periodic re-anchoring to detect calibration drift. Because all components are standard laboratory techniques, the method offers a feasible and explicitly scoped tool for two-source EV process analytics, with clear criteria for success and known failure modes.

label: baseline
text: Extracellular vesicle (EV) manufacturing requires reliable methods to quantify the fractional contribution of different producer cell lines within mixed preparations, yet existing tagging approaches assume that per-vesicle tag copy number remains stable across changing process conditions. Here we propose a ratiometric peptide barcode system in which each producer line displays a shared, mass spectrometry–optimized reference peptide together with a line-specific barcode peptide co-embedded on a common EV-targeted scaffold, such that both peptides reside on the same polypeptide and are affected jointly by fluctuations in expression, EV loading, and proteolysis. The central innovation is a screen-and-lock design phase in which candidate scaffold–peptide pairs are expressed and evaluated across a matrix of process conditions, including different media, stressors, culture formats, and passage numbers, so that only designs exhibiting minimal variation in the barcode-to-reference ratio are retained. Mixed EV samples are then analyzed by targeted multiple-reaction-monitoring mass spectrometry, and the empirically validated ratios are used within a simple linear model to recover the proportion of tag-carrying EVs from each line. This approach replaces the implicit assumption of tag stability with an enforced design criterion, providing an internal control for expression and sorting drift that reduces the need for frequent process-matched recalibration. The method is biologically and analytically lightweight, requiring one scaffold, two short peptides per line, and only a few transitions with a small linear solve. By yielding bulk, process-scale origin ratios that remain valid across media and manufacturing scales, the system offers a robust, laboratory-ready route to integrating EV origin quantification into existing mass spectrometry–based quality control assays.

label: baseline
text: We propose a minimal, process-integrated barcoding method that quantifies the contribution of individual producer cell lines to mixed exosome (extracellular vesicle, EV) batches using a single small-molecule lipid tracer per line. Each tracer is a chemically identical, membrane-incorporating lipid analog distinguished only by its isotopic composition, allowing unique assignment to a producer line without altering EV proteins or nucleic acids. Tracers are quantified in EVs by targeted liquid chromatography–multiple reaction monitoring and normalized to standard quality-control metrics, such as particle counts or total protein, to define a line-specific tracer-per-EV calibration parameter. Mixed batches are then deconvolved with a simple linear model that combines these calibration values with measured tracer signals to estimate each line's fractional contribution. Because the calibration parameter can drift with passage or process changes, the method is designed to be self-monitoring through periodic single-line calibration runs, with predefined bounds that flag process deviations. We deliberately limit scope to two to four lines with clean isotopic separation and validate cross-labeling empirically under defined manufacturing conditions. This approach offers a non-genetic, non-proteomic labeling modality that integrates naturally into existing EV quality-control pipelines, particularly for therapeutic products where genetic or protein barcoding is disfavored.

label: baseline
text: This proposal describes a genetically encoded, luminal identity and quality-control system for tracking the origin of exosomes produced by distinct cell lines in demanding manufacturing settings where surface markers are intentionally modified and endogenous cargo signatures cannot be guaranteed to remain stable. Each producing cell line expresses a distinct luminal barcode, either a short synthetic RNA with exosomal sorting motifs or a small peptide tag fused to the luminal domain of an EV-enriched protein, together with minimal reference cargos. Because barcodes are loaded stochastically and reside inside the vesicle, they are protected from surface engineering and downstream processing, allowing origin fractions to be recovered even after pooling, transport, or post-release mixing. For each validated process, replicate production runs are used to learn a joint distribution of simple observables, such as barcode-to-protein ratios, reference cargos, and size profiles, that characterizes in-specification behavior. Before deconvolving a blended batch, the system checks whether its measurements fall within this validated region, flagging out-of-specification batches and thereby converting silent calibration drift into an explicit, monitorable parameter. Batches that pass these self-diagnostics are then deconvolved via probabilistic inference to estimate mixing ratios with associated uncertainty, providing a complementary, internally encoded identity and QC layer for high-value, distributed manufacturing contexts.

label: baseline
text: We present a non-genetic, chemically defined method for quantifying the mixing ratio of exosomes derived from two known producer cell types. Each purified exosome population is labeled after isolation with a distinct, orthogonal small-molecule handle at a controlled density, using NHS-ester chemistry that targets abundant surface amines and copper-free click chemistry pairs such as azide–DBCO and TCO–tetrazine. Rather than treating handle density as an intrinsic biological constant, we define it as an empirically measured assay parameter, established during calibration runs on pure populations and subject to quality-control acceptance ranges. When labeled populations are mixed, dual-channel reporter signals read out by fluorescence or targeted mass spectrometry are related to vesicle contributions through a simple linear model whose proportionality and density constants are determined from pure-population calibration, allowing direct algebraic recovery of the mixing ratio. Cross-label controls quantify and correct residual background, ensuring orthogonality and robustness. This marker-agnostic, standardized workflow is applicable across many cell-type pairs with minimal redesign, offering a practical solution for rapid, accurate ratiometric quantification at laboratory and manufacturing scales without reliance on genetic modification or endogenous surface markers.

label: baseline
text: Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) offers a promising route to label-free quantification of two-source exosome mixtures, but variability across cartridges and days undermines its reliability for quality control. This project asks what the simplest calibration strategy is that yields robust cross-cartridge mixture quantification within a constrained regime of moderate ratios and low-to-moderate load. Rather than adopting a complex pipeline at the outset, we pursue a sequential search for the minimal effective intervention, escalating complexity only when justified by measured performance gaps. We first empirically define a safe operating window in which the ensemble-averaged mixture spectrum behaves as a near-linear combination of endmember spectra, then test whether per-cartridge two-point static calibration combined with simple regression meets predefined quality-control criteria. If this baseline underperforms, we add incremental static refinements—internal standards, a single mid-ratio reference, or mixed-effects modeling—one layer at a time, and only as a last resort introduce short time-series SERS features to address residual failure modes. Throughout, we quantify which factors and interactions drive prediction error without assuming clean mechanistic separability. The outcome is a minimal, empirically grounded calibration prescription for exosome quality control that specifies precisely when dynamics are necessary and when they are not.

label: baseline
text: This proposal develops a hardware-agnostic statistical framework for inferring the mixing ratio of exosomes derived from two known sources using joint measurements of particle size and electrophoretic mobility from resistive pulse sensing. Rather than introducing new device geometry, the approach centers on a measurement protocol, a generative mixture model, and a quantitative characterization of when the mixing fraction is identifiable. For each experimental campaign, pure source populations are measured to empirically calibrate their joint size–mobility distributions, and an unknown mixture is then modeled as a weighted combination of these distributions, with the mixing fraction inferred by maximum likelihood or Bayesian methods that propagate sampling noise and calibration uncertainty. Because the source distributions are empirical and may overlap, the framework explicitly reports wide credible intervals when the fraction is poorly identifiable, avoiding overclaimed resolution. The method is benchmarked against labeled ground-truth assays across different buffers, donors, and event counts to produce a performance map delineating conditions under which label-free measurements can reliably recover the mixing ratio. Optional multi-pore hardware is framed solely as a throughput enhancement rather than a conceptual advance. The resulting identifiability maps and error models inform both basic exosome physics and practical assay design, clarifying when labels remain indispensable.

label: baseline
text: This proposal investigates whether defined Lactobacillus adhesin constructs can mediate measurable, strain-selective binding and retain function when tethered within an antifouling polyethylene glycol (PEG) matrix, thereby testing the plausibility of engineered probiotic seeding on synthetic surfaces. Rather than assuming that an arbitrary monomeric adhesin fragment behaves as a bacterial analogue of the RGD peptide, the work adopts a biology-first, staged framework that first establishes the valency and molecular context required for adhesion before introducing antifouling constraints. In Stage 1, a single MUB/SpaC-type adhesin domain will be expressed and engineered into monomeric, dimeric, and trimeric forms, and their binding to a target Lactobacillus strain versus staphylococcal and irrelevant controls will be quantified in a PEG-free assay to determine binding strength and strain selectivity. In Stage 2, the best-performing constructs, alongside a validated positive-control ligand and negative controls, will be tethered to a well-characterized planar PEG substrate to test whether specific adhesion survives PEG steric effects. This design deconvolves adhesin unsuitability, valency limitations, and PEG incompatibility, yielding mechanistic insight regardless of outcome. Titanium translation is deferred until selective, PEG-compatible binding is demonstrated, ensuring the core study remains tightly scoped and feasible within three months.

label: baseline
text: Titanium implant infections remain a persistent clinical challenge, and probiotic-derived cell-free supernatants (CFS) have emerged as candidate anti-adhesive additives for implant coatings. However, it is unclear whether crude CFS offer specific bioactivity or merely reflect generic acidity and surfactant effects that could be reproduced with simpler defined agents. This project develops functionally matched postbiotic hydrogels on titanium and evaluates them in a two-phase design that normalizes conditions by physicochemical properties rather than raw protein mass. In the first phase, native probiotic CFS, pH-neutralized CFS, non-probiotic CFS, and a minimal synthetic acid-plus-biosurfactant mixture are matched for pH and surface tension and tested on titanium and polystyrene for their ability to reduce early adhesion of Staphylococcus aureus and Staphylococcus epidermidis. In the second phase, the most discriminating conditions are incorporated into GelMA or alginate–GelMA coatings on titanium and challenged with staphylococci to quantify early adhesion and short-term biofilm formation. By treating the hydrogel as a burst-release interfacial host and controlling generic acid and surfactant effects, the study will determine whether crude probiotic CFS carry specific bioactivity warranting further development or whether purified, defined additives represent the more rational path. All experiments are achievable within a three-month in-vitro window, yielding decision-relevant guidance for postbiotic implant coatings.

label: baseline
text: This proposal develops a titanium surface engineering strategy designed to bias early microbial colonization toward beneficial probiotic species over pathogenic staphylococci relevant to orthopedic implants. Two nearly identical surfaces are compared: an antifouling titanium coating bearing a neutral or zwitterionic polymer brush, and the same coating augmented with a low density of longer chains that display mucin-inspired glycan motifs as protruding antennas, making the presence of these glycans the sole intentional variable. Before any surface modification, candidate glycan ligands are validated in solution using binding assays to identify motifs that bind strongly to Lactobacillus or Bifidobacterium strains and weakly to Staphylococcus aureus and Staphylococcus epidermidis, ensuring that only confirmed hits proceed to surface engineering. Biological testing then advances in stages, beginning with single-species adhesion in protein-free buffer, followed by adhesion under defined protein conditioning, and culminating in a minimal mixed competition assay that quantifies the probiotic-to-staph adhesion ratio on antenna versus baseline surfaces. The mechanistic rationale holds that probiotic mucus-binding adhesins gain specific footholds on the antennas while staphylococci, dependent on adsorbed host proteins, receive little advantage. A positive outcome would establish ligand-validated glycan antennas as a new design axis beyond global antifouling or bactericidal coatings, while a negative outcome would indicate that a single glycan cue is insufficient and motivate combined strategies.

label: baseline
text: Encapsulated probiotics have been proposed as dynamic antimicrobial coatings for implants, yet it remains unclear whether they can generate chemical defense fields quickly enough and over sufficient distances to influence early bacterial colonization at realistic coating thicknesses. This proposal develops a planar hydrogel model to quantify how fast and how far antimicrobial fields produced by encapsulated Lactobacillus or Bifidobacterium extend as a function of coating thickness, nutrient availability, and metabolic state. GelMA or alginate slabs of implant-relevant thicknesses (approximately 10–200 µm) will be cast with live or heat-killed cells at defined densities under low- and high-carbon regimes, treating geometry as a primary experimental variable. Local pH will be mapped over 0–6 hours using ratiometric fluorophores, and functional antimicrobial activity will be assessed at defined distances by challenging a test bacterial strain, capturing the combined effect of acids and secreted factors. Simple one-dimensional diffusion–reaction models will extract effective diffusion lengths and build-up time constants and extrapolate to ultrathin coatings. Comparing live versus metabolism-off conditions will distinguish sustained metabolic production from front-loaded release. The resulting kinetic, geometric, and nutrient-dependent characterization will provide a decisive assessment of whether probiotic-loaded coatings can plausibly serve as early chemical defense layers.

label: baseline
text: Implant-associated infections remain a major clinical challenge, motivating strategies that combine antifouling surfaces with beneficial microbial occupancy. Carboxybetaine (CB) zwitterionic coatings provide excellent resistance to bacterial fouling, but it is unclear whether they can simultaneously support the attachment of protective probiotic species without sacrificing this antifouling performance. This proposal introduces a minimal gatekeeper test to answer that decision-critical question before committing to complex titanium fabrication and imaging work. In a first stage, flat CB surfaces will be modified with a small set of known probiotic-adhesive motifs, such as a peptide and a sugar, presented at several discrete densities, and evaluated using simple readouts of Lactobacillus or Bifidobacterium attachment alongside Staphylococcus aureus and Staphylococcus epidermidis adhesion. A predefined quantitative gate requires at least a tenfold increase in probiotic attachment with no more than a twofold increase in staphylococcal adhesion relative to unmodified CB. Only ligand regimes that pass this gate will advance to a focused second stage on CB-coated titanium coupons, where confocal imaging and comparative adhesion assays will test whether hosted probiotics confer net ecological protection against staphylococci. Either outcome yields a clear, quantitatively grounded conclusion about the feasibility of probiotic-on-zwitterion strategies for implant surfaces.

label: baseline
text: This proposal investigates whether brief activation of the succinate receptor SUCNR1 by extracellular succinate installs a durable pathological state in key effector cells, including fibroblasts, stellate cells, and macrophages, that cannot be reproduced by canonical cytokines, other early G protein-coupled receptors, or intracellular succinate-driven dioxygenase inhibition. To establish this rigorously, we experimentally separate three mechanistic layers—receptor-mediated signaling using selective agonists, antagonists, and SUCNR1-knockout cells; metabolic and epigenetic effects manipulated through succinate dehydrogenase inhibition and α-ketoglutarate ratios independent of the receptor; and generic cytokine amplification via matched doses of transforming growth factor-β, interleukin-1, and angiotensin II. We define two falsifiable hysteresis signatures: a SUCNR1-dependent bistable shift in the transforming growth factor-β activation threshold with persistent memory after washout, and a receptor-dependent chromatin imprint at a predefined panel of fibrosis-critical loci. A single high-leverage perturbation, disabling autocrine transforming growth factor-β maintenance, tests whether SUCNR1 acts by pushing cells over a self-sustaining threshold or through a distinct hysteresis module. One representative in vivo fibrosis model measures early activation-state distributions and chromatin patterns to confirm imprinting. This design determines whether SUCNR1 is a genuine metabolic remodeling checkpoint or merely an early amplifier, providing clinically relevant insight into interception strategies.

label: baseline
text: Residual metabolic dysfunction frequently persists after obesity and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease have been partially corrected through weight loss or glycemic control, yet the particulate danger signals responsible for maintaining this "improved but not cured" state remain poorly defined. This proposal tests whether extracellular ASC specks, protein aggregates released downstream of NLRP3 inflammasome activation in myeloid cells, constitute a distinct and quantitatively important particulate scar, or whether they act merely as one redundant danger signal among neutrophil extracellular traps, nucleic acids, crystals, and oxidized lipids. In a first, diagnostic phase, we will use diet-induced obesity and steatohepatitis models followed by partial normalization to quantify competing particulate burdens alongside non-myeloid dysfunction readouts, including endoplasmic reticulum stress, endothelial and stellate cell activation, caspase-8/11 signaling, and insulin resistance, and will apply multivariate and causal modeling to determine whether speck burden explains unique variance in residual pathology. If specks emerge as leading predictors, a second phase will apply minimal, orthogonal perturbations—extracellular speck neutralization versus extracellular trap clearance, with NLRP3 and IL-1R blockade as reference arms—to test whether reducing speck burden produces mechanistically distinct improvements in interleukin-1-independent endpoints. This design efficiently partitions the contributions of different particulate scars to late metabolic disease. Whether positive or negative, the study will deliver a rigorous, mechanistically grounded map that either establishes ASC specks as a targetable late metabolic checkpoint or redirects future efforts toward other danger signals.

label: baseline
text: This proposal investigates whether a coenzyme A–shared coupling between fatty acid oxidation (FAO) and pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH)/TCA activity constitutes a structurally distinct metastable control circuit within the mitochondrial matrix. We hypothesize that competition for a finite CoA pool between FAO and PDH, together with realistic regulatory constraints, produces hysteresis in FAO and PDH fluxes that cannot be reproduced by simpler motifs based on FAO-only CoA bistability or respiratory-chain–centric nonlinearities with monotone PDH inhibition. To test this, we will perform comparative bifurcation and steady-state analyses across three model classes under physiologic parameter bounds, seeking regions where only the CoA-shared FAO–PDH architecture supports coexisting steady states, thereby establishing a topological rather than parameter-fitting criterion for distinctness. We will pre-register qualitative signatures—such as two stable states with similar FAO but divergent PDH flux, switchable by transient changes in CoA buffering—and evaluate which architectures can generate them. Experimentally, we will use short-timescale fatty acid ramps and modest CoA-buffering perturbations in cultured cells, measuring FAO-linked respiration, PDH phosphorylation, and labeled substrate oxidation, with targeted acylation and acyl-CoA profiling as supporting evidence. Success would define a novel CoA-coupled metabolic checkpoint and identify CoA buffering capacity as a rational lever for shifting mitochondrial fuel-use states.

text: Metabolic-associated fatty liver disease progresses toward fibrosis through poorly controlled macrophage programs, yet whether specific immunometabolic pathways can be selectively targeted to favor regression over scarring remains unclear. This proposal investigates KLASH, an axis linking lactoylglutathione (LGSH) to histone lactylation, as a candidate druggable checkpoint that may bias macrophages away from scar-associated TREM2+ states toward resolution-associated states. Rather than relying on technically fragile metabolite and post-translational modification measurements in scarce human macrophages, we first define KLASH-responsive transcriptional modules by perturbing the glyoxalase system and LDHA in cultured and mouse macrophages, benchmarking selectivity against broader glycolytic and cytokine-targeting interventions and other metabolic pathways. We then project these model-derived modules onto single-cell transcriptomes from liver biopsies of patients with matched baseline fibrosis but divergent outcomes, testing whether KLASH signatures distinguish regressors from progressors within defined macrophage subsets and add non-redundant predictive value. KLASH will be classified as a selective metabolic checkpoint only if perturbation reconfigures fibrosis-relevant macrophage programs more specifically than generic interventions and the same signatures track human outcomes. This human-anchored, comparative design either identifies a tractable target for LGSH/lactylation-directed macrophage therapies or intelligently narrows the field by demoting KLASH to an informative biomarker.

text: Fibrotic states often persist even after profibrotic cues subside, yet the matrix properties governing this irreversibility remain incompletely defined. This proposal tests whether resistance to permanent extracellular matrix remodeling constitutes a metabolic hysteresis element that locks cells in a pathological state independent of stiffness and short-term viscoelasticity. Using well-characterized hyaluronic acid–based dynamic hydrogels that already recapitulate stiffness-driven YAP/TAZ activation and partial regression upon softening, we will engineer conditions matched in initial elastic modulus and short-term stress relaxation but differing in plasticity and proteolytic degradability, achieved by tuning the ratio of reversible to stable covalent crosslinks. Each condition will be characterized for two persistence metrics, a plasticity index and a degradation half-time, and paired with cell-based hysteresis assays in fibroblasts or hepatic stellate cells measuring YAP/TAZ localization, profibrotic gene expression, and metabolic flexibility during activation, cue removal, and re-stiffening. We hypothesize that matrices more resistant to plastic and enzymatic remodeling will retain a larger fraction of persistently activated, metabolically inflexible cells. Contingent on positive results, we will correlate these findings with long-lived crosslink content in native fibrotic versus regressing tissues, identifying candidate bonds for future therapeutic modulation.

text: Reactive carbonyl species such as methylglyoxal and 4-hydroxynonenal accumulate under diabetic and lipotoxic conditions, yet it remains unclear when cellular stress responses transition from reversible adaptation to irreversible dysfunction. This proposal aims to define and functionally validate carbonyl-driven metabolic commitment checkpoints: dynamical regimes in which cells lose the capacity to recover despite reduced stress and supportive intervention. In an initial, clinically focused tissue context, such as pancreatic β-cells or kidney microvascular endothelium, we will use multiplex endogenous reporters of adaptive defense, proteostasis, redox balance, and cell fate to record longitudinal single-cell trajectories under physiologically relevant carbonyl stresses. From these data we will operationally define commitment regions as trajectory subsets where recovery probability collapses in a manner not explained by baseline vulnerability, using lineage barcoding and baseline profiling to distinguish dynamical lock-in from pre-existing weakness. We will then apply timed, translationally plausible interventions to test whether rescue efficacy changes sharply across these regions, thereby separating true commitment checkpoints from continua of vulnerability. Finally, contingent on discovering actionable timing structure, we will construct compressed commitment proxies using recombinase or barcoding cassettes for long-horizon and in vivo studies. This program offers a mechanistically grounded, falsifiable framework for identifying and exploiting optimal interception windows in carbonyl-driven metabolic disease.

text: Fibrosis is often described as a point of no return, yet whether specific metabolic signals actively gate the transition from reversible to irreversible fibroblast activation remains untested. This proposal asks whether CD73-generated adenosine acts as a genuine dynamical checkpoint on fibroblast and hepatic stellate cell reversibility, rather than serving merely as a graded amplifier of injury-driven activation. Using primary hepatic stellate cells and cardiac fibroblasts, we will first identify a narrow, borderline injury band in which some cultures revert and others remain activated after washout of a controllable injury signal. Within this band, we will manipulate adenosine signaling during defined priming, maintenance, and recovery windows to determine whether transient perturbations can flip fate between reversible and irreversible states at fixed injury load. Critically, we will apply explicit dynamical tests, comparing increasing versus decreasing signal ramps and matched injuries with distinct adenosine histories, to detect hysteresis and path-dependence that distinguish a true checkpoint from a steep but graded response. Targeted fibroblast-specific CD73 knockout and receptor modulation in a mild, reversible in vivo injury model will validate relevance. Whether positive or negative, the results will sharply define adenosine's role as either an independent decision layer or a modulator of an injury-driven program.

text: This project critically evaluates whether the insulin receptor (IR)–Galectin-3 (Gal-3)–MGAT5 glycan lattice functions as a true bistable metabolic checkpoint or is better described as a graded modulator subject to slow adaptation and independent cellular damage. Rather than assuming that a checkpoint exists, we pose a precise question about whether this module can sustain bistability and hysteresis in IR fate under realistic biological constraints. We first construct two minimal dynamical models: a feedforward model in which Gal-3/MGAT5 lattice strength directionally shapes IR surface residency and signaling while slow damage accumulates independently, and an extended model incorporating hypothesized IR-embedded feedback capable of generating closed-loop bistability. Bifurcation and sensitivity analyses will determine whether robust bistability can persist given transcriptional delays and noise, and will define distinguishing signatures such as hysteresis loops, bimodality, and path-dependent outcomes. We then perform acute, inducible in vitro perturbations, including bidirectional lattice ramp assays and history-matched, state-split experiments, quantitatively fitting both models with pre-committed criteria that require feedback only if graded control cannot explain residual history dependence. A contingent, narrowly targeted in vivo probe using timed Gal-3 inhibition will test for path-dependent benefits. This parsimonious, model-driven design will decisively classify Gal-3 lattices as checkpoints or graded tuners, reshaping how Gal-3-targeted therapies are positioned for metabolic disease interception.

text: Post-diet weight regain is driven in part by rebound hyperexcitability of hunger-promoting AgRP neurons, and although central circuits can be manipulated to suppress this activity, coupling such plasticity to the natural timing of nutrient intake over prolonged periods remains a challenge. This proposal develops a three-node strategy that uses a single gut segment as a naturalistic, absorption-locked handle on a functionally defined lateral parabrachial nucleus (LPBN) ensemble that suppresses AgRP activity. We will first identify, in dieted mice, an LPBN population whose brief activation during meals reduces AgRP firing and rebound feeding without aversive responses, and map the spinal and dorsal root ganglion inputs through which specific gut segments naturally engage this gate. We will then establish a central closed-loop conditioning protocol, pairing meal consumption with LPBN activation to demonstrate durable reductions in AgRP hyperexcitability and weight regain. Next, we will modestly increase mechanosensory gain in the selected gut segment using viral targeting of Piezo2-positive enteroendocrine and neuropod cells, biasing normal post-meal distension toward reliably crossing the LPBN activation threshold while preserving motility. Finally, during refeeding, meal-driven distension will substitute for external triggers to strengthen inhibitory control over AgRP neurons. This approach reframes the gut as a chronically engaged timing and gain handle for physiologically grounded resetting of hunger circuits after dieting.

label: baseline
text: Post-diet weight regain is frequently attributed to sustained AgRP neuron hyperactivity, and it has been speculated that gut-derived signals influence this rebound through hypothalamic metabolic pathways. This proposal tests, quantitatively and with explicit falsification criteria, whether a tanycyte/astrocyte-to-POMC monocarboxylate support module accessible from the gut side causally determines post-diet AgRP hyperdrive and weight regain. We will first map how dieting alters tanycytic and astrocytic glycolytic enzymes, monocarboxylate transporters, and lactate delivery to POMC neurons, relating these measures to AgRP/POMC firing and refeeding behavior in weight-stable versus weight-reduced animals. We will then use viral and chemogenetic tools to enhance this central axis and define its maximal plausible effect size on POMC activity, AgRP reactivation, and weight regain, establishing a gold-standard benchmark. Only if the module proves both diet-sensitive and powerful will we test whether dietary fermentable fibers, amino acid mixes, or short-chain fatty acid supplements can approximate this effect by shifting portal precursor profiles that feed tanycyte metabolism. Direct comparison across baseline, central, and gut conditions, with pre-specified decision rules, will determine whether the pathway constitutes a tunable gut-accessible lever or should be abandoned in favor of more proximal neuronal or hormonal targets. Either outcome yields a decisive, mechanistically informative result.

label: baseline
text: Weight regain after diet-induced weight loss is driven in part by rebound activation of hunger-promoting AgRP neurons in the mediobasal hypothalamus, yet the potential for glial signaling to leave a lasting protective imprint on this circuit remains untested. This proposal asks whether a temporally limited increase in astrocyte-derived adenosine tone, delivered during the period of caloric restriction, produces durable changes in AgRP neuron rebound and weight regain that persist after the manipulation is withdrawn. Using an astrocyte-targeted Gq-DREADD delivered to the arcuate nucleus and median eminence, combined with pharmacological A1 receptor probing, we will activate glia in diet-induced obese mice during and briefly after weight loss, then follow animals for months to determine whether AgRP rebound remains attenuated after ligand washout. We will assess pre-specified candidate substrates of a "satiety memory," including AgRP intrinsic excitability, synaptic excitation-inhibition balance, glial coverage and morphology, and transcriptional changes in adenosine, pro-excitatory, and structural plasticity pathways. A parallel arm directly manipulating AgRP excitability will test whether glial targeting confers distinct persistence or a more favorable side-effect profile than neuronal intervention. The design ensures that attenuated, unchanged, or worsened rebound each yields mechanistically interpretable insight into whether transient modulation of an inhibitory glial axis can durably blunt hunger-driven weight regain.

text: Perineuronal nets (PNNs) surround subsets of enteric nervous system (ENS) neurons, yet whether these structures confer distinct and net-dependent functional properties, as they do in the central nervous system, remains untested. This proposal establishes a single-cell-resolved framework in ex vivo ENS preparations to determine whether PNN-ensheathed neurons possess a stable electrophysiological and synaptic phenotype that depends on the integrity of their nets. Within individual myenteric or submucosal ganglia, we will identify PNN-positive and PNN-negative neurons using lectin staining or tagged matrix components and perform paired electrophysiological or calcium-imaging recordings before and after highly localized PNN disruption via focal or photoreleased enzymatic degradation, using neighboring PNN-negative cells as internal controls. Readouts will include intrinsic excitability, synaptic integration, and short-term plasticity, allowing direct comparison of baseline phenotypes and the consequences of targeted net removal while minimizing confounds from global matrix changes, inflammation, or motility. A negative result would indicate that ENS PNNs act as generic extracellular matrix rather than perisomatic filters, whereas a positive result would demonstrate longer-lived, cell-specific tuning. This decisive local test will clarify whether ENS PNNs merit treatment as structural controllers of enteric neuron function, providing a rigorous foundation for future studies of gut reflexes, motility, and gut–brain signaling.

text: Post-diet weight regain is driven in part by persistent adaptations in hypothalamic feeding circuits, yet most mechanistic work has focused on neurons or on astrocytes and microglia, leaving the tanycyte interface largely unexplored. This project tests the hypothesis that specific, endogenous tanycyte state variables—particularly insulin-signaling tone and ACBP/endozepine gliotransmitter output—can persist across phases of overfeeding and caloric restriction, thereby encoding aspects of caloric history that causally bias arcuate hunger circuits and modulate post-diet hyperphagia and regain through glial, non-incretin, non-vagal mechanisms. Using a three-phase dietary design, we will longitudinally map tanycyte, neuronal, astrocytic, and systemic markers and determine whether tanycyte signatures at dieting onset predict later regain beyond neuronal and astrocytic readouts. We will then use tanycyte-targeted CRISPR activation/interference and chemogenetics to minimally tune each candidate pathway during dieting, asking whether single, monotonic changes are sufficient to shift regain. Conditional, inducible manipulations restricted to tanycytes, contrasted with systemic perturbations, will distinguish cell-autonomous history from global metabolic milieu. From these data we will define a minimal protective tanycyte configuration and test whether inducing it in naïve animals reduces hyperphagic rebound without provoking anorexia or sickness behavior. A positive result would yield a defined, parsimonious tanycyte target against yo-yo dieting, while a negative result would sharpen the boundaries of glial contributions to regain.

text: This proposal tests whether a time-limited change in the state of microglia within the arcuate nucleus can produce a durable shift in defended body weight, functioning as a cellular satiety "memory" rather than as ongoing pharmacological action. Prior work shows that microglial activation state influences pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) and agouti-related peptide (AgRP) neuron function and susceptibility to diet-induced obesity, yet it remains unclear whether lasting effects reflect a self-maintaining glial phenotype or irreversible neuronal remodeling. To address this, we will use an inducible, arcuate-biased intervention to transiently drive microglia into a POMC-supporting, satiety-like state during a weight-reduced, low-leptin phase, then completely withdraw the intervention and confirm its off-state at molecular and cellular levels. Animals will then be re-exposed to an obesogenic diet and tracked for months, with body weight trajectories, feeding behavior, melanocortin circuit activity and structure, microglial transcriptional state, and leptin signaling compared against pair-fed, leptin-matched, and sham controls. Persistent reductions in defended weight after washout would provide falsifiable evidence for a hypothalamic engraving mechanism, whereas reversion to control values would constrain microglial targeting to reversible pharmacology. Either outcome yields a decisive, mechanistically informative result that establishes whether central cell-state changes can counteract the biological drive to regain lost weight.

text: Weight regain after dieting is often driven by an early hyperphagic phase in which animals overeat relative to energy needs, reflecting heightened AgRP neuron activity and altered leptin signaling. This proposal tests whether a stable microRNA-encoded bias in hypothalamic feeding neurons can measurably attenuate this hyperphagic component of regain, and, if so, whether a diet-coupled peripheral carrier can approximate that effect without direct central nervous system intervention. In a first stage, we will use AgRP- and POMC-specific viral and CRISPR/dCas9 tools to perturb individual microRNAs implicated in energy balance and leptin responsiveness, measuring the magnitude and duration of refeeding hyperphagia, neuronal activity, and central leptin sensitivity during the regain window. A clear reduction in hyperphagia or improved leptin sensitivity establishes a defined central benchmark, whereas the absence of effects provides a principled endpoint that prunes further work. Conditional on a positive result, a second stage will compare peripheral delivery strategies—synthetic brain-targeted nanoparticles and tissue-derived extracellular vesicles, including gut- and enteric nervous system–derived vesicles—against this benchmark for efficacy and practicality. This staged design isolates the core biological question before pursuing gut-derived vesicles as a potentially diet-tunable, minimally invasive route to buffering hunger-driven weight regain.

text: Delivery of protein therapeutics across the blood–brain barrier (BBB) remains a central challenge, and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) have been proposed as an alternative shuttling axis to receptor-mediated transcytosis. However, it is unclear whether specific HSPG engagement offers any advantage over generic cationic adsorption, or whether HSPG-biased carriers can compete with transferrin receptor (TfR)-based shuttles. This proposal will build a small, mechanistically characterized panel of 30–50 nm protein nanocarriers bearing an identical payload, comparing a charge-only cationic construct, a charge-matched HSPG-motif construct, a variant adding a generic endosomal-escape helper, and a high-avidity motif variant used to map the avidity–flux relationship in vitro, all benchmarked against a TfR shuttle. Binding kinetics and avidity to HSPG mimetics and brain endothelial monolayers will be quantified so that any comparison between HSPG specificity and charge is anchored to measured engagement rather than assumed from surface potential. In vitro assays will resolve uptake, intact transcytosis, and lysosomal trapping, while in vivo studies in mice will assess parenchymal delivery, anatomical fate by cleared-brain imaging, and safety proxies. Using a pre-defined decision framework, the study will deliver a fair-chance falsification test that distinguishes intrinsic HSPG limitations from suboptimal design, thereby guiding whether HSPG-centric BBB shuttles merit continued investment.

text: This project aims to develop and validate a mechanics–optics design framework for non-invasive, patterned corneal reshaping using existing PiXL/LIRIC-type tools that spatially modify the stiffness and refractive index of the anterior stroma without ablation or implants. The central scientific question is whether such epi-on treatments can achieve a maximum safe, stable central refractive change of two to three diopters, treated here as an explicit hypothesis rather than a presupposed outcome. In a first phase, we will define realistic modification limits from clinical and ex vivo data, apply conservative homogeneous and annular patterns in finite-element and optical models and in donor eyes, and estimate an upper bound on achievable central myopic correction while monitoring induced astigmatism, higher-order aberrations, stress concentrations, and transparency. Conditional on this bound approaching two to three diopters, a second phase will optimize pattern families—including annular, bow-tie, and low-order Zernike-like geometries, optionally combined with removable pre-deformation—and test them head-to-head in inflation and OCT-based elastography setups. Whether the ceiling proves low or moderate, the project will deliver a quantitative, safety-constrained characterization of this refractive lever and a lab-ready strategy clearly differentiated from orthokeratology, atropine, and standard broad-beam crosslinking.

label: baseline
text: This proposal addresses a foundational feasibility question for non-incisional myopia correction: whether realistic whole-eye mechanics permit a durable corneal flattening of at least three diopters without cutting, ablating, or implanting tissue. We propose to develop a constraint-aware whole-eye finite-element framework that represents the cornea together with the limbus and sclera under physiologic intraocular pressure and boundary conditions, reusing established models but re-parameterized around small, non-incisional stromal perturbations. The framework encodes empirically grounded bounds on local changes in stromal thickness, stiffness, and hydration, derived from perturbations already shown to be clinically tolerable without haze, ectasia, or unacceptable higher-order aberrations, and it permits modest non-axisymmetric and decentered annular patterns. Using optimization as a feasibility test, we will search the admissible perturbation space for the maximum achievable myopic correction while respecting optical-quality and stress constraints, and we will repeat this across a family of plausible material parameter sets to bracket uncertainty in corneal biomechanics. Where existing in vivo crosslinking data leave critical gaps, one or two targeted ex vivo experiments will anchor the small-perturbation regime. The outcome is a decisive, uncertainty-aware verdict: either a robust "stop signal" indicating that non-incisional reshaping is mechanically insufficient, or concrete mechanical targets that any future biological or photochemical therapy must meet.

label: baseline
text: This proposal investigates whether Donnan-governed swelling of the corneal stroma can serve as a meaningful lever for non-invasive refractive correction, asking how much refractive power change is physically achievable within hydration ranges that preserve transparency and while accounting for hydration-dependent tissue stiffness. We adopt a data- and model-first pipeline that begins by aggregating existing clinical and experimental datasets—diurnal swelling, contact lens–induced edema, and osmotically driven changes—to define a functional transparency window and to obtain a first inverse-modeled estimate of refractive change per allowable hydration shift. We then calibrate swelling-aware finite element models against controlled ex vivo uniform-bath experiments that jointly measure thickness, curvature, backscatter, and stiffness, establishing a validated mapping from hydration state to mechanical and optical response. Using this calibrated model, we predict best-case refractive leverage from idealized axisymmetric hydration patterns and test, through minimal ex vivo perturbations, how much radial heterogeneity survives diffusion and lateral smearing. The synthesized results yield a quantitative upper bound on Donnan-mediated refractive change, determining whether it is clinically meaningful (on the order of one to two diopters) or negligible. This outcome either motivates integration of hydration steering into patterned crosslinking protocols or provides a justified rationale to prioritize stiffness and refractive index modulation instead.

text: Keloids are fibrotic lesions that respond poorly to current therapies, and repeated intralesional injections impose patient burden while risking off-target effects. This proposal develops a single-application dissolvable microneedle patch that delivers a small-molecule PPARγ agonist directly into keloid tissue to provide sustained, lesion-restricted anti-fibrotic activation. The approach is grounded in the well-established capacity of PPARγ agonists to inhibit TGF-β1-induced collagen synthesis, suppress Smad2/3 signaling, and downregulate pro-fibrotic factors in keloid fibroblasts. In the primary tier, the agonist is formulated directly within an inert microneedle matrix, exploiting patch geometry and the intrinsic hypovascularity of keloids to concentrate drug within the lesion while limiting systemic and normal-skin exposure. The central experimental aim is quantitative: to determine whether a one-time dose achieves intralesional concentrations exceeding in vitro anti-fibrotic thresholds for a clinically meaningful duration, assessed through depth-resolved tissue sampling, local versus systemic pharmacokinetics, and markers of PPARγ activation and fibrosis, benchmarked against injections and standard care. Only if exposure or safety limits emerge would a second tier introduce ECM-interacting carriers that leverage dense keloid collagen as a passive pharmacokinetic trap. This staged, mechanism-first design offers a practical, selective, and efficiently testable keloid therapy.

text: Centrosome-amplified (CA) cancer cells depend on TACC3–HSET/KIFC1-mediated clustering to organize supernumerary centrosomes into bipolar spindles, and disrupting this axis selectively induces multipolar spindles and mitotic catastrophe in CA-high tumors while sparing many normal cells. Existing peptide or truncated dominant negatives that target the short interaction motifs underlying clustering suffer from poor stability, aggregation, and uncontrolled valency. Here we propose a small, de novo-designed intracellular protein that localizes to spindle poles through a minimal, non-perturbative targeting motif and presents multiple copies of experimentally validated inhibitory short linear motifs derived from TACC3 or HSET on a rigid, computationally designed scaffold. The scaffold is engineered so that its geometry and copy number maximize avidity-driven sequestration of one side of the clustering interfaces while preventing the motifs from forming productive crosslinks, thereby titrating essential interactions without stabilizing microtubules. Because CA cells have a heightened dependence on functional TACC3–HSET complexes, this valency-controlled competition is expected to collapse clustering selectively in CA cells while normal cells tolerate residual activity. The approach demonstrates how de novo protein design can yield compact, stable, precisely valenced intracellular dominant negatives against defined protein–protein interfaces, offering a programmable new modality for exploiting a validated cancer-specific vulnerability.

label: baseline
text: Neurodegenerative proteinopathies present a persistent challenge because current intracellular clearance tools operate in a single mode, typically routing bound clients toward lysosomal degradation regardless of aggregate stage or salvageability, which risks premature destruction of recoverable structures and imposes a difficult safety–efficacy trade-off. We propose to design minimal synthetic dual-arm adaptor proteins that combine a pathology-biased binder for disease-relevant tau, polyQ, or Aβ conformers with two weak effector motifs, one recruiting chaperones and one engaging the autophagy machinery. The central hypothesis is that, because these motifs are individually too weak to trigger their pathways but respond to multivalent, avidity-driven cues, the relative dominance of repair versus degradation will shift with local adaptor density on aggregates, favoring chaperone-mediated repair on small early species and progressively engaging autophagic clearance on large, entrenched inclusions. We will construct chaperone-only, autophagy-only, and dual-arm adaptors, and at matched binding and expression compare aggregate dynamics, neuronal health, and global proteostasis impact in neurons. Our falsifiable prediction is that dual-arm adaptors match the best degradation-only constructs in clearing entrenched aggregates while preserving recoverable structures and reducing global stress. Success would establish a new paradigm of density-dependent triage between repair and destruction using self-regulating intracellular protein therapeutics.

text: We propose the design of a synthetic transcriptional router protein that operates specifically during periods of chronically elevated autophagy to modestly bias how endogenous transcription factor activity is allocated toward organelle biogenesis and repair. Rather than sensing flux directly, the router relies on established autophagy flux reporters and flux-integrating transcription factors to gate its own expression through inducible or promoter-based control, restricting its activity to well-defined high-flux conditions. The router itself is a modular, de novo scaffold with two functional faces: a tunable-affinity face that multivalently binds a subset of native stress-responsive transcription factors and coactivators, and a DNA-binding face that tethers them to synthetic operators upstream of a curated set of mitochondrial, endoplasmic reticulum, and lysosomal genes. By capturing only a fraction of available transcription factor molecules, the router acts as a local hub that increases their effective concentration at engineered promoters while preserving their combinatorial logic and native regulation. This protein-level approach complements CRISPR activation and synthetic promoters by modulating transcription factor complex formation without genome editing, making it suitable for primary cells and payload-constrained settings. The resulting tool provides a tunable, mechanistically clean instrument to probe how modest reallocations of transcription factor output influence organelle homeostasis under chronic stress, while pointing toward therapeutic strategies for conditions marked by autophagy-driven organelle loss.

label: baseline
text: Targeted protein degradation offers powerful control over intracellular clients, yet many disease-relevant proteins present a fundamental challenge: the same low-complexity or aggregation-prone domain required for normal function also drives pathological high-order assemblies, making conventional degraders unacceptably destructive to essential functional pools. This proposal develops a modular, client-tailored degrader—an intracellular "security guard"—that discriminates between functional and pathological assembly states rather than merely recognizing the shared epitope. The guard is a single fusion protein combining a client-specific binder, a tunable weak self-association module, and a minimal E3 recruitment tail, so that robust ubiquitination is triggered only when guards are recruited at high local density within persistent oligomers or aggregates, while sparsely bound guards on functional monomers and small complexes remain below the activation threshold. The self-association strength is explicitly calibrated against measured native and pathological assembly distributions, and graded variants are screened to identify regimes that preferentially degrade pathological assemblies while sparing physiological pools. Beyond providing a mechanistically transparent template for assembly-state–selective degradation, the system furnishes an experimental framework to determine, per client, whether a usable difference in epitope density, geometry, or persistence exists. Where no such regime is attainable, the approach clarifies that topology-based selectivity is biophysically inaccessible, guiding rational choice among degradation strategies for dosage-sensitive targets.
