text: The RAF–MEK–ERK cascade is organized in part by scaffold proteins such as KSR1, yet it remains unclear whether the architectural role of a scaffold provides control over signaling that cannot be replicated by tuning the activity or abundance of the kinases themselves. This proposal poses an existence-proof question: does acute removal of KSR1 as a structural module generate spatially defined ERK dynamics and cell-fate outcomes that no pattern of kinase degradation can reproduce under identical degradation chemistry and input conditions? To test this, we will tag endogenous KSR1, MEK1/2, and ERK1/2 with the same inducible degron in a common cellular background, monitor ERK activity at the plasma membrane and a second, KSR1-relevant compartment using targeted biosensors, and quantify a defined ERK-sensitive fate decision. Under a small number of well-controlled input regimes, we will record the local ERK signatures and fate outcomes produced by KSR1 loss and then attempt to phenocopy them by varying the timing and dose of kinase degradation. Identifying any regime in which kinase demolition cannot match both local dynamics and fate would establish scaffold architecture as a distinct axis of signaling control. This minimal design isolates architectural from catalytic contributions and, if successful, would motivate scaffold-directed therapeutic strategies beyond conventional kinase inhibition.

text: Biomolecular condensates formed through liquid–liquid phase separation are strongly influenced by ATP and ions, yet current understanding rests on idiosyncratic native systems that carry many overlapping binding sites and regulatory motifs, making it difficult to extract general sequence-level principles. We propose to build a systematic family of de novo, genetically encoded protein reporters that quantify how defined sequence features shape ATP- and ion-dependent behavior across distinct intracellular condensates. Each reporter combines a stable de novo core, parametrically designed intrinsically disordered segments in which charge, charge patterning, and aromatic sticker content are varied independently, a dual weak anchoring system that enriches the reporter in a chosen condensate only when two features coincide, and an intramolecular FRET readout of compaction or clustering. In vitro reconstitution with model condensates will generate calibrated response surfaces relating ATP, magnesium, salt, and RNA to reporter conformation and partitioning, while in-cell deployment alongside genetically encoded ATP and ion sensors will constrain interpretation under physiological perturbations. Integrating these measurements will yield a sequence–ATP–condensate atlas linking designed sequence parameters to condensate behavior. This platform converts qualitative observations into portable, quantitative design rules, providing a mechanistic foundation for future efforts to control condensate physics.

text: We propose to develop a modular, laboratory-ready platform for permanently inactivating specific intracellular proteins through a single engineered proteolytic cut. The approach combines two elements: an inactivating recognition site for an orthogonal protease inserted into a defined loop or hinge of the target protein, and an intrabody-protease fusion that recruits the protease directly to that site upon binding. Because cleavage is proximity-driven, inactivation can be restricted to specific alleles, domains, subcellular locations, or cell types, avoiding the confounds of freely diffusing protease and preserving beneficial functions of multifunctional proteins that full degradation would eliminate. We will establish general design rules for cut-site placement and fusion geometry, build validated exemplar libraries for kinases, transcription factors, and scaffolding proteins, and quantitatively benchmark cleavage kinetics, phenotypic outcomes, and side effects against degradation and inhibitor strategies. A narrow exploratory branch will test whether binding geometry can bias cleavage toward particular protein conformers. The central contribution is to transform scattered protease-based tricks into a predictable, reusable modality that occupies the space between transient inhibition and complete degradation, making single-cut inactivation immediately actionable in research models and engineered cell therapies.

text: Ubiquitin chains of different linkage types, notably K48 and K63, encode distinct instructions that govern the phase separation of the receptor protein UBQLN2, yet it remains unclear whether this linkage “code” is controlled predominantly by the geometry of the ubiquitin chain or by the multivalent architecture of the reader itself. This proposal directly compares multivalent topology engineering on both sides of the polyubiquitin–UBQLN2 interaction to determine where the more powerful and specific control resides. We will design a minimal panel of chimeric UBQLN2 variants that alter the number, spacing, and linker length of ubiquitin-binding modules while preserving the native UBA pocket chemistry and low-complexity character, alongside a matched set of polyubiquitin hub constructs that vary ubiquitin–ubiquitin spacing, flexibility, and valency without altering the ubiquitin surface. For every combination we will measure phase separation onset, condensate fraction, material state by fluorescence recovery, and partitioning of both partners, quantifying the shift in linkage response relative to wild-type components at comparable collateral changes in basal phase separation, oligomerization, and inclusion penalty. This symmetric, mechanistically transparent comparison tests whether reader-side topology can remap the linkage code or whether geometry is effectively locked into the chain. The results will identify the true design degrees of freedom in ubiquitin-encoded condensate logic and indicate whether node-specific, protein-scale control of condensate decisions is achievable through reader rewiring or must rely on chain engineering.

label: baseline
text: This proposal develops a two-stage experimental platform in the rat restraint water-immersion stress (RWIS/WIRS) model to test whether the timing of vagal bursts within the respiratory cycle is a meaningful design axis for protective neuromodulation of stress-induced gastric injury. In the first stage, we establish a single cervical vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) burst pattern that reliably reduces gastric lesion formation without causing problematic hypotension or bradycardia. In the second stage, we deliver this identical pattern while varying only the alignment of burst onset to respiration, comparing exhalation-locked, inspiration-locked, pseudo-random, and sham conditions. Rather than isolating afferent from efferent mechanisms, we treat vagal drive, the dorsal vagal complex, and gastric outcomes as a coupled axis and ask whether respiratory phase reconfigures this axis under severe stress. Primary and secondary outcomes include gastric lesion index, c-Fos and GFAP expression in the NTS and DMV as indices of neuronal and glial activation load, and autonomic safety measures. Total pulse counts and cumulative charge are recorded and included as covariates so that observed differences reflect timing rather than gross temporal statistics. Whether exhalation-locked stimulation proves superior or dose and pattern dominate over phase, the results will provide mechanism-anchored, repeatable guidance for designing future vagal neuromodulation therapies.

text: Stress-induced gastritis reflects a breakdown of epithelial barrier integrity, yet the molecular drivers of gastric paracellular leak and the therapeutic trade-offs of targeting them remain poorly defined. Building on evidence from intestinal epithelium, this proposal develops a gastric-specific mechanistic platform to test whether stomach epithelium relies on MLCK1–FKBP8-mediated recruitment to tight junctions as a dominant driver of stress-induced leak, and whether spatially targeted recruitment blockade offers a therapeutic window distinct from global MLCK inhibition. Using human and animal gastric organoids and ex vivo mucosa, we will characterize MLCK1 and FKBP8 biology, image stress-induced junctional recruitment, and construct quantitative trade-off curves relating barrier protection to restitution, extrusion, and toxicity across reversible pharmacologic and transcriptional interventions. We will then integrate pharmacokinetic and toxicity data to determine whether a clinically desirable region of barrier protection lies beyond the reach of systemic or topical small molecules. Only if such a constrained region exists will we engineer MLCK1-recruitment–resistant organoid-derived epithelial patches and compare their barrier–restitution profiles against the best pharmacologic regimens. This staged, parsimonious design yields a gastric MLCK1 trade-off map and a mechanistically grounded decision point for developing local, repeatable therapies for chronic stress-induced gastritis.

text: Stress-induced gastritis is associated with long-term vulnerability of the gastric mucosa, but it remains unclear whether this vulnerability is sustained by persistent systemic and niche factors or by durable, cell-intrinsic changes within gastric stem cells. This project proposes a minimal, decisive causal test to discriminate between extrinsic and intrinsic models of "stress memory" in a single, well-defined stem-cell population: the fast-cycling corpus isthmus stem cells that drive day-to-day regeneration. Mice will be subjected to a standardized chronic psychological stress paradigm and compared with canonical chemical injury and infection benchmarks; after defined recovery periods, the isthmus stem compartment will be isolated and cultured as organoids under identical, neutral conditions and challenged with acute glucocorticoid, catecholamine, oxidative, and inflammatory stimuli to measure survival, repair, barrier integrity, and lineage output. To determine whether any differences are actively maintained, key extrinsic axes—glucocorticoid, sympathetic, inflammatory, and reactive oxygen species signaling—will be modulated during culture, complemented by coarse bulk RNA-seq and low-depth ATAC-seq profiling. Full normalization would indicate extrinsic-dominant vulnerability favoring systemic interventions, whereas a persistent residual difference would provide clean evidence of an intrinsic, durable stem-cell state, motivating chromatin-focused therapeutic strategies. By foregrounding upstream-axis perturbations and avoiding transplantation and extensive atlasing, this focused design yields a crisp mechanistic conclusion with direct therapeutic implications.

text: This project addresses whether sophisticated autonomic monitoring provides genuine benefit over simple heuristics for preventing water-immersion restraint stress (WRS)–induced gastritis, framing the question as a decision problem rather than an engineering challenge. In WRS, sustained vagal efferent overdrive contributes to mucosal breakdown, yet different vagal components differentially regulate acid secretion, motility, and protective blood flow, so global suppression may carry trade-offs that timed, partial modulation could avoid. We propose a staged design in which we first map the lesion time course against simple physiological variables, including heart rate variability, core temperature, and basic gastric metrics, to identify pre-lesion windows and test whether trivial predictors already suffice. We then compare fixed-time vagus nerve stimulation aimed at attenuating vagal drive against maximal suppression by atropine or vagotomy, measuring lesion severity and mucosal perfusion. Only if timed attenuation shows benefit that varies across animals do we test whether autonomic-triggered, closed-loop stimulation outperforms fixed-time delivery in sparing suppression or improving individualized timing. This lean, escalating framework will clarify whether autonomic monitoring earns its complexity and will guide the design of future preemptive neuromodulation strategies for stress-induced gastritis.

text: Stress-induced gastritis remains a therapeutic challenge because current approaches provide only transient or broadly suppressive protection in a continuously renewing mucosa rather than durable, locally stored resilience. This proposal tests the hypothesis that repeated, biased activation of EP4 signaling in human gastric stem and progenitor cells, potentiated by specialized pro-resolving mediators acting as positive allosteric modulators, can stably reprogram these cells so their progeny form an epithelium that resists injury and resolves damage faster even after treatment stops. Using human gastric organoids, we will first confirm that stem and progenitor compartments are EP4-competent by mapping receptor expression and acute cAMP and early-gene responses, then apply EP4-biased or EP4 plus mediator conditioning across multiple self-renewal cycles. After washout, we will assess whether persistent transcriptional shifts, optional chromatin changes at protective and pathway genes, and altered lineage output define a genuine, mediator-independent memory. Conditioned and naive organoids will then undergo standardized repeated neurogenic and acid injury without added mediators to measure barrier integrity, restitution speed, and endogenous pro-resolution activation. An optional arm will test whether reprogrammed epithelium imprints a durable pro-resolving phenotype in macrophages. Positive results would justify periodic local EP4 and mediator formulations for chronic gastritis, while negative results would localize memory to stromal or neural niches.

text: Stress-induced gastritis lacks an on-demand, patient-controllable means of engaging gastric protection during predictable stressors. This proposal tests whether contingently pairing gastric-focused transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) with a single standardized slow-breathing pattern can train a cueable vagal safety mode that biases autonomic output toward a gastric-protective configuration, characterized by preserved mucosal blood flow, maintained barrier integrity, and reduced dyspeptic symptoms. We hypothesize a systems-level, state-dependent gain change whereby repeated contingent pairing strengthens the trained breathing state's ability to trigger protection, beyond what breathing, taVNS, or their non-contingent co-application achieves. Using both animal models and human participants, we will randomize subjects to paired, taVNS-only, breathing-only, and dose-matched non-paired groups, then evaluate a cue-only test after washout and a clinically realistic stress test to assess protection, efficiency, and reliability. Outcomes include direct measures of mucosal perfusion and barrier integrity in animals and non-invasive physiological surrogates, gastric motility imaging, and symptom reports in humans, with explicit monitoring for maladaptive effects. Even a negative result would clarify whether simple acute protocols suffice, while a positive result would yield a low-burden, patient-controllable tool for managing stress-induced gastritis.

text: This proposal tests whether luminally confined modulation of adenosine A2A or purinergic P2X7 receptors at the gastric surface provides mucosal protection in stress- and NSAID-induced gastritis that is competitive with, and clinically distinct from, existing therapies. Using standard rat gastritis models, we will first confirm that fully absorbed A2A agonists and P2X7 antagonists protect the mucosa from the serosal side, establishing a benchmark efficacy range, and then evaluate simple high-contact luminal vehicles such as viscous suspensions that transiently coat the gastric surface. Local pharmacodynamic readouts, including mucosal blood flow, early signaling, and gene expression changes, will provide proof-of-contact to distinguish genuine mechanistic limits from mere apical inaccessibility, while lesion scores, permeability, blood flow, and systemic immune and acid-secretion measures will quantify protection and off-target effects. Luminal strategies will be compared against systemic A2A agonism, proton pump inhibitors, and prostaglandin analogues using pre-defined decision rules requiring both non-inferior protection and a demonstrable advantage in reduced systemic immune modulation, acid sparing, or NSAID co-therapy compatibility. Refined mucoadhesive formulations and detailed receptor mapping are reserved as second-stage work contingent on initial success. Either a clear advantage or clear non-superiority will meaningfully inform future treatment strategies for stress-induced gastritis.

text: Psychological stress impairs gastric mucosal perfusion and barrier integrity, but the neural bottleneck responsible for this injury remains uncertain. This proposal tests the hypothesis that stress-induced downregulation of the potassium-chloride cotransporter KCC2 in gastric-projecting neurons of the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (DMV) weakens or reverses GABAergic inhibition, disrupting protective vasodilatory programs and driving perfusion and barrier failure. Using a single, well-characterized psychological stress model with documented DMV involvement, we will determine whether KCC2-dependent disinhibition is both necessary and sufficient for mucosal injury by preserving KCC2 function selectively in gastric-projecting DMV neurons during stress and by mimicking the disinhibited state in unstressed animals. We will further benchmark DMV-targeted correction against simpler peripheral vasodilator support and sympathetic attenuation to establish whether central intervention offers any therapeutic advantage. If DMV disinhibition proves central and correctable, the findings would redirect translational efforts toward preserving balanced inhibitory control and KCC2 function rather than simply enhancing vagal tone; if peripheral approaches outperform it, the results would equally clarify where future interventions should focus. This decision-structured design provides a sharp, causally interpretable test of a defined brainstem mechanism in stress-induced gastritis.

text: Water-immersion restraint stress (WRS) in rats produces acute gastric erosions that are closely tied to reductions in gastric blood flow and mediated through vagal–cholinergic pathways. While bilateral vagotomy and atropine reliably prevent these lesions, it remains unknown whether the vagus can serve as a useful therapeutic target in its intact form. This proposal tests whether a simple, clinically plausible cervical vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) protocol applied during WRS reduces gastric lesions relative to sham stimulation and approaches the protection achieved by vagal silencing, without producing obvious systemic side effects. Using a minimal acute experimental setup, we will induce stress gastritis, continuously monitor gastric blood flow at a defined corpus site, and record systemic variables such as heart rate and blood pressure across sham, VNS, and vagotomy/atropine benchmark groups. One or two fixed, translationally relevant stimulation patterns will be delivered throughout WRS, and lesion scores and blood-flow dynamics will be compared across conditions. Rather than dissecting afferent versus efferent contributions, the design provides a decisive, translationally relevant filter: it will determine whether vagal neuromodulation is a viable avenue worth deeper investigation or should be deprioritized in favor of pharmacologic and sensory–mediator strategies.

text: Obesity-associated adipose tissue inflammation is driven in part by a metabolic circuit in which lactate produced by adipocyte lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) accumulates in the interstitium, inhibits prolyl hydroxylase 2 in adipose tissue macrophages, stabilizes HIF-1α, and promotes interleukin-1β expression. This project asks which therapeutic lever—adipocyte LDHA or the macrophage HIF-1α/PHD2/IL-1β axis—delivers greater suppression of macrophage inflammatory programs per unit of realistically achievable, safe perturbation. We first define drug-realistic perturbation windows from existing toxicology and clinical data, then implement partial adipocyte-specific LDHA reduction and clinically relevant myeloid HIF-1α/PHD2 modulation or IL-1β blockade in diet-induced obese mice, benchmarking effect sizes on macrophage inflammation and systemic insulin sensitivity as the primary evidence. Targeted adipocyte–macrophage co-cultures, exposed to palmitate, hypoxia, lipopolysaccharide, and necrotic debris at matched fractional perturbations, are used only to interpret in vivo findings and identify contexts where lactate is or is not the limiting driver, with organ-on-chip and single-cell approaches reserved for unresolved discrepancies. By anchoring perturbations to plausible therapeutic ranges and prioritizing in vivo effect sizes, the study accounts for lactate pleiotropy and concurrent inflammatory inputs. The result is a bounded, decision-grade comparison that justifies pursuing or deprioritizing adipose-targeted LDHA inhibition relative to macrophage- and IL-1β-directed strategies.

text: Obese adipose tissue promotes chronic inflammation through adipocyte-derived signals that push macrophages toward a pro-inflammatory, insulin-resistant state, including extracellular vesicle miR-155 and a concurrent depletion of specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs). Although multiple therapeutic strategies have been proposed, the field lacks a direct comparison of how much leverage adipocyte-side SPM production offers relative to disarming a dominant pathogenic vesicle signal. This proposal uses a minimal adipocyte–macrophage co-culture system to mechanistically rank three interventions under matched conditions: adipocyte ALOX15 overexpression to boost SPM synthesis, adipocyte miR-155 knockdown to remove a key inflammatory signal, and direct SPM addition to macrophages to define the ceiling of SPM responsiveness. Conditioned media from primary or bone marrow–derived cells will be applied to naïve macrophages, with phenotypes assessed by flow cytometry surface markers and targeted transcriptional panels, complemented by focused lipidomics to confirm SPM production. Treating adipocyte output initially as a black box, the design defers vesicle fractionation and construct-localization experiments unless ALOX15 overexpression yields a meaningful macrophage shift. This lean, decision-oriented experiment will determine whether engineering adipocytes as SPM producers is a mechanistically competitive strategy, directing future work toward the strongest lever using the smallest necessary experimental footprint.

text: In obese adipose tissue, macrophages form prolonged contacts with adipocytes at crown-like structures, but whether contact duration itself amplifies inflammatory signaling independently of the lipid and damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) cargo transferred during those interactions remains unresolved. This proposal tests, through a staged design, whether extended macrophage–adipocyte contact intensifies NF-κB activation beyond the effect of cargo uptake. In Stage 1, a simplified, non-exophagic system uses fixed adipocyte ghosts or immobilized lipid droplets with standardized surface lipid and DAMP density, allowing contact time to be manipulated via reversible motility and adhesion modulators while cargo availability is held constant. By matching cells with comparable cumulative lipid/DAMP uptake and tracking NF-κB dynamics with live reporters, we determine whether dwell time contributes independently. In Stage 2, obese adipose explants and three-dimensional co-cultures forming crown-like structures are examined with explicit measurement of per-cell lipid flux, and NF-κB activation is analyzed against contact time with lipid flux as a covariate. Together these stages establish whether physical contact dynamics represent a distinct, targetable amplifier of adipose inflammation.

text: Obesity-associated inflammation is driven in part by miR-155 activity in adipocytes, yet global inhibition of this microRNA risks impairing beneficial processes such as adipogenesis and thermogenesis. This proposal tests whether selectively shielding a minimal set of key targets from miR-155, rather than suppressing the microRNA itself, can decouple its harmful from its adaptive effects. In a first stage, we will use adipocyte-specific overexpression or 3′UTR truncation of well-validated targets, including SOCS1, SHIP1, and fibrosis-related genes, in diet-induced obesity to identify which targets, alone or in combination, most strongly blunt inflammation and fibrosis while preserving adipocyte quality and systemic metabolism. In a second stage, we will apply CRISPR base editing or Cre-dependent knock-in to generate physiologic, miR-155-resistant alleles for the top-ranked targets, comparing their effects against microRNA knockout and overexpression models using metabolic phenotyping and single-cell transcriptomics. This staged design tests the minimal brake set as an explicit hypothesis and reserves complex editing for the best-supported nodes. The expected outcome will reveal whether protecting specific network edges offers a cleaner therapeutic axis than erasing miR-155, or whether its beneficial and harmful roles are too entangled to separate.

text: Obesity subjects adipocytes to chronic endoplasmic reticulum and metabolic stress, activating the sensor IRE1α, whose kinase and RNase outputs balance inflammatory signaling against adaptive metabolic function. Although inhibiting IRE1 kinase or favoring XBP1s-mediated signaling improves adipose inflammation and insulin sensitivity, it remains unclear whether particular IRE1α output patterns leave adipocytes in a durable "primed" state that amplifies future inflammatory and lipolytic responses even after acute stress resolves. This project treats IRE1α as a potential bias encoder and asks whether distinct balances of kinase, XBP1s, and RIDD activity install a lasting pro-inflammatory bias in adipocytes. We will first define a minimal, IRE1-dependent gene signature that persists after conventional stress markers normalize and correlates with heightened responsiveness to later challenge. Using arm-selective perturbations in cultured adipocytes, we will determine which IRE1α outputs install and maintain this signature, comparing them against non-IRE1 inflammatory stimuli to test for pathway-specific persistence. Finally, an adipocyte-specific inducible IRE1α model will compare early versus late intervention in obese mice to establish whether timing dictates prevention of bias installation. The results will clarify what to target and when to reduce adipocyte-driven inflammation in obesity.

text: Obesity promotes phospholipid peroxidation in adipocytes, which paradoxically drives both harmful NLRP3 inflammasome activation and a beneficial, thermogenic, anti-obesogenic program mediated by ferroptotic signaling through the 5,15-DiHETE–HIF1α–c-Myc–PGC1β axis. This project tests whether these two branches respond differently to the time course and magnitude of peroxidation, hypothesizing that inflammation is more sensitive to brief, high peaks whereas thermogenesis depends on sustained, moderate exposure, such that flattening peaks could reduce inflammation while preserving thermogenic signaling. Using diet-induced obese mice with inducible adipocyte-specific GPX4 overexpression and pharmacological ferroptosis inhibitors, we will compare three sharply contrasting regimens—chronic, early-only, and late-only inhibition—at matched cumulative exposure, measuring peroxidation dynamics, NLRP3-dependent inflammation, and thermogenic markers. A pre-specified nonlinearity test will determine whether inflammatory and thermogenic outcomes track peak versus cumulative peroxidation. Only if temporal patterning demonstrates clear advantages will a second phase refine practical pulsed schedules and depot-specific delivery. This falsifiable, tool-ready design delivers value either way: it either defines low-complexity regimens for healthier, thermogenic adipose tissue or establishes that simple static ferroptosis inhibition is already near-optimal.

text: Adipocyte hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α) promotes chemokine production and adipose inflammation, but its transcriptional program is tightly interwoven with NF-κB, mTOR, and chromatin context, leaving unclear how selectively chemokine output can be dampened without perturbing broader HIF-dependent adaptive functions. This project quantifies the cell-intrinsic modularity boundary in adipocytes by directly comparing chemokine-restricted enhancer perturbations against global HIF-1α loss under matched stress inputs. In vitro, we will engineer adipocytes carrying CRISPRi or hypoxia-response-element deletions at Ccl2 and a representative Cxcl locus alongside adipocytes with global Hif1a knockout, expose all genotypes to identical hypoxic and macrophage-conditioned conditions, and profile chemokines, canonical HIF targets, and NF-κB/mTOR signatures by bulk or single-cell RNA sequencing. By isolating cell-intrinsic transcriptional consequences and removing macrophage and vascular confounders, this design distinguishes whether chemokine-targeted edits act as a scalpel or behave like a blunt HIF knockout. Contingent on evidence of high locality in vitro, an adipocyte-specific chemokine-edited mouse line and matched Hif1a knockout will be challenged with high-fat diet to test how intrinsic modularity manifests within intact tissue. The immediate output is a quantitative constraint on how far adipocyte inflammatory output can be retuned at the chromatin level before adaptive HIF programs are unavoidably affected.

text: Obesity leaves a persistent inflammatory imprint on adipose tissue that promotes rapid pathological reactivation upon weight regain, yet the adipocyte-intrinsic factors that sustain this enhancer memory remain undefined. This project aims to identify precision maintenance nodes at obesogenic inflammatory enhancers and to test whether their brief, adipocyte-restricted perturbation during weight loss can durably reset pathological priming. Using a transgenic mouse model of controlled weight cycling together with an adipocyte-only organ-on-chip, we will profile chromatin accessibility, NF-κB occupancy, and H3K27ac across lean, obese, post-weight-loss, and re-challenge states to define memory versus non-memory inflammatory enhancers within the same cell type. We will then extract minimal distinguishing features, focusing on transcription factor motifs and occupancy and on temporal chromatin dynamics, to prioritize candidate maintenance factors whose binding coincides with slower decay and faster reactivation. Candidates will be tested with adipocyte-specific, temporally narrow perturbations applied only during the resolution window, benchmarked against transient BET or HDAC inhibition to assess locus specificity and durability. A qualifying factor must normalize memory enhancers toward a lean-like state while sparing non-memory and identity enhancers, yielding a blunted inflammatory response that persists through drug-free re-challenge.

text: Obesity-associated adipose inflammation is characterized by reduced specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs) and downregulation of their receptors, including ChemR23, yet it remains unclear which node in this pathway is the dominant limiting factor for resolution. This proposal tests whether adipocyte-intrinsic ChemR23 abundance is a controlling bottleneck by restoring and modestly amplifying ChemR23 signaling specifically in adipocytes and asking whether this disproportionately reprograms the adipocyte–macrophage inflammatory axis when ample pro-resolving ligand is available. We will generate a moderate, adipocyte-specific ChemR23 gain-of-function perturbation and evaluate its effects in defined ligand environments using organ-on-a-chip and 3D co-culture systems, comparing wild-type and ChemR23-overexpressing adipocytes with or without RvE1 supplementation and under modulated chemerin conditions. Because ChemR23 responds to both pro-resolving RvE1 and pro-inflammatory chemerin, we will explicitly quantify and manipulate chemerin to isolate RvE1-biased signaling in a lipotoxic milieu. Complementary in vivo experiments will use an adipocyte-specific ChemR23-overexpressing mouse line challenged with a high-fat diet with or without controlled RvE1, assessing adipose inflammation, macrophage phenotype, and systemic metabolic outcomes. Positive results would establish adipocyte ChemR23 as a cell-type-specific druggable target, whereas negative results would indicate that resolving obesity-associated inflammation requires multi-node or deeper adipocyte reprogramming strategies.

text: Chronic white adipose tissue (WAT) inflammation is a central driver of obesity-associated metabolic dysfunction, yet it remains unclear whether mature adipocytes can be intrinsically reprogrammed toward a low-inflammatory, resolution-supporting state without triggering cell death or compensatory inflammation. This proposal asks whether such a state is achievable and, if so, what minimal set of gene-level changes is required. Using obese versus lean WAT transcriptomic and single-cell datasets, we will pre-select a bounded set of roughly ten to fifteen adipocyte-expressed nodes, including pro-inflammatory chemokines and cytokines alongside pro-resolving adipokines and receptors, and test single, pairwise, and small multiplex CRISPRi/a perturbations across progressively complex platforms: two-dimensional adipocyte–macrophage co-cultures, three-dimensional organ-on-chip systems, and adipocyte-specific perturbations in high-fat-diet mice profiled by single-cell RNA sequencing. Readouts will include adipocyte viability and stress, secreted inflammatory profiles, macrophage recruitment and polarization, and systemic insulin sensitivity. By defining explicit failure criteria, we will systematically map the trade-off surface between chemokine suppression and adipocyte survival rather than pursuing anecdotal interventions. The project will thereby establish clear design rules indicating whether adipocyte-intrinsic reprogramming is a viable anti-inflammatory lever or whether macrophage, stromal, or systemic routes are obligatory.

text: Leukocyte hitchhiking, in which drug-loaded nanoparticles bind circulating immune cells to reach diseased tissue, raises an unresolved design question: whether payload release should occur inside the carrier leukocyte or in the surrounding extracellular space, and whether the added complexity of engineering extracellular release is justified. This proposal addresses that question through a two-stage, modeling-guided decision test focused on payload classes where the locus of release plausibly matters. In the first stage, simple compartmental pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic models incorporating leukocyte trafficking, nanoparticle internalization, payload permeability, and intracellular degradation are used to predict when intracellular versus extracellular release meaningfully alters therapeutic index, distinguishing membrane-permeant small molecules from non-permeant or degradation-prone biologics. Only where the model predicts a benefit does the second stage proceed to a focused in vivo comparison, testing an extracellular-release hitchhiker against an intracellular-release variant on the same scaffold, alongside a simpler non-cellular comparator such as free drug or a depot nanoparticle. Readouts include active drug distribution, spatial localization, efficacy, and toxicity, interpreted against explicit, model-derived decision rules. The contribution is not a new platform but a mechanistically grounded, bounded answer to when extracellular-release backpacks are worth their added complexity.

text: The three-dimensional organization of the genome, mediated by CTCF and cohesin, gates specific enhancer–promoter contacts that drive oncogene expression, yet it remains unclear whether directly editing chromatin architecture offers any practical advantage over conventional enhancer- or transcription factor-centric interventions. This proposal tests whether a single, minimal structural manipulation—dCas9-tethered CTCF boundary editing—can achieve superior architectural selectivity and therapeutic index at a disease-relevant enhancer–promoter loop with an established CTCF gating mechanism, such as those at TAL1, TLX3, or MYC in B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Using dCas9–CTCF fusions to strengthen or dCas9-KRAB to erase a defined boundary implicated in gating the pathogenic loop, we will quantify changes in loop strength by locus-focused chromosome conformation capture and compare them against enhancer deletion, dCas9-KRAB at the enhancer, and BET or transcription factor inhibitors. Success is defined by pre-specified benchmarks, including an architectural selectivity ratio exceeding a stringent threshold and equal or better efficacy with equal or lower collateral transcriptomic and viability effects in mixed-culture assays. A positive result would establish a simple, generalizable 3D genome editor for enhancer-driven pathologies, while a negative result would demonstrate that even a best-case structural axis confers no practical benefit, thereby guiding future design choices. This focused, quantitative test provides a conceptually crisp evaluation of whether 3D genome editing can outperform established gene-regulatory tools.

text: At oncogenic loci where erosion of a single validated CTCF boundary element permits pathogenic enhancer–promoter fusion, it remains unclear whether the boundary’s function reflects CTCF occupancy at the physical site or deeper sequence-encoded chromatin context. We propose to test whether enforced CTCF-like occupancy, achieved without altering DNA, can restore insulation and normalize transcription to the same extent as CRISPR-based sequence repair. To this end, we will build a minimal, reversible boundary restorer based on an inducible dCas9–CTCF fusion targeted to the eroded motif, with optional oligomerization tags to titrate effective occupancy strength. Working only at loci where single-element control has been empirically demonstrated in colorectal and nasopharyngeal cancers, we will compare three matched interventions—CRISPR motif repair, inducible dCas–CTCF, and an unrepaired control—using focused Hi-C or HiChIP, transcriptional profiling, and histone-mark analysis. This design cleanly decouples structural restoration from permanent sequence correction and allows dose- and valency-dependent mapping of boundary strength against occupancy, which sequence repair cannot parametrize. The results will quantify how much boundary-erosion–driven oncogenic mis-wiring can be reversed by restoring three-dimensional structure alone, revealing whether occupancy is sufficient or a sequence-encoded component is essential.

text: This proposal addresses a specific class of pathogenic loci in which a single enhancer drives both a pathological promoter, causing harmful misexpression such as oncogene activation, and one or more physiological promoters required for essential, dosage-sensitive functions. In these settings, destroying or silencing the enhancer is unacceptable, and promoter-proximal sequence editing is constrained by sequence conservation and incomplete regulatory knowledge. We propose a "3D safety valve" strategy that selectively uncouples the pathological promoter from the shared enhancer by biasing its participation in the local three-dimensional enhancer hub rather than abolishing enhancer activity. The approach combines minimal, locus-confined CTCF motif edits to tilt loop-extrusion paths away from the pathological promoter, a single class of dCas9-based structural effector to modestly increase local compaction near that promoter, and optional submaximal epigenetic tuning to further shift promoter competition. Rather than claiming perfect isolation, we frame this as an iterative design-and-test program that measures three-dimensional contacts and transcriptional output to reweight promoter-enhancer engagement. Success, even if partial, would demonstrate that minimal local topology edits can achieve functional, promoter-specific uncoupling within complex shared hubs, offering an orthogonal control axis for clinically relevant enhancer-hijack contexts.

text: Reduced-intensity and non-myeloablative (RIC/NMA) allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation spares marrow architecture and donor engraftment but sacrifices the myeloablative anti-leukemic effect needed to eradicate leukemia stem cells (LSCs). This proposal develops a hypothesis-driven platform that asks whether an LSC-biased CAR-NK therapy layered onto RIC/NMA conditioning can restore myeloablative-equivalent LSC control without compromising donor hematopoietic stem cell engraftment. The program is structured as a hierarchy of effector arms—unmodified donor NK cells, simple LSC-biased CAR-NK targeting antigens such as CD123 or CLEC12A, and bone-marrow-tropic CAR-NK bearing homing enhancements—compared under identical transplant conditions to isolate the contributions of CAR specificity and marrow tropism. Two quantitative datasets serve as explicit go/no-go filters before escalation: mapping of candidate antigen expression windows between LSCs and healthy stem cells, and modeling of NK versus donor stem cell homing and niche occupancy. Antigen-tethered CD47 interference is reserved as a modular, contingent add-on only if optimized CAR-NK cannot reach the target. Success is benchmarked against myeloablative-equivalent relapse control with preserved multilineage donor reconstitution in transplant-faithful models. The result is a disciplined, laboratory-ready experimental architecture that keeps the marrow niche intact while transforming the recognition landscape within it.

text: Relapse after reduced‑intensity conditioning (RIC) allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is driven in part by leukemia stem cells (LSCs) that persist within protective bone marrow niches, but it remains unclear whether the principal barrier to graft‑versus‑leukemia activity is spatial—donor T cells failing to engage LSCs in their sanctuaries—or qualitative T‑cell dysfunction and stromal suppression. This proposal develops a replication‑defective, marrow‑localized gene delivery vector that transiently programs niche stromal and myeloid cells to secrete an affinity‑tuned, dual‑antigen bispecific T‑cell engager (BiTE) directed against LSC‑biased antigens and CD3, thereby concentrating HLA‑independent T‑cell redirection inside the niche itself. The BiTE employs reduced‑affinity tumor‑binding arms so that efficient killing occurs preferentially when two LSC‑associated antigens are co‑expressed or when a single antigen reaches very high density, creating a quantifiable avidity gate that spares normal single‑positive myeloid and endothelial cells and preserves engraftment. Because the vector is non‑replicating and episomal, BiTE secretion wanes as donor hematopoiesis reconstitutes, limiting chronic activation and endothelial stress. As a mechanistic preclinical probe, the study will compare RIC combined with systemic versus marrow‑localized dual‑antigen BiTE delivery at matched systemic exposure to determine whether niche‑restricted recognition provides incremental graft‑versus‑leukemia benefit. A positive result would identify niche visibility as a discrete, addressable bottleneck, whereas a negative result would redirect attention toward intrinsic T‑cell dysfunction and stromal resistance, while also mapping antigen density distributions and niche transduction heterogeneity central to this design.

text: This proposal outlines a tiered pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic program designed to determine whether local production of leukemic stem cell (LSC)–directed biologics by marrow-resident cells can achieve a bone-marrow exposure and target-engagement pattern that is unattainable through any tolerable systemic or regional dosing strategy, particularly in the context of reduced-intensity and non-myeloablative allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. We first define a quantitative "non-replicable" signature, specifying a threshold of sustained LSC target occupancy in marrow that must be maintained for a defined interval while plasma concentrations remain below a predefined safety ceiling. The program then proceeds through three sequential tiers of increasing complexity: escalating systemic and regional delivery of engagers such as CD123 or CLEC12A bispecifics and SIRPα fusions; direct intramedullary or intra-arterial infusion without genetic modification; and, only if warranted, engineered marrow-resident secretion of a tagged engager used explicitly as a pharmacokinetic stress-test rather than a therapy. Across all tiers, serial marrow and plasma sampling quantifies drug concentration, target occupancy, LSC clearance, and toxicity to establish whether local production yields a substantially higher, sustained engagement window at acceptable systemic levels. This least-complex-first design ensures that cellular engineering is invoked only when simpler routes fall short, producing an actionable result regardless of outcome. A negative finding would justify concentrating resources on systemic and regional strategies, whereas a positive finding would define a clear quantitative target for future graft-based approaches to LSC control.

text: This proposal addresses whether the spatial topology of CD47 modulation influences the therapeutic index of leukemic stem cell (LSC) control in the context of non-genotoxic conditioning for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in acute myeloid leukemia. We propose a three-arm comparison built on a fixed, clinically realistic conditioning backbone combining anti-CD117 antibody with a low-intensity cytoreductive scaffold such as a hypomethylating agent, holding donor source, dosing windows, and supportive care constant across all arms. The arms differ only in CD47-axis manipulation: no modulation, global CD47 blockade, or localized CD47 inversion achieved by a CD123–SIRPα fusion antibody that silences "don't-eat-me" signaling specifically on CD123-positive blasts and LSCs while sparing CD47 function elsewhere. Primary endpoints quantify therapeutic index through functional LSC control measured by limiting-dilution secondary transplantation and minimal residual disease assays, hematologic toxicity, and donor engraftment with immune reconstitution. Secondary mechanistic probes will test whether augmenting effector function rescues LSC clearance, distinguishing effector limitation from targeting topology as the principal barrier. By isolating CD47 topology as the sole variable, this study provides the first structured head-to-head evaluation to determine whether localized CD47 inversion justifies its engineering complexity and to guide the optimization of LSC-selective, non-genotoxic conditioning.

text:
# NK-Restricted Homing Enhancement as a Test of Spatial Bottlenecks in Leukemic Stem Cell Eradication

Relapse after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation using non-genotoxic conditioning remains a central challenge, and it is unclear whether residual leukemic stem cells (LSCs) persist because donor memory-like natural killer (ML NK) cells fail to access the marrow niches that harbor them or because they reach LSCs but cannot kill them. This proposal aims to distinguish spatial from phenotypic limitations within a fixed backbone combining anti-CD117-based reduced-intensity conditioning and donor ML NK cells. We will first map the spatial and temporal distribution of ML NK cells and residual LSCs in AML models using high-resolution bone marrow imaging to determine whether the two compartments co-localize or remain segregated. We will then introduce a single, targeted perturbation—transient expression of the homing-enhancing variant CXCR4R334X on ML NK cells—and compare niche occupancy, NK–LSC contact frequency, functional LSC frequency, and relapse-free survival against standard ML NK cells. Forced-contact three-dimensional killing assays and parallel fitness analyses will isolate localization effects from intrinsic changes in NK function, with pre-specified quantitative thresholds guiding interpretation. By resolving whether improved niche access alone suppresses relapse-initiating LSCs, this work will indicate whether future non-genotoxic conditioning should prioritize homing engineering or effector and antigen strategies.

text: We propose a CD47-anchored, peri-transplant intervention to enhance innate graft-versus-leukemia activity against residual leukemia stem cells in acute myeloid leukemia patients undergoing reduced-intensity or non-myeloablative conditioning. The central rationale is that the peri-conditioning and early engraftment period represents an underused therapeutic window in which residual leukemia stem cells are stressed, partially dislodged from protective niches, and vulnerable to phagocytic clearance, yet current approaches focus either on intensifying genotoxic conditioning or on post-engraftment maintenance. The core intervention is a brief, timed course of CD47 blockade spanning conditioning and graft infusion to unmask residual leukemia stem cells to macrophage and dendritic-cell clearance while enhancing antigen presentation without directly manipulating T-cell checkpoints. Two optional, modular enhancers—low-intensity CXCR4 antagonism to loosen niche retention and conservative myeloid priming to boost phagocytic function—are treated as testable modifiers rather than mandatory components. Dosing and timing are designed to maximize coverage of host-residual leukemia stem cells while minimizing exposure of incoming donor hematopoietic stem cells, with preclinical models quantifying engraftment and niche occupancy. A hierarchical hypothesis structure allows clean deconvolution of CD47 blockade alone versus combinations, supporting straightforward Phase I/II designs that restore anti-leukemic effect through immune-mediated, non-genotoxic mechanisms.

text: We propose a subset-focused allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation strategy for CD123/CD33-high acute myeloid leukemia that pairs non-genotoxic antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) conditioning with temporally tuned, leukemic stem cell (LSC)-biased CD47 blockade to eradicate quiescent LSCs that survive reduced-intensity regimens. The approach uses CD117/CD45-targeted ADCs to debulk leukemia and open marrow niches without busulfan or total body irradiation, while a SIRPα–CD123 or SIRPα–CD33 fusion biologic is delivered in a defined peri-conditioning window to selectively unmask antigen-high LSCs to innate immune clearance. The central mechanistic hypothesis is that ADC conditioning creates a transient state of low leukemic burden, opening niches, and partially intact but less-suppressed phagocytic and antigen-presenting activity, during which antigen-biased CD47 unmasking is disproportionately effective per cell. Patients would be selected by CD123/CD33 expression on LSC-enriched compartments, with antigen-low clones managed through minimal residual disease surveillance and fallback therapy. We will test whether adding peri-conditioning fusion therapy increases LSC depletion, reduces early relapse, and preserves donor engraftment and acceptable cytopenia profiles relative to ADC conditioning alone. Preclinical dose–effector modeling will define the therapeutic window, and failure to demonstrate benefit or dominance of antigen-low escape would appropriately restrict or abandon the strategy.

text: Relapse of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) remains a major challenge, particularly as the field moves toward gentler, non-genotoxic conditioning regimens that spare patients the toxicity of busulfan or total body irradiation but may leave residual leukemia stem cells. This proposal tests whether a short, front-loaded course of an existing CLEC12A-biased interleukin-15 (IL-15) natural killer (NK) cell engager, such as a MIC12-like immunocytokine or a CLEC12A-directed trispecific killer engager, can restore graft-versus-leukemia activity when delivered during the early engraftment window on an anti-CD117-based reduced-intensity conditioning backbone. The central innovation is the timing and context of antigen-biased IL-15 delivery rather than the creation of a new molecule, targeting the vulnerable interval immediately after CD117-mediated niche opening when donor stem cells are homing and residual CLEC12A-positive leukemia stem cells persist at low burden. We will assess whether this brief NK-support module reduces leukemia stem cell-driven relapse without impairing donor stem cell engraftment or provoking excessive graft-versus-host disease, using mechanistic readouts of CLEC12A antigen and clonal dynamics, engraftment kinetics and marrow niche health, and the graft-versus-leukemia versus graft-versus-host disease balance. By deliberately measuring IL-15 spillover onto stem cells, stroma, myeloid antigen-presenting cells, and T cells, the study interrogates the dominant unknown for translating these agents into transplantation. A positive result would define a concrete protocol for restoring relapse protection under gentler conditioning, while a negative result would precisely map the limiting toxicity and redirect the field toward post-engraftment, cell-intrinsic strategies.

text: Myeloablative conditioning (MAC) prior to hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) contributes to durable leukemic stem cell (LSC) depletion but carries substantial genotoxic and organ toxicity. This proposal tests whether embedding a bone marrow–tropic, cooperative chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) effector into the donor graft can functionally replace MAC's anti-LSC role under reduced-intensity or non-myeloablative conditioning (RIC/NMA). We will engineer donor-derived CLEC12A×ADGRE2 logic-gated CAR-T cells that require dual antigen recognition to sharpen the LSC-versus-normal-progenitor window, and that overexpress CXCR4 and E-selectin ligands to promote marrow residency, together with an inducible safety switch to limit graft-versus-host disease. The central contrast compares graft-integrated CAR-T cells co-infused with the donor graft against serially infused CAR-T cells at matched total dose, with the hypothesis that only co-engraftment harnesses lymphodepletion and empty niche access to establish a durable, marrow-resident effector compartment. Using leukemia xenograft models and a subsequent clinical pilot, we will benchmark functional LSC depletion, CAR-T persistence and spatial distribution, engraftment quality, and toxicity against a MAC plus standard HSCT reference. Success would demonstrate that conditioning's anti-LSC function can be reassigned from genotoxic ablation to a persistent, selective cellular effector. This could redefine HSCT conditioning around RIC/NMA plus a CAR-integrated graft, reducing treatment-related toxicity while preserving leukemia control.

text: Relapse from residual leukemic stem cells (LSCs) remains a central challenge after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for AML and MDS, and non-genotoxic conditioning with agents such as JSP191 offers a novel backbone whose interaction with LSC-targeting strategies is poorly understood. This proposal develops a staged, single-agent "mobilize-and-hit" phase I/II program to determine whether pharmacologic LSC mobilization under JSP191-based conditioning creates a clinically usable window for targeted LSC killing without destabilizing engraftment, damaging donor progenitors, or worsening graft-versus-host disease and infection. In Stage 1, carefully titrated CXCR4 and E-selectin blockade using plerixafor and uproleselan is introduced after initial engraftment to map effects on LSC burden and phenotype, donor progenitor distribution, chimerism, and endothelial and immune safety. In Stage 2, initiated only if Stage 1 demonstrates acceptable tolerability, a single pre-selected CD33/FLT3-directed agent, such as an allogeneic CAR-NK product, is administered in tight temporal coupling to mobilization and compared against mobilization alone using cautious dose escalation. Efficacy endpoints include measurable residual disease negativity, relapse rates, and LSC depletion, alongside engraftment and safety measures. This design yields a quantitative, JSP191-specific map of how mobilization, donor hematopoiesis, and targeted killing interact, reserving advanced HSPC-sparing logic-gated constructs for future, data-driven refinement.

text: This proposal tests whether slow, glia-mediated modulation of extracellular potassium in the locus coeruleus and lateral hypothalamus constitutes a distinct mesoscale control regime over sleep–wake state that cannot be replicated by electrical or pharmacologic interventions within safety-bounded parameter ranges. The central novelty is a decision-theoretic, state-dependent comparison across modalities rather than any individual tool. For a small set of literature-validated behavioral targets, such as wake promotion and sleep stabilization, we will define behavioral endpoints alongside population-level network metrics including mean firing rate, variance, pairwise correlation, and spatial recruitment. Three intervention arms—electrical stimulation, pharmacologic or potassium-conductance modulation, and direct extracellular potassium manipulation—will each be tuned within pre-specified safety bounds to achieve matched behavioral efficacy, allowing comparison of network geometry, synchrony, state-dependence, and adaptation over repeated use. A potassium-specific regime is judged to exist only if potassium manipulation achieves comparable behavioral effects with a measurably more confined, less synchronous, or slower-adapting network signature that no electrical or pharmacologic condition matches within its bounds. Only if this falsifiable uniqueness criterion is met will we pursue a minimal, state-triggered iontronic actuator to reproduce the identified regime chronically, ensuring that both positive and negative outcomes yield decisive, mechanistically honest conclusions.

text: Adaptations in adenosine A1 and A2A receptor systems following chronic drug treatment are commonly attributed to total drug exposure, cumulative sleep loss, or circadian phase, yet these metrics leave substantial variance unexplained. This proposal tests the hypothesis that receptor plasticity is selectively driven by biochemical "mismatch signals"—periods when drug-induced receptor drive is persistently out of phase with the local extracellular adenosine environment. In a first stage, rodents will receive chronic aligned versus misaligned dosing schedules of adenosine-linked agents, matched for exposure, peak concentration, circadian window, and total sleep time, allowing us to test whether precomputed mismatch indices predict behavioral tolerance and receptor-level changes (density, phosphorylation, β-arrestin recruitment, and downstream cAMP/PKA signaling) in basal forebrain, prefrontal cortex, and nucleus accumbens better than canonical metrics. Only if mismatch indices explain additional variance will a second, conditional stage employ implanted adenosine biosensors to compute mismatch in real time and to refine dosing with higher temporal and individual specificity. This staged, mechanistically grounded design avoids premature commitment to invasive closed-loop control while directly evaluating whether local adenosine timing is a distinct driver of receptor adaptation. The findings will clarify whether synchronizing receptor drive with homeostatic signals offers a principled route to tolerance-resistant, homeostat-aware sleep–wake interventions.

text: This project develops a sleep-laboratory platform for steering sleep–wake transitions using stage-locked vibrotactile stimulation, combined with polysomnographic staging and wrist- or ankle-mounted actuators. The primary objective is to optimize practical control of sleep induction and wake promotion by systematically varying stimulation timing across sleep stages together with stimulus intensity and envelope, aiming to shorten sleep onset latency and reduce micro-arousals during induction while minimizing time to waking and sleep inertia during wake promotion. Within these optimized regimes, a secondary tier tests whether aligning pulses to specific cardiorespiratory phases—derived from respiratory and cardiac cycle timing—adds practically relevant modulation of arousal probability and latency beyond stage and intensity alone. Phase is examined only in narrow, hypothesis-driven windows grounded in known locus coeruleus–norepinephrine and baroreflex timing mechanisms, comparing phase-locked pulses against matched phase-agnostic metronomic delivery. A pre-specified threshold of roughly 10–15% relative improvement determines whether phase sensing is worth incorporating into consumer devices. Because both positive and negative outcomes directly inform engineering decisions, the study functions as a mechanistically grounded, bounds-setting evaluation that prevents unjustified complexity while advancing bidirectional, non-invasive sleep–wake control.

text: The regulation of sleep pressure, quantified as slow-wave activity (SWA) accumulation and decay according to Process-S models, arises from a distributed circuit whose individual nodes may differ in their capacity to influence the homeostat itself rather than global arousal. This proposal asks whether a single node offers privileged leverage over sleep homeostasis by comparing the locus coeruleus, an arousal hub, with a more sleep-proximal node such as the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus or a cortico-thalamic hub. We will impose standardized sleep-deprivation protocols and apply matched, sub-saturating opto- or chemogenetic biases to each node during a critical window, adjusting stimulation so that added wake time and acute spectral content are equated across conditions. Per-animal Process-S models will then be fit to extract SWA build-up and decay time constants expressed as functions of actual wake history, yielding a history-normalized controllability metric that isolates node-specific influence from generic wake effects. Repeating the protocol across days, with independent readouts of each node's functional state, will disentangle actuator fatigue from network-level homeostatic reweighting. The results will reveal whether any single node constitutes a viable target for thermostat-like sleep interventions or whether homeostatic control is fundamentally distributed.

text: This proposal investigates whether a simple, clinically usable marker of distal vasodilation failure can guide the personalized application of thermal sleep interventions. The mechanistic basis is that a higher distal–proximal skin temperature gradient (DPG) around bedtime facilitates sleep onset, and distal warming can enhance this process in many individuals. The work proceeds in three falsifiable steps: first, we operationalize and validate a minimal, categorical DPG abnormality phenotype using home wearables in insomnia patients, oversampling those reporting cold extremities; second, we test whether this phenotype predicts enhanced benefit from an optimized fixed-timing distal warming protocol, yielding a physiologically grounded stratifier for existing thermal aids; and third, only within the enriched DPG-abnormal subgroup, we compare coarse, threshold-triggered DPG feedback control against the best fixed protocol. Primary outcomes include sleep onset latency and early-night wakefulness, alongside subjective sleep quality and comfort. At each stage a negative result remains interpretable, clarifying whether DPG-based personalization or feedback control is justified. By defining who should receive thermal aids and when physiology-guided feedback adds value, the program offers a sharper, mechanistically leveraged alternative to building increasingly sophisticated devices without evidence of benefit.

text: Impaired distal vasodilation, common among older adults and individuals with "cold extremities" or vascular dysregulation, is associated with prolonged sleep onset and fragmented sleep, likely because a weak or delayed rise in the distal-proximal skin temperature gradient (DPG) hinders the thermoregulatory processes that promote sleep. While pre-bed distal warming can shorten sleep latency and improve autonomic balance in healthy sleepers, it remains unclear whether efficacy in impaired vasodilators depends primarily on warming dose or on its timing relative to circadian and behavioral phase. This proposal describes a two-stage, within-subject mechanistic study in adults with documented reduced DPG. In Stage 1, we determine a dose-response surface by varying the intensity and duration of distal warming at a single favorable pre-bed time, identifying a mechanistically effective and comfortable dose. In Stage 2, we apply that optimized dose at early, mid, and late phases relative to habitual bedtime and estimated dim-light melatonin onset, comparing effects on DPG trajectory, heart rate variability, and early NREM stability, with sleep latency as a secondary outcome. By separating dose optimization from phase optimization, the study clarifies whether warming efficacy is strongly phase-dependent and whether the optimal phase is shifted in impaired vasodilators. Using standard, safe measurement tools, this work aims to establish whether circadian-phase-targeted warming provides an actionable, personalizable intervention and to lay the foundation for future timing-sensitive protocols.

text: We propose a closed-loop experimental platform that systematically maps how the efficacy of small, safe sleep-relevant nudges depends on peripheral physiological state. Using consumer-grade wearables, the system continuously senses distal and proximal skin temperature to derive the distal–proximal gradient, heart rate variability from photoplethysmography, movement via accelerometry, and circadian phase, while gentle actuators deliver brief thermal and light or sound interventions to facilitate sleep onset or promote wakefulness. Rather than committing to a sophisticated controller upfront, the platform employs a randomized perturbation engine that schedules low-dose nudges within user-defined pre-sleep and pre-wake windows, densely logging instantaneous state, short-window slopes, and volatility around each perturbation. Outcomes including sleep-onset latency, wake inertia, and subjective comfort are then related to peripheral state through causal-inference and regression methods, producing a state–effect map that estimates the conditional effect of each nudge across regions of the physiological state space. This design tests whether physiologically privileged windows exist where nudges are markedly more effective or carry fewer side effects. If strong state-dependence is found, the results guide targeted, mechanistically justified control policies; if not, they justify parsimonious time- or threshold-based protocols. By shifting complexity to offline analysis, the platform provides quantitative, shared empirical guidance for future controllers rather than another untested heuristic.

text: This proposal tests whether the prior-night homeostatic sleep state (Process S) modulates the brain's circadian phase response to light, under tight control of light history and circadian phase. Using a within-subject design, participants complete several condition days embedded in a fixed light and behavioral regimen, during which homeostatic state is experimentally manipulated through partial sleep restriction and sleep extension, with an optional subset receiving closed-loop auditory stimulation or pharmacological modulation to alter slow-wave activity independent of total sleep time. On each condition day, a standardized light pulse is delivered at a phase-matched time, and circadian phase shifts are quantified from a marker such as dim-light melatonin onset. A minimal, data-driven model then characterizes how the magnitude and variability of phase shifts depend on manipulated sleep state, examining possible global scaling, phase-region specificity, or threshold effects, and whether fine-grained slow-wave indices improve prediction beyond coarse metrics of sleep duration and efficiency. A robust dependence would justify sleep-state-conditioned phase-response mappings and homeostatically aware light-scheduling policies, whereas a null result would constitute a valuable negative finding that prevents over-engineering of such controllers. The design is laboratory-implementable with standard tools and emphasizes strong, focused perturbations over sprawling observational modeling, providing a causal foundation for whether last night's sleep alters today's circadian malleability.

text: This proposal develops a closed-loop transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) system to test whether the temporal organization of weak electric fields, independent of polarity or spatial configuration, can bidirectionally modulate slow-wave dynamics during sleep. Using a single fixed-polarity frontal montage, the system tracks the ongoing slow oscillation from a frontal electroencephalography lead and delivers short, intermittent stimulation bursts locked to predefined phase windows, while sham blocks with identical detection but no current serve as controls. The central hypothesis is that a modest, phase-aligned excitability bias shifts the probabilities of UP and DOWN state transitions, so that some phase windows favor longer, larger slow-wave trains while others favor shorter, fragmented ones. The study first maps phase–response relationships at a fixed burst structure, then applies stringent, preregistered criteria to determine whether a genuinely bidirectional phase pair exists, requiring reliable, opposite-signed, replicable changes in slow-wave train length and event incidence across nights. An optional extension varies burst density to probe temporal dosing effects. By isolating temporal targeting as the sole manipulated variable, the work clarifies the shape of the phase–response curve under realistic wearable dosing and establishes a mechanistically explicit, safe, and reproducible foundation for future sleep neuromodulation protocols.

text: Non-pharmacologic tools for controlling human sleep and wakefulness remain limited by the absence of a standardized arousal intervention with a known magnitude and time course, leaving prior attempts to infer homeostatic effects from unquantified perturbations difficult to interpret. This project develops and tests a calibrated morning arousal module based on transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) in healthy adults across two phases. In Phase 1, a within-subject design will define a taVNS parameter set that reliably produces a quantifiable arousal signature, indexed by pupil diameter, EEG alpha attenuation, heart rate variability, salivary alpha-amylase, and subjective alertness, benchmarked against pharmacologic comparators such as caffeine and against extended-wake blocks. This yields a parameterized arousal unit with explicit titration rules and characterized inter-individual variability. In Phase 2, the calibrated module will be applied in the morning under controlled wake, light, and caffeine conditions to test whether it systematically alters that night's slow-wave activity and N3 sleep, as measured by polysomnography, and daytime vigilance assessed by psychomotor vigilance testing. Because the perturbation magnitude is quantified, both null and directional outcomes will be interpretable, informing whether realistic arousal pulses are better suited to controlled wake promotion or to broader homeostatic manipulation. The result is a validated, lab-implementable building block for future bidirectional sleep–wake control strategies.

text: We propose an injectable, fully resorbable, cell-free hydrogel that forms a temporary regenerative niche for volumetric muscle loss and critical-size bone defects, using local oxygenation history as an intrinsic surrogate for vascular competence to govern its own degradation. Built from standard PEG/HA backbones, MMP-cleavable peptides, hydrolyzable linkers, and hypoxia-sensitive protecting groups, the material undergoes slow baseline hydrolysis that guarantees eventual clearance while a second, oxygen-informed pathway biases the rate of breakdown. During early hypoxia, reductively labile protecting groups are gradually removed, unmasking latent degradable sites without collapsing the network, so that only after vascular ingrowth restores moderate oxygen tension do these sites become efficiently cleavable by proteases and hydrolysis, accelerating degradation preferentially where perfusion and cellularity are highest. Because the key variable is cumulative exposure rather than a sharp threshold, the system is robust to moment-to-moment fluctuations and ties niche lifetime to the hypoxia-to-reoxygenation sequence that characterizes successful healing. This design allows the scaffold to persist longer in slow-healing, poorly vascularized defects while clearing earlier in well-perfused ones, offering a patient-adaptive alternative to fixed-schedule or indiscriminately enzyme-responsive hydrogels. We will calibrate unmasking kinetics under controlled oxygen histories in vitro, map oxygen trajectories and outcomes in animal models, and tune degradation rates so niche lifetime tracks vascular recovery across realistic comorbid conditions.

text: We propose a mechanically adaptive, cell-free scaffold that organizes early tissue repair and then progressively relinquishes its mechanical role as native tissue matures, addressing a central limitation of conventional degradable scaffolds whose fixed degradation timelines cannot match the spatial and temporal variability of healing. The scaffold combines a slowly resorbing backbone that maintains volume and connectivity with an interpenetrating soft phase built from reversible, dynamic crosslinks that are sensitive to cell-associated proteases and sustained deformation from cell traction. In regions where progenitors, endothelial cells, and matrix accumulate, these crosslinks relax and soften preferentially in the pericellular space, decoupling synthetic stiffness and shifting load onto newly deposited tissue, whereas underpopulated zones retain support until regeneration advances. An optional, tightly scoped inhibitor module transiently sequesters a single validated fibrotic factor to preserve access to the aligned architecture during the acute window. This design uses native tissue maturation itself as the signal for mechanical hand-off rather than relying on a global degradation clock, mitigating stress shielding and premature loss of support. Because the required chemistries and fabrication methods are established, the approach is feasible and testable through finite-element modeling and cyclic loading of cell-seeded constructs, offering a new paradigm of scaffolds that co-evolve mechanically with regenerating muscle or bone.

label: baseline
text: Bone repair of critical-size defects and fibrotic nonunions often defaults to disorganized fibrous tissue rather than functional bridging, and many current periosteum-mimetic scaffolds counter this by occupying substantial defect volume and persisting as long-term biochemical or mechanical participants. This proposal advances an alternative design philosophy centered on a minimal, fully resorbable periosteal sleeve conceived as a transient catalyst for spatial organization rather than a durable matrix. The construct is a thin hyaluronic acid/gelatin membrane that conforms to cut bone ends and adjacent periosteum, crosslinked with matrix metalloproteinase-degradable and hydrolytically labile linkers so that it persists only a few weeks with bioactivity front-loaded to the first days. A short pulse of pro-resolving cues, combining adenosine-releasing chemistry with interleukin-10-mimetic peptides, briefly biases local inflammation toward a resolving, endochondral-permissive state, while a soft, hyaluronic acid-rich interface encourages condensation-like clustering of endogenous progenitors along bone margins. As active remodeling proceeds, the membrane fragments and resorbs, allowing native tissue to define mature matrix and mechanics. We hypothesize that this "organize then leave" strategy converts a fibrotic trajectory into an endochondral-like bridging trajectory, and we will test it in head-to-head comparisons against stiffer, slower-degrading, or non-immunomodulatory periosteal controls.

text: We propose a single, anisotropic, fully resorbable scaffold for critical-size bone defects and volumetric muscle loss whose mechanical influence recedes preferentially where regenerating tissue becomes mechanically competent, rather than on a fixed degradation schedule. The scaffold combines an aligned, porous architected network with porosity and stiffness gradients, protease-cleavable crosslinks, and tethered adhesive and lineage-specific peptides, creating a cell-free tertiary niche that recruits and spatially organizes immune cells, vasculature, and endogenous progenitors. The central innovation is to treat load-sharing between scaffold and tissue as the primary design objective, exploiting two robust behaviors: cells upregulate proteases where they bear higher traction, and maturing extracellular matrix redistributes strain away from the scaffold. As a result, regions of stiffening, competent tissue draw more load and self-accelerate local scaffold softening, while regions of delayed healing retain mechanical support. We will use in vitro co-culture and loading studies, finite-element and network modeling, and longitudinal mechanical imaging to calibrate crosslink density, protease sensitivity, initial modulus, and architecture per site and defect type. This yields a mechanics-first, experimentally testable framework for self-terminating regeneration that avoids both stress shielding and premature loss of support, coupling scaffold dissolution to functional restoration.
