text: We propose a cell-free, fully resorbable hydrogel that functions as a transient regenerative niche for volumetric muscle loss and critical-size bone defects by rebalancing the local platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) versus transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) signaling axis that governs macrophage–stromal crosstalk and regenerative versus fibrotic outcomes. Rather than switching signaling on or off, the scaffold applies a moderate, temporally constrained bias: tunable-density TGF-β–binding motifs buffer excess TGF-β during fibrotic skew while physiological levels are preserved, and pre-loaded PDGF or PDGF-mimetic cues, together with supportive stiffness, adhesion, and microarchitecture, sustain progenitor recruitment and vascularization. Simple static spatial organization—stiffer osteoconductive cores for bone and anisotropic aligned structures for muscle—guides tissue formation without complex spatial logic. Using standard degradable backbones, the gel self-terminates on a pre-set schedule matched to the critical PDGF/TGF-β window, shedding its affinity motifs and clearing as native tissue matures. We will test whether this axis-biased gel outperforms non-biased and generic inflammation-responsive controls in muscle and bone defect models, assessing signaling profiles, progenitor recruitment, fibrosis, vascularization, and functional recovery. Success would establish a new design principle centering regenerative scaffolds on a specific signaling axis that both drives cell fate and defines the appropriate lifetime of a transient niche.

text: This proposal aims to develop a fully degradable, cell-free scaffold for the repair of large volumetric muscle loss and critical-size bone defects by integrating four functional design elements. The scaffold combines tissue-appropriate architecture that physically organizes incoming cells and vasculature, a fixed local immunoregulatory program that biases the inflammatory milieu toward pro-resolving and anti-fibrotic behavior, and matrix metalloproteinase–sensitive crosslinks that couple scaffold clearance to productive tissue remodeling. The central innovation is a pH-sensitive self-deactivation mechanism, in which acid-labile linkers mask the scaffold's most potent bioactive domains or accelerate degradation within persistently acidic, hostile microenvironments, and permit fuller expression of regenerative cues as local pH drifts toward neutrality. Rather than assuming a universal pH threshold, the work treats the relevant pH window and response slopes as empirical parameters to be tuned in defect models. The central testable hypothesis is that adding pH-sensitive self-deactivation reduces fibrosis and chronic inflammation and improves functional regeneration relative to architecture-only and pH-insensitive immunoregulatory scaffolds. Using established biomaterials fabrication and imaging, histological, and immune-phenotyping readouts, the project will determine whether pH-driven self-protection constitutes a meaningful design lever for next-generation, self-terminating regenerative niches in large musculoskeletal defects.

text: This proposal addresses a foundational question in human hematopoietic stem cell transplantation: whether introducing small, precisely placed noncoding edits at candidate safe-harbor loci measurably perturbs long-term hematopoietic reconstitution. We propose an ultra-minimal editing scheme with internal controls at two genomic loci, using homology-directed repair to generate three allelic states in a single mixed graft: unedited cells, sham-edited cells carrying only a repair scar, and tag-edited cells bearing a short, fixed, unexpressed noncoding insert. Donor CD34⁺ cells will be edited ex vivo without selection, transplanted under standard conditions, and sampled longitudinally from peripheral blood and bone marrow, with short amplicon sequencing quantifying the relative contributions of each allelic state across lineages and time points. By comparing tag, sham, and unedited compartments, the study can disentangle whether observed effects arise from the insert, the editing process itself, or locus-dependent constraints, thereby testing both locus and procedure neutrality. Integrating edit status with natural mitochondrial and nuclear barcodes further enables separation of pre-existing clones from transplant-origin edited clones, demonstrating the added value of a time-stamped genomic mark. If neutrality is supported, these validated loci and minimal designs will provide vector-agnostic, reusable anchors for future clonal tracking tools; if not, the study will clearly delineate the limits of safe-harbor assumptions in primary human cells.

label: baseline
text: Hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) monitoring currently relies on a patchwork of separate assays for engraftment chimerism, minimal residual disease or clonal hematopoiesis, and retrospective donor testing, leaving clinically critical questions—whether an emerging mutation reflects donor-derived clonal hematopoiesis, residual host clones, or relapse—difficult to resolve routinely. We propose a single duplex/UMI-based targeted next-generation sequencing panel whose primary outputs are, for each driver-defined clone detectable down to approximately 10⁻⁴ variant allele frequency, its clonal origin (donor versus recipient) and its distribution across myeloid, lymphoid, and megakaryocytic/erythroid lineages over the first post-transplant year. The assay combines an error-corrected driver-gene backbone covering common hematologic and clonal hematopoiesis genes with a minimal scaffold of high-heterozygosity SNP blocks positioned near recurrent hotspots, enabling origin attribution through direct read-level phasing, statistical co-segregation with lineage-specific chimerism dynamics, and confirmatory fallback sequencing when needed. Applying the same panel to modestly fractionated lineage compartments at serial timepoints yields chimerism metrics for free and produces a longitudinal, origin-aware lineage occupancy profile for every clone. Because panel complexity is bounded by the driver set and a small number of SNP blocks rather than genome-wide tiling, sequencing depth and cost remain comparable to existing duplex clonal hematopoiesis and SNP-based chimerism assays. This clone-centric platform replaces three fragmented workflows with one standardized, clinically translatable assay, and its design can be empirically optimized in pilot cohorts to maximize confident origin calls without altering its conceptual structure.

label: baseline
text: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) requires longitudinal monitoring of donor engraftment and clonal behavior, yet current tools rarely capture platelet lineage contributions or provide affordable serial surveillance across many patients. Here we propose a clinically compatible sequencing framework that relies exclusively on endogenous genetic variation—mitochondrial DNA polymorphisms and, where present, nuclear somatic mutations—to define persistent, cross-lineage donor clones over the first post-transplant year without engineered barcodes or genome editing. The approach uses a two-tier design: a training cohort of 20 to 50 diverse HSCT cases empirically establishes which variant patterns reliably mark stable clones and under what conditions platelet mtDNA is informative, yielding a semi-standardized targeted panel and explicit interpretation rules. A clone is operationally defined by consistent detection across multiple timepoints and presence in more than one mature compartment, thereby filtering out transient stress-responsive expansions. The validated panel is then deployed for routine, platelet-inclusive clonal monitoring, quantifying donor chimerism, clonal persistence, dominance, and lineage bias while distinguishing donor clonal hematopoiesis from recipient variants. By integrating mtDNA lineage tracing, clonal hematopoiesis profiling, and SNP-based chimerism into a coherent framework with defined failure modes, this platform adds a continuous, lower-cost surveillance layer that flags patients for more intensive investigation.

label: baseline
text: We propose a prospective clonal tracking platform for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in high-risk and investigational settings, including gene therapy, gene-edited grafts, novel conditioning regimens, and graft-manipulation protocols where clonal behavior is a central safety concern. The approach introduces a high-diversity, promoterless barcode cassette into a clinically vetted safe-harbor locus in donor CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, so that each persistent barcode serves as a proxy for a functional long-term repopulating unit rather than a literal stem cell count. Serial peripheral blood samples are fractionated into major hematopoietic lineages, and targeted sequencing of the barcode region quantifies clonal richness, evenness, and per-clone lineage bias over at least one year, enabling early detection of emergent or lineage-restricted dominant clones even when they remain subclonal by cell counts. Neutrality and safety of the insertion are treated as empirical questions, validated through competitive co-transplantation in immunodeficient mouse and non-human primate models before human deployment. An optional methylation micro-module reading lineage-biased CpG markers extends monitoring to predefined scenarios such as cell-free DNA-only sampling or erythroid and megakaryocytic outcomes. Positioned as a vector-agnostic, standardized overlay complementing chimerism and integration-site analysis, the platform delivers higher clonal resolution to inform trial design, dosing, and stopping decisions.

label: baseline
text: Lentiviral barcoding is widely used to track clonal dynamics in hematopoietic stem cell transplantation and gene therapy, yet barcode read counts are commonly treated as directly proportional to clone size despite the fact that cells frequently carry multiple integrants. This introduces a systematic but poorly quantified copy-number bias that inflates apparent clonal dominance and underestimates true clonal richness, particularly when viral dose deviates from an ideal single-copy regime. This project builds a focused, quantitative correction model for this distortion using a single, clinically relevant self-inactivating lentiviral vector to barcode primary human CD34⁺ cells transplanted into NSG mice. We systematically vary the multiplicity of infection, characterize barcode copy number and integration sites at single-cell resolution before transplant, track barcodes longitudinally in primary and secondary recipients, and use limiting-dilution secondary transplants as functional constraints on long-term hematopoietic stem cell clones. A hierarchical statistical model then links pre-transplant copy-number distributions, observed barcode counts, and functional readouts to infer underlying clone number and size with credible intervals. The resulting framework provides a validated multiplicity-of-infection window and a practical correction function, enabling copy-number–aware clonal inference with known, bounded distortions for the design and interpretation of barcoding-based transplantation studies.

text: Obesity worsens psoriasis, yet whether metabolic status meaningfully reshapes actionable disease pathways remains uncertain. This proposal tests whether obesity re-weights adenosine receptor biology—particularly the A2B–EGFR–IL-6 axis in keratinocytes—such that A2B becomes a privileged, obesity-stratified therapeutic lever, as opposed to canonical IL-17/TNF and lipid/hormonal drivers that operate irrespective of metabolic state. We will first mine existing human psoriatic skin transcriptomic datasets stratified by body mass index to assess whether CD73, A2A, A2B, and downstream EGFR/IL-6 signatures shift with obesity, then functionally probe adenosine-driven, A2B-dependent IL-6 and EGFR signaling in primary keratinocytes from obese versus lean psoriatic donors. In parallel, an imiquimod-induced dermatitis model in chow- and high-fat-diet-fed mice will provide cell-type-resolved mapping of adenosine enzymes, receptors, and A2B–EGFR–IL-6 coupling, with a small, conditional topical A2B-antagonist experiment triggered only if human and mouse mapping suggest an obesity-linked pathogenic shift. A pre-specified decision rule will classify results into scenarios where A2B is amplified, homeostatically protective, or unchanged by obesity. Because any outcome yields a clear translational conclusion, this efficient, human-anchored program will determine whether adenosine-targeted strategies warrant obesity stratification or should be deprioritized.

label: baseline
text: Psoriasis is frequently accompanied by obesity, insulin resistance, and hepatic steatosis, and systemic IL-23/17-axis cytokines are assumed to mediate much of this metabolic burden. However, it remains unclear whether psoriatic, IL-23/17-high skin exports additional mediators that reprogram adipocytes and hepatocytes beyond the effects of canonical cytokines, and how obesity reshapes this secretome. This project addresses that question through an ex vivo strategy combining unbiased secretome mapping with incisive comparative reconstitution tests. We will generate conditioned media from control and psoriatic skin in lean and obese contexts, characterizing cytokines, chemokines, secreted proteins, lipids, and extracellular vesicle cargo, and use data-driven clustering to define co-varying mediator groups. In parallel, we will treat adipocytes, hepatocytes, and organoids with full conditioned media versus recombinant cytokine cocktails matched to measured IL-17, TNF, IL-6, and IL-22 levels, quantifying insulin signaling, lipid accumulation, and inflammatory activation. Minimal add-on experiments will test whether supplementing cocktails with top non-canonical candidates, such as LCN2, S100 proteins, or vesicles, closes any residual gap. The result will be a quantitative estimate of how much psoriasis-driven metabolic reprogramming reflects canonical cytokines versus additional, obesity-rewired, potentially targetable secretome components.

label: baseline
text: This proposal establishes a comparative, mechanistic pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic program to determine whether short-acting agents that reduce uterine contractility or sympathetic drive can achieve clinically useful uterus-to-systemic selectivity when delivered by vaginal or intrauterine routes. The central strategy treats route and formulation as the global control variable and applies it across a panel of mechanistically distinct drug classes, including nitric oxide donors, α1-blockers, uterine-relaxant β-agonists, low-dose calcium channel blockers, and prostaglandin-pathway modulators. For each drug and route combination, we will measure uterine tissue and plasma exposure over time, local contractility and perfusion effects, and systemic safety indices such as blood pressure and heart rate, then construct exposure–effect surfaces relating local concentration to therapeutic benefit and plasma concentration to systemic risk. Predefined therapeutic targets and systemic no-effect boundaries convert the question into a clear feasibility test: does any feasible dosing range meet uterine goals while respecting systemic limits? Studies will proceed from animal models and ex vivo human myometrium to carefully controlled low-dose human bridging work. The deliverable is a comparative uterus-targeting landscape that either identifies a translatable class and route for a simple ring, pessary, or intrauterine device, or definitively shows this mechanistic approach is not viable, redirecting the field accordingly.

label: baseline
text: This proposal describes a first-in-human feasibility study to determine whether image-guided low-intensity ultrasound (LIUS) can differentially modulate uterine vascular reactivity in the deep pelvis under realistic clinical safety constraints. Currently, no validated non-invasive method exists to test organ-specific vascular modulation of clinically important indices such as uterine artery resistivity and pulsatility. We hypothesize that, during a standardized pharmacologic uterine vasoconstrictive challenge, LIUS directed at a uterine artery segment will measurably alter that vessel's resistivity and pulsatility response relative to a nearby, non-insonated pelvic comparator artery exposed to the same systemic drug conditions. Using a research-enabled clinical ultrasound platform, we will co-register a LIUS focus with a uterine artery, deliver short bursts at diagnostic-adjacent intensities in a randomized, blinded active-versus-sham design, and apply a difference-in-differences analysis comparing target and comparator vessels. The internal spatial control addresses the insensitivity of systemic hemodynamic measures and treats mechanism as a black box at this stage. A positive result would provide the first evidence of spatially selective, non-invasive uterine vascular modulation, whereas a rigorous null would constrain expectations and prevent overinvestment in implausible targeting strategies.

label: baseline
text: Excessive Gq-driven uterine contractions contribute to disorders of labor, yet current strategies to suppress them lack uterine selectivity. Regulator of G-protein signaling 2 (RGS2) acts as an endogenous brake on Gq-mediated calcium signaling in myometrium and could, in principle, be exploited to dampen contractility, but its expression is embedded within cAMP/CREB and calcium-dependent transcriptional programs that also drive pro-labor inflammatory outputs such as COX-2. This project asks whether RGS2-mediated braking within EP2-linked pathways can be causally and meaningfully separated from inflammatory signaling to yield a distinct long-term contractile phenotype in human myometrium. Using a lean three-part ex vivo program, we will first compare a small panel of EP2-family ligands for their RGS2 versus COX-2 outputs, calcium and force responses, and integrated contractile behavior over hours to a day; second, directly manipulate RGS2 by overexpression and knockdown at matched cAMP levels to test whether RGS2 alone reshapes long-term contractility; and third, perturb EP2 spatial signaling to probe whether cAMP microdomains bias the RGS2/COX-2 balance. Predefined thresholds for quantitative and functional separation will determine whether RGS2 constitutes a distinct, exploitable axis. The outcome will serve as a gatekeeper decision, either justifying RGS2-centric therapeutic development for uterus-selective contraction control or redirecting efforts toward alternative mechanisms.

label: baseline
text: This proposal investigates whether non-noxious stimulation of cervix-related and sacral afferents can directly modulate uterine mechanics in awake humans through segmentally organized spinal circuits, independent of pain relief or systemic sympathetic suppression. The central hypothesis is that low-threshold, Aβ-dominant stimulation of afferents converging on lumbosacral segments shifts the balance of excitatory and inhibitory drive to uterine efferents, thereby altering peristalsis and contractility in a segment-biased fashion. Two complementary paradigms share the same logic and controls: in healthy, pain-free volunteers, cine MRI will quantify junctional zone peristalsis during surface stimulation, while in individuals undergoing labor induction or augmentation, intrauterine pressure catheters will record contraction amplitude, frequency, and patterning. Both paradigms compare sacral stimulation configurations that emphasize different sacral segments against remote-dermatome stimulation and sham, with subjective sensory intensity matched across conditions and pelvic floor electromyography monitored to exclude co-activation artifacts. By studying pain-free volunteers and analgesia-controlled clinical periods, the design distinguishes direct segmental control from effects mediated by pain relief or generic arousal. Confirming a reliable, segment-dependent, pain-independent lever would establish a mechanistically grounded, non-invasive platform for later therapeutic development in dysmenorrhea and related conditions.

label: baseline
text: This proposal develops a minimal, differential experimental framework to test whether enforced three-dimensional chromatin proximity provides controllable causal leverage over transcription, beyond what passive chromatin fluctuations and actuator biochemistry already contribute. Using a reversible CRISPR/dCas9 dimerization system to induce two-point chromatin loops, the study focuses on a small panel of three to four extremal loci spanning active, poised, repressed, and boundary-proximal contexts. The central innovation is a three-condition comparison performed at each locus: passive dynamics with no actuator, a topology-on configuration in which dimerization shortens the enhancer–promoter path, and a topology-null configuration in which actuator occupancy is matched but contact probability is minimally altered. Live contact and transcription imaging, nascent RNA measurements at a few time points, and coarse early and late chromatin checks provide the principal readouts, while polymer-informed modeling verifies expected contact changes and relates transcriptional responses to contact gains. This within-locus, within-actuator differential design cancels most locus-specific biochemical effects and reframes the question as a practical dose–response between enforced contact and transcriptional timing and burst statistics. By combining parsimony with calibrated causal comparison, the project quantifies how much additional, controllable transcriptional modulation topology can supply across distinct chromatin environments.

label: baseline
text: The relationship between three-dimensional chromatin architecture and transcriptional output remains poorly understood, in part because raw enhancer–promoter distance is an incomplete predictor of gene activity. This proposal reframes the problem around an effective enhancer–promoter communication strength: a latent parameter capturing how efficiently regulatory information is transmitted between loci, integrating local chemistry, condensate dynamics, and chromatin state. We ask how much of this communication strength, and thus of transcriptional bursting, can be explained by measurable geometric features within a fixed biochemical looping context. Using an established dCas9-based looping system to generate multiple configurations at a single enhancer–promoter pair in epithelial cells, we will first correlate static geometry metrics from live-cell imaging with bursting parameters from single-molecule RNA measurements, fitting a communication strength parameter for each condition. A targeted second stage will apply time-resolved, multicolor imaging to informative configurations to determine which geometric descriptors, such as time spent below distance thresholds or co-residence within condensates, best predict communication strength. By treating geometry as a contributor rather than a surrogate, this staged, platform-anchored framework will quantify how strongly and in what form spatial arrangement governs transcriptional dynamics.

label: baseline
text: Gene activation at native promoters can be driven by multiple, often entangled mechanisms, including direct RNA polymerase II (Pol II) recruitment, coactivator condensate formation, and chromatin looping, yet their relative contributions in differentiated cells remain unclear. This proposal asks how far biased recruitment of endogenous Pol II complexes at native promoters can drive gene activation and phenotype, compared with architectures that primarily enhance condensate formation or enhancer–promoter contacts. We will construct a small, theory-driven panel of dCas9-based promoter-tethered architectures, each emphasizing a distinct mechanistic regime: a neutral scaffold control, a Pol II-biased low-condensate module, a condensate-biased Pol II-neutral module, a looping-biased module, and a full CRISPRa/LAMPS-like benchmark. Each architecture will be targeted to identical gRNA sites at a set of lowly expressed promoters that retain measurable basal Pol II activity in epithelial cells and neurons, controlling for sequence and chromatin context. We will assess Pol II occupancy and CTD phosphorylation, condensate imaging, targeted chromatin contacts, and nascent transcription and phenotype, emphasizing relative comparisons across the panel. This sparse, mechanistically explicit design directly tests when biased Pol II engagement is sufficient and when condensates or looping become necessary for activation.

label: baseline
text: This proposal investigates whether three-dimensional enhancer–promoter proximity can function as an independent, time-resolved information variable in gene regulation when classical chromatin-based memory is structurally minimized. We ask whether distinct histories of spatial contact can generate stable transcriptional states that cannot be reproduced by equivalent transcription factor exposure alone. To test this, we will build a minimal enhancer–promoter reporter cassette placed in a globally simplified chromatin environment, using either a nucleosome-poor episomal context or a cell background depleted for major histone-mark writer axes, thereby reducing the dominant channels for long-term epigenetic memory. Enhancer–promoter proximity will be controlled independently of transcription through an inert, inducible CRISPR-based dimerization system that enforces looping without recruiting activators or chromatin modifiers, allowing purely geometric perturbation. We will compare acute transcriptional responses, then contrast matched transcription factor exposure protocols that differ only in their looping history, and finally vary the temporal pattern and ordering of contact while holding integrated inputs constant. Divergent stable expression states arising from looping history alone would establish 3D architecture as a semi-autonomous control variable, whereas interchangeability with biochemical exposure would constrain claims about topology-based coding, making either outcome informative for understanding spatial regulation in epithelial cells and neurons.

label: baseline
text: Transcriptional control at enhancer–promoter pairs depends on three-dimensional genome architecture, but existing synthetic looping tools treat the looping scaffold as a black box, making it impossible to distinguish effects arising from enforced geometry from those introduced by the protein scaffold itself. This proposal develops a calibrated, model-constrained system to quantitatively partition these contributions. We will engineer a family of finite-valent dCas9 loopers that bind identical guides at the same locus but vary systematically in tether length and stiffness, spanning from a compact contact-like configuration to a maximally offset architecture, each equipped with a reversible on/off switch and carrying no activation domains. In parallel, we will specify an explicit biophysical model linking geometric parameters, an effective scaffold engagement term, and transcriptional bursting. At one or two well-characterized loci in epithelial cells or neurons, we will measure enhancer–promoter distance distributions and contact frequencies by live imaging and targeted 3C/FISH, burst frequency and amplitude by MS2 tagging, and co-regulator occupancy by targeted ChIP and proteomics, then fit these data to the model. The result will be a quantitative structure–function map estimating how much contact change is required for a given change in bursting and how much additional effect derives from scaffold engagement, with explicit confidence bounds and honest acknowledgment of biophysical limits.

label: baseline
text: Transcription bursting at genes embedded within super-enhancer hubs may be controlled by the pairwise three-dimensional distance between enhancers and promoters or, alternatively, by a shared hub state defined by coactivator condensate properties, with distance serving as a secondary correlate. Distinguishing these possibilities is critical for 3D genome engineering, since it determines whether interventions should target specific chromatin loops or condensate chemistry. We propose a minimal, perturbation-informed imaging and modeling framework applied to a well-characterized mouse embryonic stem cell super-enhancer locus, using four-channel live imaging to simultaneously track enhancer position, nascent transcription at two promoters via orthogonal RNA reporters, and a fluorescently tagged coactivator reporting hub state. From baseline movies we will quantify pairwise distances, dwell times, burst kinetics, and co-bursting statistics, and relate them to hub state over time. Two quasi-orthogonal perturbations will then bias either condensate material properties or looping geometry while leaving the other largely intact, allowing us to test which variable causally reorganizes bursting. Fitting distance-only, hub-state-only, and combined models across all conditions with information criteria and variance partitioning will reveal the unique predictive contribution of each factor. This work delivers a generalizable decision framework indicating whether future efforts should prioritize distance engineering or hub-state engineering to control gene expression through chromatin architecture.

label: baseline
text: The relationship between three-dimensional enhancer–promoter interactions and transcriptional bursting remains poorly understood, in part because most studies correlate contact probability with mean expression rather than distinguishing among competing causal mechanisms. This proposal develops a single-locus, model-driven experimental system that uses established forced-loop platforms as controllable perturbations to discriminate among alternative contact-to-burst models in epithelial cells or neurons. At one carefully chosen enhancer–promoter pair with a known natural loop, we combine a non-catalytic forced-looping tool to strengthen or weaken the loop, an MS2 reporter to quantify transcriptional bursts in live cells, and dual-color fluorescent labeling to track enhancer–promoter positioning over time. We define a small family of explicit mechanistic hypotheses—including a distance-threshold model, a condensate-mediated model, and a multi-enhancer integration model—each predicting distinct statistical relationships between locus distance trajectories and bursting dynamics. Using hidden Markov and Bayesian inference, we fit and compare these models against joint imaging and MS2 data across baseline, strengthened, and weakened loop conditions, treating effective contact as a latent state. The primary outcome is identification of which mechanisms are consistent with the data, transforming forced looping from a demonstration tool into a rigorous mechanistic probe and establishing a tractable, hypothesis-driven foundation for later extension to additional loci, chromatin marks, and phenotypes.

label: baseline
text: The three-dimensional organization of the genome shapes gene expression, yet how graded changes in native chromatin architecture translate into transcriptional output, and whether restoring physical contacts alone can rescue compromised loci, remain poorly understood. This proposal addresses these questions at the CFTR locus, whose regulation depends on epithelial enhancers and CTCF/cohesin boundaries that have previously been studied mainly through binary deletions. We will engineer a small, pre-defined panel of CFTR alleles in 16HBE cells that vary enhancer strength and insulation across a few maximally informative states, and quantify promoter–enhancer contacts, steady-state and single-cell expression, and epithelial chloride conductance to construct a coarse dose–response map linking scaffold strength to function. In selected compromised architectures, we will then introduce a minimal, effector-free dCas9-based synthetic loop between the promoter and a key enhancer to test whether restoring contact probability is sufficient to rescue expression. We predict a contact-limited regime in which looping substantially restores output and a scaffold-encoded regime in which enforced contacts fail to rescue despite restored proximity. By combining graded perturbations with an explicit sufficiency test, this work will transform qualitative statements about element importance into a quantitative, mechanistic account of CFTR’s architecture–function relationship.

label: baseline
text: Transcriptional activation by CRISPR-based looping systems could reflect either the enforcement of three-dimensional enhancer–promoter proximity or the recruitment of condensate-like coactivator assemblies, yet existing studies typically vary looping and coactivator activity together, obscuring their relative contributions. This proposal develops a minimal, mechanistically focused framework to determine whether enforced looping retains marginal control over transcriptional bursting once condensate machinery is partially compromised. Using a single inducible dCas9 looper targeted to one or two MS2-tagged reporter loci, we will tune looper strength across discrete levels and directly measure loop occupancy by live imaging or targeted chromatin conformation capture, while quantifying burst frequency, duration, and size. We will fit an empirical relation linking measured contact metrics to bursting parameters in condensate-competent cells, then introduce an acute, selective perturbation of condensate competence, such as degron-mediated BRD4 or MED1 depletion, and re-measure both occupancy and bursting at each looper strength. Because loop occupancy is measured rather than assumed, indirect effects of condensate perturbation on contact are explicitly captured. The analysis will reveal whether the contact–burst relationship collapses under diminished condensate function or whether a contact-dominated regime persists. The deliverable is a quantitative constraint defining how far three-dimensional rewiring alone can drive transcription.

label: baseline
text: Enhancer–promoter (E–P) communication depends on three-dimensional genome architecture, yet the functional limits of engineered looping tools and the potential contribution of biomolecular condensates remain poorly defined. This proposal poses a concrete, falsifiable question: at E–P pairs where classical inducible looping systems fail to sustain durable proximity and transcription, can locus-targeted condensates rescue these same readouts at the same loci? Using matched enhancer–promoter targets in keratinocytes and neurons, we will first map the failure regime of dCas9-based inducible looping across a defined distance band and compact chromatin contexts, measuring E–P dwell time, contact frequency, and nascent transcription. We will then deploy a phase-separation-competent scaffold to the same elements and quantify whether it converts non-responsive loci into responsive ones, while a high-valency, phase-separation-defective control distinguishes condensate-specific effects from increased tether strength. Where rescue occurs, a lean polymer-physics analysis will test whether condensate behavior systematically deviates from the distance–contact relationship inferred without phase separation. Whether positive or negative, the outcome will clarify how condensates extend the functional range of 3D genome control.

label: baseline
text: This proposal investigates whether pattern recognition receptor (PRR) signaling, specifically RAGE and TLR4 pathways, undergoes tolerance-like adaptation within neurovascular compartments relevant to diabetic neuropathy, including the dorsal root ganglia (DRG), sciatic nerve, and spinal cord. Using established mouse models of diabetic polyneuropathy combined with global and myeloid-restricted PRR perturbations, we will characterize nerve-associated macrophages and endothelial cells across disease stages through a focused panel measuring signaling kinetics, negative regulator induction, receptor handling, and chromatin tone, complemented by side-by-side ex vivo ligand stimulation to distinguish cell-intrinsic adaptation from ligand gradient effects. A tiered design ensures interpretable outcomes: persistent high-gain activation would support systemic PRR blockade, whereas evidence of regional adaptation, particularly divergence in the DRG, would motivate region-targeted interventions, which we will functionally test by modulating the identified adaptive axis. In parallel, we will conduct a pragmatic translational experiment delivering a PRR or NF-κB modulator with biased regional exposure to determine where modulation yields the greatest improvement in pain, nerve conduction, and structural outcomes. This lean, mechanism-centered approach delivers actionable guidance under all outcome scenarios, clarifying whether neurovascular PRR circuits in diabetic neuropathy are fundamentally adaptive or persistently activated, and where therapeutic targeting should be focused.

label: baseline
text: Diabetic neuropathy involves methylglyoxal (MGO)-driven damage to dorsal root ganglion (DRG) nociceptors, where reactive carbonyl species modify key ion channels and activate cellular stress pathways to produce neuropathic pain. Although global manipulation of the MGO-detoxifying enzyme glyoxalase 1 (GLO1) influences neuropathy, it remains unclear whether therapeutic leverage lies in systemic, liver-centered detoxification that lowers circulating MGO, or in enhancing local detoxification capacity within nociceptors themselves. This proposal develops a minimal in vivo framework using AAV-mediated, compartment-specific GLO1 overexpression to distinguish these possibilities, contrasting liver-only versus DRG-only manipulation alongside a catalytically dead GLO1 control that isolates MGO-specific effects from generic overexpression stress. Primary endpoints are intracellular, cell-type–resolved readouts in IB4+ nociceptors, including integrated stress response activation and MGO/AGE adducts on channels such as TRPA1 and Nav1.8, complemented by systemic MGO, redox markers, and behavioral and electrophysiological measures. Redox and glutathione markers are explicitly monitored to account for pleiotropic effects, and compartmental targeting is validated to ensure that conclusions reflect the intended detoxification shift. By determining whether normalizing intracellular nociceptor stress requires systemic or local intervention, this work will prioritize the more efficient therapeutic axis for MGO-driven diabetic neuropathy.

label: baseline
text: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) is a common and disabling complication, yet the cellular origins of dorsal root ganglion (DRG) vulnerability remain unclear. This proposal tests the hypothesis that glial programs—principally the satellite glial cell LCN2–PPARβ/δ–PDK2 axis and coupled sphingolipid and complement/inflammatory remodeling—largely determine structural and functional DRG resilience in diabetes, potentially rendering complex neuron-centric metabolic engineering unnecessary. In an initial stage, we will re-analyze existing single-cell, single-nucleus, and bulk transcriptomic datasets from rodent and human DRG and peripheral nerve to test whether these glial signatures consistently align with structurally defined resilience proxies, including preserved axonal integrity and reduced chronic damage markers. We will then conduct glia-centric head-to-head perturbations in a DRG-on-chip co-culture platform and one in vivo diabetic model, comparing satellite glial modulation of the LCN2–PDK2 axis against sphingolipid/complement correction, with at most a single minimal neuronal metabolic adjunct. Readouts will encompass axonal integrity, neuronal excitability and conduction, energetic status, and redox and inflammatory markers to determine which glial strategy best reproduces resilience. Only if glial interventions leave a substantial gap will we build a minimal one- to two-gene neuronal module as a mechanistic probe. This falsification-aware, deliberately lean design will clarify whether fine-tuned glial programs constitute a transferable DRG resilience strategy.

label: baseline
text: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy involves both microvascular dysfunction and pathological changes in dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons and satellite glial cells, yet it remains unclear how long correcting vascular impairment can still reset neural and glial trajectories before these changes become self-sustaining. This proposal defines the reversibility of vascular contributions to neuropathy as a graded, mechanistically measurable property rather than an absolute point of no return. Using a tamoxifen-inducible, endothelial-specific manipulation that restores DRG and nerve microvascular perfusion, barrier integrity, and reduces local inflammation under constant systemic hyperglycemia, we will normalize vascular state at staged times after diabetes induction and quantify vascular trajectories through pre-specified metrics of early deviation, cumulative burden, and peak injury. A two-phase readout strategy first maps rescue, partial-rescue, and non-rescue outcomes across timing groups using simple neuronal, glial, and behavioral markers, then applies single-cell RNA sequencing at selected boundary conditions to test whether glia remain activated and vulnerable neuronal subsets remain lost despite restored vascular health. By tying intervention timing directly to measured vascular state rather than calendar duration, this design will identify when DRG neurons and glia become autonomous from their microvascular environment. The results will yield a data-driven, time-bounded window during which vascular correction can still reshape neural outcomes, and beyond which direct neuro-glial targeting becomes necessary.

label: baseline
text: Painful diabetic neuropathy (PDN) can be mitigated by endothelial-directed interventions, but it remains unclear whether their benefits derive solely from restoring the blood–nerve barrier and lowering inflammation, or whether a distinct trophic/metabolic endothelial output is additionally required for durable nociceptor stabilization. This project tests these competing hypotheses using a deliberately minimal design centered on a single well-characterized mouse model of PDN. In Stage 1, we contrast a barrier/inflammation-dominant intervention with fenofibrate, which robustly engages PPARα–AMPK–PGC-1α–eNOS signaling, and measure predefined panels along two axes: barrier/inflammation markers and trophic/metabolic markers, together with nociceptor mitochondrial, ion-channel, and behavioral readouts. If both arms normalize barrier and inflammatory measures yet only the metabolic arm improves nociceptor state and pain durability, the trophic/metabolic dimension is implicated as necessary. Stage 2 then defines a minimal candidate module and tests its sufficiency in diabetic-like dorsal root ganglion cultures by incrementally adding or removing components on an anti-inflammatory baseline. The outcome will clarify whether endothelial protection reduces to barrier/inflammation control or requires a compact, targetable metabolic/trophic module relevant to modeling pain remission.

label: baseline
text: In established type 2 diabetes, capsaicin-sensitive small-fiber afferents innervating the pancreas and liver may not simply be damaged but instead occupy a disease-shifted activity regime whose net effect on glucose homeostasis becomes catabolic. We propose that these afferents can be therapeutically retuned, such that shifting their activity toward a mid, quasi-physiological window improves glycemia in diabetic animals while producing neutral or harmful effects in non-diabetic controls. To test this, we will first classify disease-state–dependent structural and functional changes in pancreatic and hepatic afferents in diabetic versus control mice, distinguishing sprouting, pruning, and remodeling using fiber mapping, activity markers, and ex vivo calcium imaging. We will then use organ-specific chemogenetic and optogenetic actuators to apply graded inhibition and excitation, constructing activity–glycemia curves that identify a diabetic-specific "sweet spot" and compare the therapeutic window across pancreas and liver. Finally, contingent on a robust non-linear, state-dependent effect, we will determine whether local CGRP and NK1 signaling is necessary within that window using targeted peptide antagonists. This framework moves from binary knockout approaches to a continuous, tunable model of neuropathy, defining diabetic sensory afferents as a dynamic and druggable driver of metabolic state.

label: baseline
text: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy remains a poorly treated complication of diabetes, and although Nrf2-activating therapies show promise, the cellular locus of their protective action is unresolved. This project asks whether Nrf2 activity within dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons accounts for most of the benefit of Nrf2-activating drugs and, conditionally, whether β-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) contributes a distinct metabolic–epigenetic program that Nrf2 alone cannot provide. In the first part, we will treat diabetic mice with a fumarate-class Nrf2 activator and profile DRG using bulk transcriptomics, targeted metabolomics, and separation of neuronal versus non-neuronal fractions, then use Advillin-Cre–based genetic models to elevate Nrf2 specifically in DRG neurons and quantify how much of the pharmacologic protection is recapitulated. In the second part, contingent on demonstrating meaningful neuronal Nrf2 protection, we will apply an in vitro gate in high-glucose, methylglyoxal-stressed DRG neurons to test whether physiologic BHB induces histone β-hydroxybutyrylation and a transcriptional module distinct from Nrf2, followed by in vivo comparison of Nrf2 alone versus Nrf2 plus BHB. Readouts will span neuropathy behavior, nerve function, cell-type-resolved gene expression, and locus-specific histone modifications. By coupling stepwise, decision-gated experiments with minimal but sufficient cell-type resolution, the study will either establish DRG-biased Nrf2 enhancement as a dominant therapeutic axis or reveal a mechanistically distinct Nrf2–ketone interaction, providing field-level clarification in either outcome.

label: baseline
text: Diabetic sensory neurons appear to operate within a narrow ATP–calcium safety window, in which limiting mitochondrial calcium entry through partial MCU inhibition and enhancing metabolic capacity through AMPK/PGC-1α activation both improve neuropathy phenotypes. Whether the spatial organization of endoplasmic reticulum–to–mitochondria calcium delivery at membrane contact sites offers additional therapeutic leverage remains untested, and this proposal addresses that question directly. We will first establish an optimized baseline in well-characterized diabetic dorsal root ganglion nociceptors by combining partial MCU inhibition with AMPK/PGC-1α activation to achieve near-maximal rescue of mitochondrial function and electrophysiological stability. On this background, we will introduce modest, spatially restricted, rapalog-inducible synthetic tethers to slightly tighten local ER–mitochondria proximity, while simultaneously measuring ER calcium release, mitochondrial calcium dynamics, ATP levels, and conduction fidelity, with built-in controls for mitochondrial transport, morphology, and ER stress. Membrane contact site modulation will be judged beneficial only if it improves the ATP-to-calcium ratio and functional resilience beyond the optimized baseline without provoking additional stress or organelle disruption. By converting a broad claim that contact sites matter into a precise, falsifiable test with explicit go/no-go criteria, this study will either identify a spatially specific therapeutic handle or demonstrate that therapeutically relevant control resides at calcium entry and metabolic signaling, informing future engineering priorities.

label: baseline
text: Diabetic neuropathic pain frequently persists even after hyperglycemia is corrected, yet whether this persistence reflects a self-sustaining intrinsic state within dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons and satellite glia or ongoing extrinsic maintenance by extracellular vesicle (EV)–mediated signaling remains unresolved. This proposal establishes DRG-intrinsic reversibility as a benchmark before evaluating EVs as upstream drivers. In Aim 1, we induce diabetic neuropathy in mice, restore normoglycemia until pain stabilizes, and characterize persistent epigenetic, metabolic, and ion-channel programs (including TET2–TXNIP–NLRP3, SIRT1, PARP1, and PDK2/4 axes) using single-cell transcriptomics; we then apply DRG-restricted interventions after glucose control to quantify the magnitude and time course of intrinsic pain reversal. In Aim 2, we use inducible, lineage-restricted perturbations to dampen EV output from Schwann cells, DRG neurons, and a vascular or immune source after normoglycemia, comparing behavioral and molecular changes against the intrinsic reversal trajectory to judge whether specific sources maintain the locked state. In Aim 3, minimal ex vivo add-and-remove experiments in DRG slices and co-cultures test whether source-specific EVs causally impose or sustain these signatures. By evaluating EV manipulations relative to a defined intrinsic reversibility ceiling, this trajectory-based framework interprets partial and delayed effects realistically and localizes where diabetic pain memory resides.

label: baseline
text: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy is a common and disabling complication, and β-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) has been proposed as a protective intervention, yet it remains unclear whether any benefit reflects genuine neuronal fuel utilization or receptor-mediated and systemic signaling effects. This proposal introduces a minimal discriminant design to determine whether dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons oxidize ketone bodies in a therapeutically meaningful way, using streptozotocin-induced diabetic mice maintained at fixed hyperglycemia. We first test whether modest BHB administration improves neuropathy endpoints, including pain behavior, nerve conduction velocity, neuronal excitability, mitochondrial potential, and oxidative damage, without inducing marked ketosis. We then apply 13C-labeled BHB and glucose tracing with oxygen consumption and reactive oxygen species measurements in ex vivo DRG preparations to quantify direct neuronal ketone oxidation. If both benefit and oxidation are confirmed, two cell-type-specific in vivo perturbations—neuronal OXCT1 loss to constrain oxidation and neuronal HCAR2 loss to constrain signaling—will dissociate metabolic from receptor-mediated mechanisms, with an optional Schwann-cell module addressing glial ketogenesis. The design yields falsifiable outcomes that clarify whether neuron-targeted ketone fueling, ketone signaling, or glial metabolism represents the most rational therapeutic target.

label: baseline
text: Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) signaling in keratinocytes is known to become hyporesponsive after activation, yet how responsiveness evolves over time following a single stimulus, and whether this temporal structure can be selectively tuned, remains poorly understood. This proposal aims to determine whether basal-like human keratinocytes encode a finite, time-structured tolerance profile after a brief priming pulse with a synthetic TLR2 ligand, and whether distinct kinetic classes of negative regulators reshape that profile in the time domain rather than merely altering its amplitude. Using two-dimensional basal-enriched keratinocyte monolayers, we will first map a high-resolution temporal tolerance curve by challenging primed and naïve cells at multiple intervals up to 24 hours and quantifying NF-κB nuclear dynamics alongside cytokine outputs. We will then characterize the kinetics of a fast proximal regulator (IRAK-1 degradation) and an intermediate regulator (A20) to confirm their temporal roles. Finally, we will perturb each node through controlled stabilization, overexpression, or knockdown and test whether IRAK-1 predominantly governs the early onset and recovery of tolerance while A20 shapes its mid-to-late maintenance. This design will reveal whether epithelial TLR2 signaling stores recent history through a multi-layered temporal memory kernel, or whether short-term tolerance is fundamentally amplitude-based, providing a clear mechanistic foundation for future work in more complex models.

label: baseline
text: The skin barrier is continuously exposed to bacterial extracellular vesicles (EVs), yet it remains unclear whether keratinocytes merely respond to current microbial signals or retain a durable functional memory of prior exposures that shapes subsequent inflammatory responses. This proposal develops a minimal, three-phase two-dimensional assay in primary human keratinocytes to test whether prior exposure to Staphylococcus aureus versus Staphylococcus epidermidis EVs leaves a lasting imprint analogous to innate immune training or tolerance. Cells are first primed with pathogenic EVs, commensal EVs, or no EVs, then maintained in EV-free medium during a defined recovery window to separate transient signaling from durable adaptation, and finally challenged with the same or opposing EVs or a non-EV NF-κB stimulus. Core readouts include NF-κB dynamics and cytokine output, with built-in controls for EV uptake and clearance, viability, proliferation, and differentiation state across all phases to prevent misinterpretation from toxicity or clonal selection. The inclusion of a non-EV challenge distinguishes generalized pathway rewiring from EV-specific history encoding. By treating history as an explicit functional composite rather than requiring chromatin profiling, this lean design yields a laboratory-ready proof of concept, delivering clear evidence for or against durable, stimulus-specific keratinocyte training or tolerance induced by sequential Staphylococcal EV exposure.

label: baseline
text: The skin microbiome shapes keratinocyte responses to pathogens, yet whether the sequence of exposure to commensal versus pathogenic bacterial signals produces order-dependent effects remains largely unexplored. This proposal tests whether primary human keratinocytes integrate sequential exposure to extracellular vesicles (EVs) from Staphylococcus epidermidis and Staphylococcus aureus in an order-dependent manner, and how fragile any such pattern is to metabolic versus receptor-proximal perturbation. We will first establish a quantitative, reproducible order effect by comparing commensal-first (SE→SA) and pathogen-first (SA→SE) sequences, matched for total dose and exposure time, using inflammatory cytokine and early differentiation markers as readouts. We will then determine whether this order-dependent signature is selectively altered, preserved, or globally suppressed under modest glycolytic inhibition with low-dose 2-deoxyglucose or under TLR2 blockade, with internal positive controls confirming that residual responsiveness and pathway activity are maintained. Rather than attempting to localize a molecular memory, the study delivers a falsifiable characterization of whether a robust order-dependent phenotype exists and how it deforms under two orthogonal levers. Implementable within three months using standard culture and assay methods, this work provides a foundation for deeper mechanistic follow-up on commensal modulation of pathogen responses.

label: baseline
text: The skin microbiome comprises commensal and pathobiont staphylococcal species whose signals reach host cells in part through bacterial extracellular vesicles (EVs), yet it remains unclear whether the temporal sequence of these encounters leaves a durable, chromatin-linked memory in epidermal progenitors. This proposal tests whether trainable basal-like human keratinocyte progenitors encode the temporal order of EV signals from Staphylococcus epidermidis and Staphylococcus aureus beyond transient effects of the local milieu and receptor desensitization. We adopt a two-tier design: the first tier confirms that the keratinocyte system can acquire trained-immunity-like behavior and chromatin changes using a well-characterized agonist followed by S. aureus EV restimulation, while the second tier imposes reciprocal EV exposure sequences (commensal-then-pathobiont versus pathobiont-then-commensal) under short and long washout intervals. Readouts include secreted cytokines, an inflammatory and differentiation gene panel, keratin and barrier marker ratios, and H3K27ac or ATAC signal at a pre-registered locus set in enriched KRT14-positive cells. By comparing outcomes across timescales, the design distinguishes durable chromatin-based memory from short-lived mechanisms and yields interpretable conclusions under every result scenario. This focused, feasible proof-of-concept establishes a mechanistically grounded first step toward understanding temporal logic in keratinocyte-microbe communication.

label: baseline
text: This proposal investigates whether the temporal patterning of a single inflammatory stimulus, independent of total dose, can imprint a stable and cell-intrinsic state in primary basal keratinocytes that alters their response to a subsequent challenge. To address this question, we develop a logically minimal two-dimensional history-encoding assay using primary basal keratinocytes and a single cytokine or Toll-like receptor agonist delivered under three conditions: naive, a single continuous pulse, and a dose-matched split pulse with the same integrated exposure but different temporal structure. We first empirically define a usable memory window by identifying two timepoints that lie after acute signaling has largely subsided but before differentiation drift or viability loss, confirmed through markers of inflammation, differentiation, proliferation, and viability. Cells subjected to each history are then rested and exposed to a standardized second challenge at these early and later timepoints, with inflammatory and differentiation gene expression as readouts. Comparing naive versus single-pulse histories tests for generic priming or tolerance, while comparing dose-matched single- and split-pulse histories isolates temporal encoding from cumulative dose. Persistence of differences to the later timepoint distinguishes durable encoded states from transient adaptation. By using primary cells, an explicitly defined post-acute pre-differentiation window, and a dose-matched temporal contrast, this feasible proof-of-concept design directly tests whether epidermal cells can stably encode temporal features of inflammatory history.

label: baseline
text: This proposal tests whether primary human keratinocytes, cultured in simple two-dimensional conditions and without immune cells, can undergo order-dependent, lasting reprogramming of their inflammatory responsiveness following a single defined pattern-recognition-receptor stimulus. Using a train–wash–challenge design, naïve keratinocytes from multiple donors will first be exposed to one of two mechanistically distinct Toll-like receptor ligands, carefully dose-matched to produce comparable acute NF-κB activation and early cytokine output, or to a vehicle control. After a washout period of one to three days in ligand-free medium, all groups will receive an identical standardized challenge, and their responses will be compared. Readouts include NF-κB activation kinetics, cytokine secretion, and a focused panel of inflammatory and barrier genes measured before and after challenge, with optional chromatin profiling of H3K27ac and H3K4me3 at persistently altered loci to probe cell-intrinsic mechanisms. Reproducible, donor-paired differences in the response to the identical challenge would demonstrate that keratinocytes encode first-hit identity in a durable manner. This minimal, lineage-specific assay is framed as a de-risking foundation: a positive result would justify building more complex organoid and stem-cell systems, whereas a null result would caution against over-interpreting order effects in such settings.

label: baseline
text: This proposal investigates whether pre-exposure of stem/progenitor-rich skin organoids to Staphylococcus epidermidis-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) can induce a protective epithelial state that limits damage from subsequent challenge with Staphylococcus aureus-derived EVs. In Stage 1, organoids with a defined basal layer will be primed with purified S. epidermidis EVs across a range of priming durations and rest intervals, then challenged with S. aureus EVs, using inflammatory cytokines, basal and differentiation markers, and morphology as readouts to map a reproducible protective pre-exposure window that persists after longer rest. In Stage 2, contingent on identifying such a window, we will test whether one or a few simple, mechanistically anchored measurements taken at the end of priming can predict later protection, comparing an inexpensive extracellular scalar such as medium lactate with a minimal transcriptional and secreted mini-signature linked to basal, aryl hydrocarbon receptor, and barrier programs. We will assess whether any scalar or low-dimensional composite tracks the degree of protection more reliably than trivial metrics. The study uses only standard methods, including EV isolation, organoid culture, qPCR, ELISA, and lactate assays, and is feasible within three months. Whether positive or negative, the results will clarify how far complex commensal conditioning states can be approximated by practical, low-dimensional operational surrogates in epithelial systems.

label: baseline
text: This proposal develops a function-only proof-of-concept in basal-enriched human keratinocyte monolayers to characterize the temporal dynamics and mechanistic dependence of Staphylococcus aureus-like inflammatory priming. In the first component, keratinocytes maintained in a basal-like state are exposed to a single sub-toxic pulse of a TLR2/6-biased ligand, then rested and re-challenged at multiple time points to generate a kinetic map of hyper-responsiveness across one to seven days, with parallel assessment of differentiation markers, proliferation, and viability to monitor compositional drift. In the second component, a reversible inhibitor of a defined regulatory axis (NF-κB, HAT, or BET) is applied during either an early establishment window or a later maintenance window, followed by complete washout, with inflammatory outputs read out at day seven in the absence of inhibitor in all conditions. Because perturbation and readout are temporally separated, differences in day-seven responsiveness reflect history dependence rather than acute pathway blockade, allowing a specific test of whether priming requires this axis within a time-bounded consolidation phase. The design does not resolve molecular substrates or clonal versus population effects, but it offers a tractable, reproducible scaffold demonstrating a transition from an inhibitor-sensitive to an inhibitor-insensitive primed state. This provides a temporal and mechanistic foundation for formalizing epithelial inflammatory memory that can later integrate microbiome-derived cues and higher-resolution epigenetic tools.

label: baseline
text: This proposal investigates whether single priming of human basal-like keratinocytes with Staphylococcus aureus–derived bacterial membrane vesicles (BMVs), but not Staphylococcus epidermidis BMVs, installs a persistent inflammatory state that outlives acute NF-κB signaling and aligns with gene modules relevant to hidradenitis suppurativa and atopic dermatitis. Using a controllable two-dimensional keratinocyte culture system, we operationally define memory as a basal-enriched transcriptional shift at disease-relevant modules that remains altered 24–72 hours after BMV removal, only once immediate-early NF-κB targets, generic stress and DNA-damage markers, and detectable residual BMV cargo have returned to baseline. The primary readout is a small, disease-informed expression panel including the S100A cluster and IL1 axis, complemented by a recall-challenge assay to test for a trained-like response bias. If clear differences between conditions emerge, focused chromatin assays at a minimal set of enhancers will assess whether persistent transcription reflects sustained enhancer activation consistent with epigenetic training. Explicit viability and stress-normalization prerequisites protect the claim of keratinocyte-intrinsic persistence rather than lingering damage. Within roughly three months, this proof-of-concept aims to decisively determine whether pathobiont signals uniquely stabilize a disease-like basal inflammatory bias, informing future tests of commensal rescue and microbiome-based interventions.

label: baseline
text: Intestinal epithelial cells express the serotonin transporter (SERT) and are frequently proposed to tune local immune responses by regulating basolateral serotonin (5-HT) available to lamina propria dendritic cells and T cells, yet this assumption has not been quantitatively tested. This proposal asks whether modulation of epithelial SERT can shift basolateral 5-HT enough to cross immune-relevant signaling thresholds, and whether such control persists when other local 5-HT sources are present. Using polarized organoid or Ussing-type epithelial preparations with standardized apical 5-HT input, the first stage will empirically bound the change in basolateral 5-HT achievable through acute SERT inhibition or enhancement, both under epithelium-dominated conditions and with added neuronal- or platelet-like inputs. The second stage will define receptor-specific dose-response relationships in dendritic cells and CD4 T cells across that same concentration window, measuring rapid signaling, cytokine output, and T cell differentiation bias, with pharmacological dissection of 5-HT2, 5-HT4, and 5-HT7 receptors. An integrated epithelial-immune co-culture will provide a cross-check that immune responses in a more realistic geometry match the simpler titration assays. By aligning empirical dynamic ranges, the work yields a quantitative, receptor-aware falsification window that will either constrain or substantiate epithelial SERT as a homeostatic immune gain control.

label: baseline
text: Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease encompasses genetically diverse peripheral neuropathies for which durable, subtype-agnostic therapies remain lacking, and it is unclear whether epigenetic modulation within Schwann cells can meaningfully reshape chronic disease trajectories. This proposal aims to define the smallest mechanistically coherent set of epigenetic axes capable of chronically ameliorating pathology across multiple CMT genotypes and potentially imprinting a durable preventive state. Using myelinating Schwann cell–neuron co-cultures and organotypic explants modeling CMT1A-like, CMT1B-like, and axonal defects under continuous endogenous stress, we will pursue a staged, decision-gated strategy. We first benchmark chronic modulation of well-characterized global levers, including the PRC2/H3K27me3 axis, Egr2-antisense lncRNA, the c-Jun injury program, and HDAC regulators, to establish their true therapeutic window. If these prove insufficient, we will map chronic epigenetic trajectories to identify a minimal convergent control set that distinguishes resilient from vulnerable responses, then chronically tune these axes to test efficacy and specificity. Finally, validated axes will be assessed for durable preventive imprinting through transient pre-modulation. The design yields either a small, mechanistically grounded preventive program or a principled demonstration of the limits of Schwann-intrinsic epigenetic re-baselining, redirecting effort toward combined strategies.

label: baseline
text: Acute myeloid leukemia stem cells (LSC) and normal long-term hematopoietic stem cells (LT-HSC) share most adhesion and signaling molecules, making selective LSC eradication difficult without damaging normal hematopoiesis. This proposal defines and tests a new quantitative selectivity axis termed niche-deprived stress tolerance of stemness, based on the hypothesis that LSC depend more heavily than LT-HSC on continuous niche-derived survival signals to buffer high intrinsic replication and oxidative stress. Using minimal stromal or endothelial co-cultures that supply E-selectin, CXCL12, and SCF, we will apply a fixed submaximal intrinsic stress and progressively suppress niche signaling to construct signal-level versus functional-stemness curves for primary human LSC and LT-HSC, measuring survival, colony formation, serial replating, xenograft initiation, and DNA damage markers. If curves separate, we identify a static selectivity window; if LSC-specific nonlinear or delayed effects emerge, we further test short, timed signal withdrawals to define a timing-sensitive window. Candidate regimens will then be validated in humanized xenografts co-engrafted with human HSC and AML to assess relative LSC depletion versus preserved long-term repopulation. This functional, marker-independent approach uses existing biology and tools to determine whether tuning the level or timing of niche-signal suppression can widen the LSC–HSC therapeutic gap, or conclusively exclude this axis as a lever.

label: baseline
text: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) treatment intensity is limited not only by non-hematologic toxicity but also by a conservative reluctance to enter fully marrow-destroying regimens, driven by concern for the preservation of endogenous hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). This proposal develops a treatment-design framework that reframes this constraint by asking when it is rational to treat in vivo HSCs as expendable. The central premise is that, before definitive debulking, a quantified ex vivo hematopoietic reserve—autologous, allogeneic, or cord blood—can be secured and assessed for adequacy and leukemic contamination, thereby externalizing the hematopoietic constraint. When this reserve is judged sufficient and comparatively advantageous, HSC preservation is explicitly removed as a binding design constraint, allowing regimens to be optimized solely for maximal leukemic eradication within non-hematologic toxicity limits, followed by rescue from the external reserve. We hypothesize that, given an adequate reserve, HSC-expendable regimens achieve deeper and more durable suppression of leukemic regenerative capacity than HSC-preserving protocols without exceeding global toxicity limits. Using preclinical AML models comparing reserve versus no-reserve conditions, we will measure leukemic control through secondary transplantation and host survival. The contribution is a principled decision rule and experimental scaffold that converts the HSC–LSC overlap from an intractable limitation into an exploitable design choice.

label: baseline
text: Leukemia stem cells (LSC) are thought to reside along a continuum with normal hematopoietic stem cells (HSC), raising the possibility that leukemic states might be reversible rather than only eliminable. This proposal tests whether a transient, global metabolic perturbation of the methionine–MAT2A–S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) axis can drive surviving LSC into a stable, intrinsically less-leukemic state, while allowing HSC to recover normal function. Using acute myeloid leukemia subsets with documented SAM dependence, we will apply ex vivo SAM-lowering pulses (methionine restriction with or without MAT2A inhibition) to barcoded LSC-enriched and matched normal HSC fractions, then assess clonal dynamics, serial replating, and limited xenotransplantation after recovery. A minimal first stage employs pre-specified quantitative decision rules—durable reductions in functional LSC frequency, clonal evidence of intrinsic change distinct from selection or exhaustion, and preserved HSC output—benchmarked against a positive-control differentiation therapy. Only if these criteria are met in independent patient samples will a focused second stage characterize the putative regressed state using targeted epigenetic and transcriptional markers and re-challenge experiments to distinguish a genuine state shift from damage. Both outcomes are informative, defining whether global SAM manipulation represents a reversible state lever or merely a cytotoxic vulnerability.

label: baseline
text: A central challenge in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) therapy is eliminating leukemia stem cells (LSCs) without harming long-term hematopoietic stem cells (LT-HSCs), which share overlapping immunophenotypes. This proposal asks whether realistic bone-marrow-like mechanics reveals any simple, drug-addressable perturbation that reduces LSC robustness more than LT-HSC robustness, without relying on new molecular markers. Using paired primary LSC-enriched fractions and bona fide LT-HSCs, we first perform coarse biophysical profiling of stiffness, deformability, viscoelastic recovery, and adhesion to determine whether the two populations differ enough to warrant deeper testing. We then conduct a focused vulnerability test in which a pre-specified panel of druggable mechanotransduction and structural nodes—including integrin/FAK–YAP signaling, mechanosensitive ion channels, ROCK/actomyosin contractility, and nuclear lamins—is perturbed across two to three physiologic stiffness levels, with viability, apoptosis, proliferation, and clonogenicity compared with and without mechanical context. This minimal, context-explicit, paired design is built to support a strategic decision: either identify a mechanonode offering genuine LSC-biased selectivity to guide low-myelotoxic therapies, or conclude that cell-autonomous marrow mechanics provides too narrow a selectivity window to pursue. Either outcome delivers a mechanistically grounded answer guiding future therapeutic strategy.

label: baseline
text: Acute myeloid leukemia stem cells (LSCs) depend disproportionately on amino-acid–supported oxidative phosphorylation and related metabolic pathways, yet these dependencies are shared with normal hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), limiting the therapeutic window of metabolic therapies and contributing to myelotoxicity. This project proposes to exploit timing, rather than new molecular targets, as an orthogonal axis of selectivity by mapping how LSCs and HSCs differ in the kinetics of their stress responses under clinically realistic amino-acid depletion. Using pharmacokinetically informed, time-varying depletion profiles (for example arginine deiminase–like agents or branched-chain amino-acid restriction) applied to primary human AML and HSC co-cultures, we will measure integrated stress response and mTORC1 signaling, quiescence status, and mitochondrial and reactive oxygen species stress at defined timepoints along each depletion curve. Functional outcomes will be assessed through clonogenic assays and, where feasible, xenotransplantation to evaluate long-term stem cell fitness. We will then test a small set of clinically motivated schedules for existing agents such as venetoclax or fatty-acid-oxidation and polyamine inhibitors, dosed relative to the nutrient nadir and recovery. The goal is to identify reproducible timing windows in which LSCs occupy a vulnerable, maladaptive state while HSCs remain protected, yielding practical scheduling strategies that improve leukemic selectivity and reduce myelotoxicity without requiring novel targets.

label: baseline
text: Leukemic stem cells (LSC) drive relapse in acute myeloid leukemia, yet strategies to eliminate them are limited by toxicity to normal hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) with which they share many features. Here we propose a minimal two-axis strategy that couples an established, LSC-biased metabolic vulnerability—polyamine and translation stress—to a pre-specified innate sensing pathway comprising the integrated stress response (ISR), type I interferon signaling, and endoplasmic reticulum stress–linked damage-associated molecular patterns. We hypothesize that LSC lie closer than HSC to a translation failure boundary and therefore enter a pronounced ISR/ER-stress state at lower drug doses, generating a differential immune-relevant signature rather than any new antigen. We will first map graded, sub-ablative polyamine stress in LSC- and HSC-enriched populations to identify a window in which LSC exhibit strong ISR, interferon, and DAMP outputs while HSC remain below activation thresholds and retain clonogenic potential. Within this window, we will test whether targeted modulation of ISR–interferon/ER-stress signaling preferentially amplifies immune clearance of stressed LSC in co-culture and in AML mouse models. This approach exploits differential distance-to-failure using existing drugs, offering a mechanistically defined, HSC-sparing route to selective LSC elimination.

label: baseline
text: Acute myeloid leukemia stem cells (LSC) drive relapse yet share many phenotypic features with normal hematopoietic stem cells (HSC), making selective elimination difficult. This project tests the hypothesis that LSC depend on sustained nucleolar hyperactivation and elevated ribosome biogenesis to maintain self-renewal, whereas HSC are physiologically adapted to transient nucleolar stress during stress hematopoiesis, and are therefore more resilient to a brief, sublethal nucleolar perturbation. As a first step, imaging flow cytometry and machine-learning analysis of nuclear and nucleolar morphology will be evaluated as a label-free indicator of LSC versus HSC content across primary AML grafts and normal controls, correlated with xenograft-defined stem cell frequencies. Next, a short, graded nucleolar disruption–recovery challenge, first titrated to remain within an HSC-tolerant envelope, will be applied to matched fractions, with structural, transcriptional, and functional recovery quantified by limiting-dilution xenografts. The central prediction is that HSC restore nucleolar architecture and multilineage engraftment while a disproportionate fraction of LSC lose self-renewal or leukemic reconstitution, even when short-term viability is comparable. If a robust asymmetry emerges, the approach will be developed as a scalable ex vivo graft-conditioning step and benchmarked against morphology-informed sorting and low-dose chemotherapy. Even a negative result yields a practical morphology-based LSC assessment tool and a decisive test of nucleolar stress as a selectivity lever.

label: baseline
text: Leukemia stem cells (LSCs) in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) drive relapse yet remain difficult to target selectively because they share most molecular features with normal long-term hematopoietic stem cells (LT-HSCs). Rather than searching for new LSC-specific markers, this proposal tests whether LSCs and LT-HSCs differ in how intensely they depend on a shared cytoskeleton–mitochondria coupling program that supports oxidative metabolism and self-renewal. Using single-cell RNA sequencing and proteomics on paired patient LT-HSC and AML samples, we will construct a coupling-intensity score from mitochondrial dynamics, trafficking, and actomyosin contractility genes and identify AML subsets in which high stemness co-occurs with elevated coupling intensity relative to autologous LT-HSCs.
