We will then define the dose of coupling-node perturbations (targeting DRP1, ROCK, or Miro/TRAK) that LT-HSCs tolerate without loss of quiescence or engraftment, and test whether these tolerated doses selectively erode LSC clonogenicity and leukemia-initiating capacity, benchmarked against generic oxidative-phosphorylation inhibition. As an optional probe, we will assess whether increased substrate tension intensifies this vulnerability. A positive result would establish coupling intensity as a marker-free stratification axis actionable with near-clinical compounds, while a negative result would set clear limits on this strategy.

label: baseline
text: Acute myeloid leukemia therapy is limited by overlapping metabolic and quiescence properties shared between leukemic stem cells (LSC) and normal hematopoietic stem cells (HSC), which constrains therapeutic selectivity. This proposal investigates whether the temporal pattern of well-characterized mitochondrial and differentiation pressures—pulsed versus continuous exposure—can widen the therapeutic window beyond what static dose or exposure alone achieves. The central hypothesis is that many LSC archetypes require a sustained effective duty cycle of mitochondrial support to maintain self-renewal, whereas deeply quiescent HSC can recover from transient stress when provided sufficient off-periods, predicting that intermittent pulses at fixed total dose will deplete LSC while sparing HSC. Using two to three AML archetypes with already-defined LSC and HSC compartments, the study will establish baseline continuous regimens and then test simple pulse schedules in long-term cultures and xenografts, measuring functional LSC frequency, HSC repopulating capacity, and coarse cell-cycle and stress-recovery markers around pulses. Positive results would yield mechanistically interpretable scheduling rules for specific AML subtypes without requiring new molecular targets, while negative results would define a clear boundary condition indicating that temporal structuring alone cannot resolve LSC/HSC overlap. This decision-oriented, mechanistically grounded design treats time structure as an independent control lever for reducing myelotoxicity.

label: baseline
text: Metastatic organotropism prediction remains imprecise, in part because current models treat endothelium simply as homeostatic or inflamed, ignoring physiologic heterogeneity in the endothelial glycocalyx that regulates access to adhesion molecules. This proposal develops a minimal, mechanistic testbed to determine whether changes in glycocalyx state create tipping points that reverse organ preference for a defined glycan–lectin axis, focusing on sialyl-Lewis-x interactions with E-selectin in brain versus liver endothelium in a breast cancer context. Using existing organ-specific microvascular chips, we will generate discrete, verified glycocalyx states (high, medium, low coverage) through VEGF, tumor-conditioned media, and cytokine or flow modulation, then measure rolling and firm adhesion of tumor cells and extracellular vesicles with controlled ligand density under matched shear. We will test whether adding a single categorical glycocalyx variable to standard predictors corrects known organ misrankings, and whether qualitative behaviors such as organ-specific thresholds or non-monotonic capture emerge. Only if simple binary corrections fail will we introduce minimal parametric functions relating defect area to adhesion probability, and we will bound the glycocalyx contribution relative to other factors. The deliverable is a set of experimentally anchored, axis- and organ-specific glycocalyx tipping points that can directly refine existing organotropism models.

label: baseline
text: Metastatic organotropism has long been associated with tumor cell glycosylation, yet direct evidence that a defined glycan axis biases early vascular capture toward specific organs remains limited. This proposal develops a minimal, competition-based in vitro assay to test whether a targeted change in tumor cell glycosylation alters the relative odds of early adhesion across distinct organ-derived endothelia under physiological shear. Using a single cancer context with known organotropism, we will culture two to three organ-derived endothelial types under identical flow and media conditions, generate isogenic tumor cells edited along one well-defined glycan axis (for example, sialyl-Lewis^x via fucosyltransferase editing or α2,6-sialylation via ST6GAL1), and label edited and control cells with distinct fluorophores for competitive perfusion. The primary readout is an organ-specific adhesion odds ratio, and we define a glycan organotropism signature as significant deviation of these odds ratios from a uniform-scaling null across organs. To distinguish glycan-axis specificity from generic increases in stickiness, we will apply orthogonal acute perturbations, including glycan-targeted enzymatic neutralization and integrin blockade, while phenotypically bounding endothelial identity through glycocalyx and selectin measurements. A positive result would provide a quantitative foothold for glycan-biased organotropism, whereas a negative result would meaningfully constrain the hypothesis and redirect emphasis toward integrin, chemokine, and niche-conditioning mechanisms.

label: baseline
text: This proposal develops a compact, mechanistically anchored glycobiology panel to predict organ-specific metastasis risk from baseline primary tumors and circulating tumor cells across multiple cancer types. Rather than pursuing broad pathway-wide discovery, we pre-select a small, literature-informed set of glycosyltransferases and related enzymes with strong prior evidence in organotropism, together with a matched set of measurable surface glycan motifs such as sialyl-Lewis x and α2-3 versus α2-6 sialylation. In the first stage, we will train transparent organ-specific predictors and rigorously benchmark whether this minimal enzyme panel adds value beyond clinical and transcriptomic baselines, while testing whether the same features predict a given organ across cancers; a clear decision gate determines whether the premise is supported. In the second stage, enzymes that survive as robust predictors will be mapped to specific glycan motifs in isogenic organ-tropic cell models and tested through gain- and loss-of-function assays for effects on organ-relevant adhesion, extravasation, and immune interactions under organotypic conditions. We will then validate the combined enzyme and lectin-based glycan panel in independent clinical cohorts with follow-up metastasis data. The result is a feasible, mechanistically grounded clinical assay for pan-cancer organotropism prediction with quantified incremental value.

label: baseline
text: Cancer metastasis exhibits pronounced organ specificity, and current predictive models rely on tumor transcriptomics, exosomal integrins and glycans, chemokines, and generic vascular properties. Although the endothelial glycocalyx is mechanistically plausible as a determinant of organotropism—given organ-resolved differences in selectin exposure, galectin-3, heparan sulfate sulfation, and sialylation, all modulated by tumor-derived factors and inflammation—its incremental predictive value remains untested. This project provides a clean, outcome-anchored statistical model comparison rather than a platform build or mechanistic screen, asking whether adding a parsimonious set of organ-resolved endothelial glycocalyx markers and their degradation proxies improves prediction of metastatic destinations. Using public atlases and existing datasets, we will construct organ- and, where feasible, vascular-subtype-resolved glycocalyx indices, extract matched tumor and exosome glycobiology features, compile organ-specific metastasis frequencies across major cancers, and compare baseline and extended predictive models using cross-validation and regularized, interpretable methods. A robust improvement would identify specific glyco axes and organs meriting mechanistic follow-up, whereas a negative result, obtained under transparent resolution limits, would constrain endothelial-centric theories and redirect future effort. The design is pan-cancer, avoids experimental over-engineering, and keeps both outcomes informative.

label: baseline
text: Circulating tumor cell (CTC) arrest within organ-specific microvasculature is a critical determinant of metastatic organotropism, and endothelial glycocalyx (GCX) remodeling has been implicated in this process. However, it remains unclear whether defined endothelial glycan states exert glycan-specific effects on CTC adhesion or simply act as generic modifiers of vascular stickiness through nonspecific GCX thinning. This proposal develops a single-organ vessel-on-chip platform in which endothelial glycobiology is the primary controlled variable, using organotypic microvascular endothelial cells under physiologic shear across three defined states: a native baseline, a generic GCX shedding condition, and a biochemically defined, reproducible glycan-programmed condition. Fluorescently labeled CTCs will be perfused through each state to quantify rolling velocity, firm arrest, and early transmigration, while each state is characterized by a practical glyco-fingerprint comprising lectin panels, selectin/siglec or chemokine binding assays, and imaging of GCX coverage. By comparing the defined glycan program against tuned generic shedding under matched brush thickness, and testing whether glyco-fingerprint features add nonredundant predictive power, the platform will determine whether a true glycan gate exists. A positive result identifies a concrete endothelial glycan gate for extension to additional organs, whereas a negative result provides an interpretable finding that constrains overbuilt glyco-centric models of organotropism.

label: baseline
text: Metastatic organotropism to lung and liver is a major determinant of outcome in cancers such as triple-negative breast and colorectal cancer, yet clinical prediction of the first metastatic site remains limited. This proposal develops and validates a standardized competitive lung–liver vascular capture assay that quantifies how strongly E- and P-selectin–recognizable glycans bias early vascular capture toward lung-like versus liver-like microvasculature under controlled flow. Using a minimal dual-channel microfluidic device perfused simultaneously with matched patient-derived tumor cells, we compute a lung:liver capture ratio and, through on-assay selectin and glycan blockade, derive a context-specific functional glycan dependence score that distinguishes cells losing all adhesion from those shifting their relative organ preference. A parsimonious glyco-phenotyping panel measuring selectin binding and key sialyl-Lewis and sialylation motifs complements these functional readouts. We will test, in a longitudinal clinical cohort, whether these assay-derived metrics improve prediction of the first metastatic organ over clinical and limited omic baselines, and we will confirm mechanistic dependence in matched cell line and patient-derived models through acute glycosyltransferase modulation and, where feasible, in vivo rerouting experiments. The intended outcome is a decision-relevant classifier that stratifies patients whose lung–liver organotropism is selectin–glycan dominated from those driven by other mechanisms, identifying candidates for anti-selectin strategies or targeted surveillance.

label: baseline
text: This proposal investigates whether one or two heparan sulfate (HS) markers measured on circulating tumor cells (CTCs) provide independent, organ-specific prognostic information about the likely first metastatic site in pan-cancer patients at risk of metastasis. Treating HS as a compact glycan-state proxy rather than a mechanistically resolved adhesion signal, the study frames a purely prognostic question and compares a baseline model of clinical covariates and coarse tumor molecular subtype against the same model augmented with HS epitope levels quantified on CTCs by flow-cytometry–compatible antibodies. Predefined, clinically consequential organ contrasts—such as liver-first versus bone-first metastasis in breast cancer or liver-first versus lung-first in colorectal cancer—will be evaluated using cross-validated discrimination, calibration, and decision-curve or net-reclassification metrics in cohorts with adjudicated first-metastasis outcomes. An optional overlay module tests whether HS staining adds value on top of organ-mimetic microfluidic adhesion assays where such platforms already exist, and a small mechanistic side-study uses heparinase and enzyme perturbations to inform interpretation. By restricting the panel to one or two antibodies and prioritizing a single contrast per indication, the design remains feasible for multi-center validation. This minimal, honest experiment will determine whether static HS states on CTCs offer actionable organotropic prognostic value beyond standard clinical data, or are ultimately redundant with existing measures.

label: baseline
text: Organ-specific metastasis reflects multiple determinants, yet the contribution of glycan-mediated tumor–endothelium recognition remains poorly quantified. This proposal introduces GlycoOrganMap, a two-tier, stratified framework to test whether tumor–organ lectin compatibility contributes measurably to organotropism across cancers. In the first tier, focused glycomic and glyco-transcriptomic profiles of tumors within defined tumor–organ strata are combined with baseline endothelial lectin profiles derived from single-cell and proteomic atlases to compute mechanistically constrained Lectin Compatibility Scores, restricted to biochemically validated ligand–lectin pairs. Nested models predicting organ-of-first-metastasis then evaluate whether adding compatibility terms improves explanatory power beyond clinical covariates and tumor-intrinsic glycan features, with the expectation of modest but reproducible effects. In the second tier, the most robust nominated axes undergo minimal single-axis functional validation using flow and static adhesion assays with recombinant lectins, alongside enzymatic or transferase-based perturbations to establish causal concordance between predicted compatibility and binding. By stratifying analyses and enforcing biochemically justified sparsity, the framework limits confounding and yields interpretable outcomes. The study will either identify a mechanistically grounded axis of organotropism suitable for focused biomarker panels or provide a well-justified negative result constraining the role of endothelial lectins.
